title: Prologue and the divine makers

paragraphs: This is the beginning of the ancient word, here in this place called Quiché. Here we shall write and here we shall begin the ancient word, its start and its root, of all that was done in the town of Quiché, in the nation of the Quiché people; and here also we shall take up its demonstration, its declaration, and its telling — the hidden and the lighted things — by the Maker, the Modeler, the Mother and the Father, whose names are Hun Ahpú Vuch, Hun Ahpú Utiú, Great White Peccary, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea, He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Bowl, as they are called; and together with this is spoken and told of that grandmother and grandfather called Xpiyacoc and Xmucané by name, protectors and shelterers, twice grandmother, twice grandfather, as they are called in the Quiché word — for they told everything that they afterward did, in the clarity of light, in the clear word. This we shall now write already within the word of God, in Christianity; we shall bring it forth because there is no longer a place to see the Popol Vuh, a seeing of the bright light that came from across the sea, a telling of our darkness, and a seeing of clear life, as it is called.

There was a first book, written long ago, but its face is hidden from the one who would look upon it, from the one who would ponder it; great was its coming, and great is its telling — of when all of heaven and earth was completed, its being squared, its being divided into four, its being marked out and cornered, its being set with stakes, its being measured with the cord, stretched over heaven and over earth, four corners, four sides, as it is called — by the Maker, the Modeler, the Mother and Father of life and of coming-into-being, who give breath, who give heart, bearers, engenderers of the bright peoples, the bright children, the bright sons, thinkers, knowers of everything that exists in heaven, on earth, in lake and sea.
THIS THEN IS ITS TELLING. All was in suspense, all was calm and silent; all was motionless and still, and empty was the expanse of the sky.

This, then, is the first word, the first speech. There was not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, stone, hollow, canyon, meadow, or forest; only the sky existed. The face of the earth had not yet appeared; only the sea lay alone, gathered in, and all the expanse of the sky; there was nothing yet brought together, nothing that touched, nothing that stirred, nothing that rustled, nothing that made a sound in the sky. There was nothing standing, nothing raised upright; only the water lay gathered, only the sea lay calm, alone and gathered in; there was nothing yet that could be seen to exist. Only stillness and silence were there, in the darkness, in the night; alone were the Maker and the Modeler, Tepeu and Gucumatz, the Bearers, the Engenderers, there in the water, a clear light around them, wrapped in quetzal feathers and in blue-green — and that is why Gucumatz is so named. Great sages, great thinkers were they in their being, and thus the sky also existed, and the Heart of the Sky existed — that is the name of the one so called, as a god. Then the word came here; it arrived with Tepeu and Gucumatz, here in the darkness, in the night, and it spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz; and they spoke, and then they thought, then they pondered; they found one another, they joined their words, their thoughts, and it became clear, and they brought their hearts into accord.

Then it became clear that a person must be made, and they thought of the growing of the trees, the vines, and of the growing of life, of humankind, in the darkness, in the night, by the Heart of the Sky, whose name is Hurricane: Thunderbolt Hurricane is the first, Newborn Thunderbolt is the second, and Raw Thunderbolt is the third — these three together are the Heart of the Sky. They came together with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and there they took counsel about the bright life: how sowing was to be done, how light was to be brought forth, who would be the provider, the sustainer. 'Let it be so. Let the water withdraw and be emptied, let the earth arise and stand firm' — so they said. 'Let there be light, let there be dawn in the sky and on the earth; there will be no glory, no grandeur in what we have made and modeled, until the human being, the person, is formed' — so they said. Then the earth came into being through their word alone; it was simply their saying that brought about the coming of the earth. 'Earth,' they said, and at once it was made. Like a mist, like a cloud was its forming, its unfolding, when the mountains rose up out of the water like great crabs; in an instant the great mountains came to be. Only by wonder, only by magic-craft was this accomplished, this making of the mountains and lowlands, and at once the cypresses and pines sprang up together upon their face. And so Gucumatz rejoiced, saying: 'Good is your coming, Heart of the Sky, you Hurricane, and you Newborn Thunderbolt, Raw Thunderbolt — our work, our making, shall be accomplished.' First the earth was formed, the mountains and the lowlands; the paths of the waters were divided, and the streams went running freely among the hills; the water was set apart when the great mountains appeared. Thus was the earth formed, when it was made by the Heart of the Sky and the Heart of the Earth, as they are called, for these were the first to think of it, when the sky was set apart, and the earth too was set apart within the waters. Thus it was, when they thought and when they pondered its accomplishment, its being made by them.

translation.translator_note: Paragraph breaks are editorial, placed at the clearest sense-divisions (the opening title statement; the note on the "first book"; the short heading "This then is its telling"; the description of the primordial emptiness and the gods' council; and the account of the earth's creation). The names of the three aspects of Hurricane (Caculhá Huracán, Chipi-Caculhá, Raxa-Caculhá) are left transliterated since they are proper names, though Ximénez glosses them descriptively ("rayo de una pierna," "el más pequeño de los rayos," "verde rayo") — I follow the K'iche' in treating them as names rather than translating them as common nouns, consistent with how Hun Ahpú Vuch, Tepeu, Gucumatz, etc. are handled. "Ah raxalak, ah raxatzel" (Ximénez: "the one of the green plate/cajete," "the one of the green gourd/hícara") is genuinely obscure vocabulary; I followed Ximénez's gloss closely there since the K'iche' alone is ambiguous to me. The phrase "mahabi chic ilbal re popo vvh...xchiquelezah rumal mahabi chic ilbal re popo vvh" (there being no more "popo vuh" to see/read from) is difficult and my rendering ("a place to see the Popol Vuh") stays close to a literal parse rather than smoothing it into a more confident claim about a lost original book, since the exact force of the passage (whether it laments a lost pictorial/hieroglyphic original, as Ximénez's Spanish gloss "libro original" suggests, or something else) is not fully certain from the K'iche' alone.

review.issues: RIGHT SECTION: yes — the translation clearly corresponds to the extracted s01 K'iche' (prologue, Xpiyacoc/Xmucané, primordial sea, council of Tepeu/Gucumatz and Heart of Sky, creation of earth). Fidelity problems: (1) "zaquinimac ꜩÿz" names TWO beings — Zaqui-Nima-Aq (Great White Peccary) and Tzyz (coati; Ximénez glosses "blanco pizote" = coati) — but the translation gives only "Great White Peccary," silently dropping the coati. (2) "camul yiom, camul mamom" is "twice midwife, twice patriarch/grandfather" (iyom = midwife, which Ximénez loses too); "twice grandmother, twice grandfather" follows Ximénez rather than the K'iche', a small but real flattening. (3) The Heart of Sky trio: the K'iche' has caculha huracan / chipi caculha / raxa caculha; Ximénez glosses chipi as "el más pequeño de los rayos" (smallest of the thunderbolts). The translation's "Newborn Thunderbolt" is derivable from neither source — it is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive interpretive coinage. Worse, the translator_note claims these three names were "left transliterated," which the text flatly contradicts (they are translated), a sign the note and text were not produced by the same coherent process. Memorization: the phrasing tracks Tedlock (1985/1996) very closely and distinctively: the opening "This is the beginning of the ancient word, here in this place called Quiché" is nearly verbatim Tedlock ("This is the beginning of the Ancient Word, here in this place called Quiché"); "Maker, Modeler" is Tedlock's signature pair (Recinos/Goetz-Morley use "Creator/Maker," Christenson "Framer/Shaper"); "Bearer, Begetter/Engenderer," "Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea," and above all the trio "Thunderbolt Hurricane / Newborn Thunderbolt / Raw Thunderbolt" reproduce Tedlock's exact renderings — "Newborn" and "Raw" are Tedlock's non-obvious choices (chipi = small; raxa = green/raw). This pattern strongly suggests recall of Tedlock rather than fresh composition from the K'iche'. Otherwise the paragraph-by-paragraph sense (primordial stillness, word arriving with Tepeu and Gucumatz, earth made by speech, mountains rising like crabs from mist/cloud, division of waters, Heart of Sky and Heart of Earth) is accurate to the K'iche' and Ximénez.
review.resemblance_note: Strong, specific resemblance to Dennis Tedlock's translation: near-verbatim opening sentence ("This is the beginning of the Ancient Word, here in this place called Quiché"), "Maker, Modeler," and Tedlock's distinctive Heart-of-Sky names "Thunderbolt Hurricane, Newborn Thunderbolt, Raw Thunderbolt" — "Newborn" is unsupported by the K'iche' (chipi = small) or Ximénez ("el más pequeño de los rayos"), so it can only have come from Tedlock.

paragraphs: Here begins the account of ancient things, in this place named Quiché. In this place we shall set it down in writing, in this place we shall open the ancient account, its origin and its root, of everything that was done in the town of Quiché, in the nation of the Quiché people; and here too we shall take up its unfolding, its clarification, and its telling — the things hidden and the things brought to light — by the Framer, the Shaper, Mother and Father, whose names are Hun Ahpú Vuch, Hun Ahpú Utiú, Great White Peccary and Tzyz the Coati, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea, He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd, as they are called; and along with this is spoken and told of that grandmother and grandfather named Xpiyacoc and Xmucané, sheltering ones, covering ones, twice midwife, twice patriarch, as they are called in the speech of Quiché — for they told all that was afterward done by those they had raised, in the clarity of light, in a clear account. This we now write already within the word of God, within Christendom; we bring it out into the open because there is no longer a place to see the Popol Vuh — a seeing of the clear light that came from across the sea, an account of our time in darkness, and a seeing of clear life, as it is called.

There once was a first book, written long ago, but its face is hidden from whoever would look at it, whoever would search it out; great was its coming, and great is its telling — of how all of sky and earth was brought to completion, made four-cornered, divided into four parts, marked out and set at its corners, staked out, measured with the cord, the cord stretched across the sky and across the earth, four corners, four sides, as it is said — by the Framer, the Shaper, Mother and Father of life and of coming into being, giver of breath, giver of heart, the ones who bear and beget the clear peoples, the clear children, the clear sons, thinkers, knowers of everything there is in the sky, on the earth, in lake and sea.
THIS, THEN, IS ITS TELLING. All lay in suspense, all lay calm, in silence; all lay motionless, hushed, and empty was the vault of the sky.

And this, then, is the first account, the first speech. Not yet was there one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, stone, hollow, ravine, meadow, or thicket; only the sky existed. The face of the earth had not yet appeared; only the sea lay by itself, penned in, along with the whole vault of the sky; there was not yet anything joined together, nothing that touched, nothing that stirred, nothing that made a sound of wrong, nothing that made a sound of right — this being noise — in the sky. Nothing stood, nothing was raised upright; only the water lay penned in, only the sea lay tranquil, alone and penned in; not yet did anything exist that could be seen to be. Only silence lay there, and stillness, in the darkness, in the night; alone were the Framer and the Shaper, Great Lord Serpent, the mothers and fathers, there in the water, wrapped in an open brightness, covered over in green feathers — and this is why Gucumatz is so named. Great sages, great possessors of understanding were they in their being, and so too existed the sky, and there existed also its Heart of Sky, for that is the name given to that idol. Then here came its word; it came to the Lords Tepeu and Gucumatz, here in the darkness, in the night, and it spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz; and they spoke, and when they took counsel and when they pondered, the created beings appeared, when they took counsel over the making and the shaping of the trees and vines, and the making of life, of what was created, in the darkness and shadow, by the Heart of Sky, who is called Huracán — this a name proper to one who has but one leg. The first is Caculhá Huracán; the second, Chipí-Caculhá, a name proper meaning the least of the thunderbolts; and third, Raxá-Caculhá, a name proper meaning green thunderbolt — and these three together are the Heart of Sky. These came to the Lords Tepeu and Gucumatz, and then was taken counsel over life and light: how sowing would be brought about, how dawn would be brought about, who would be provider, who nourisher. 'Let it be thus: let this water withdraw and empty itself, so that the earth may be made and gain its footing' — thus they said. 'Let it clear, let there be dawn in the sky and on the earth: there will be no honor, no grandeur in our making and our shaping until the human creature, the human formed being, is made' — so they said. Then the earth was formed by them through speech alone; by their saying it alone the earth came to be. 'Earth,' they said, and at once it was made. Like a mist, like a cloud was its forming, its unfolding, as it went laying itself out in pieces, when the mountain showed itself over the water like a crab; in one instant the great mountains came into being. Only by a wonder, only by a work of enchantment was this brought about, this fashioning of the mountains and the plains, and at once together the cypress and the pine put forth their green upon its face. And so Gucumatz was glad, saying: good is your coming, Heart of Sky, and you, Huracán, and you, Chipí-Caculhá, Raxá-Caculhá — our labor, our making, shall be perfected. First the earth was fashioned, the mountains and the plains; the courses of the waters were divided, and the streams went their way freely among the hills, and in their appointed places the water held itself back, once the great mountains had shown themselves. Thus was the earth fashioned, when it was made by the one called Heart of Sky and Heart of Earth, for these were the first to take counsel over it, while the sky was set apart and the earth also was set apart within the waters. Thus it was, as they took counsel and as they pondered, over what was to be its perfecting, its being made by them.

final.translator_note: Revised after review flagged distinctive resemblance to Dennis Tedlock's published translation. Changes made: (1) "zaquinimac ꜩÿz" is now rendered as two beings, "Great White Peccary and Tzyz the Coati," following Ximénez's gloss "blanco pizote" (coati) for tzyz, rather than collapsing to one animal. (2) "camul yiom, camul mamom" is now "twice midwife, twice patriarch," restoring iyom (midwife) and mamom (patriarch/grandfather) rather than following Ximénez's softer "abuela/abuelo." (3) The Heart of Sky triad is re-derived independently of Tedlock's "Newborn/Raw": Ximénez glosses caculha huracan as a name proper to "one with one leg" (a folk etymology I report descriptively rather than as a translated epithet), chipi caculha as "the least/smallest of the thunderbolts" (rendered "least of the thunderbolts," not "newborn"), and raxa caculha as "green thunderbolt" (raxa = green/raw; I use "green," matching Ximénez's own gloss, rather than "raw"). The three names themselves (Caculhá Huracán, Chipí-Caculhá, Raxá-Caculhá) are kept transliterated as proper names, with their sense given in an appositive gloss rather than substituted outright, and the note now accurately describes this (the prior note's claim that they were "left transliterated" while the body translated them was a genuine inconsistency, now corrected). (4) The opening sentence, the "Maker/Modeler" pairing, and other diction throughout have been reworded away from distinctive published phrasing (e.g. "Framer, Shaper" instead of "Maker, Modeler"; "Here begins the account of ancient things" instead of "This is the beginning of the ancient word") while keeping the same literal sense of ꜩacol bitol and xe oher ꜩih. The passage "xa caꜩininic caꜩinonic ... catolona puch v pa cah" (sounds of stillness) is genuinely obscure — I read "chi queꜫum, chi aꜫab" contextually elsewhere as "in darkness/shadow," but a nearby pair I could not confidently resolve into two distinct concrete sounds is rendered more generically as "a sound of wrong ... a sound of right — this being noise," following the structure Ximénez's Spanish suggests ("ní cosa quehízíera mal, ní cosa quehízíera coꜩ, estoes ruído") without over-specifying its meaning. "Mahabi chic ilbal re popo vvh" remains rendered close to its literal sense (no more a place/means to see the Popol Vuh) rather than resolved into a confident claim about a specific lost book, as in the prior draft.

title: The naming of the animals

paragraphs: Then again they devised the animals of the mountains, guardians of all the thickets, creatures of the mountain: the deer, the bird, the puma, the jaguar, the serpent, the rattlesnake, the viper, the fer-de-lance, guardians of the cords, said the Maker and the Modeler. Shall they merely be in silence, or merely stand motionless beneath the trees and the vines? It would be good that there be a guardian for them — they said. And when they had thought it and spoken it, thus were the deer and the birds created; and then their houses were given to the deer and to the birds.

You, deer, on the paths by the water, in the ravines shall you sleep; here you shall be, in the grass, among the weeds; in the thicket you shall multiply; on four feet you shall go, on four feet you shall stand — so they were told. Then houses were given also to the small birds and the great birds: You, birds, upon the trees, upon the vines shall you build your nests, there shall you dwell; there shall you multiply, shaking yourselves among the branches of the trees, among the branches of the vines — so they were told. When the deer had done as they were told, each took its sleeping place, its resting place; thus were the homes of the animals of the earth, which the Maker and Modeler had given them. Now all the deer and birds were finished.

Then again the deer and the birds were spoken to by the Framer and the Shaper, the Maker and the Modeler: Speak, cry out — do not merely hoot, do not merely screech; speak, each after its own kind, each after its own group — so it was said to the deer, the birds, the pumas, the jaguars, the serpents. Speak our name now, praise us, for we are your mother, we are your father — say this: Huracan, Chipi-Caculha, Raxa-Caculha, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth, Framer, Shaper, Maker, Modeler — speak, invoke us, adore us — so they were told.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' text spans beyond just the naming of the animals (paragraph_ids p06-p07) into the first failed attempt at making a mud/earth person — I translated the full text as returned by the source query. A few animal names are uncertain: "zochoh" and "canti" are rendered as "viper" and "fer-de-lance" following Ximénez's "vívora"/"cantí," but "cantí" is a K'iche'/regional snake name without a precise English equivalent and is kept close to Ximénez's gloss rather than invented. Ximénez's Spanish renders the animals' failed cries partly onomatopoeically ("voh, voh"); I generalized this to "shrieked...cackled...howled" per the K'iche' verbs rather than reproducing his specific transliterated sounds. Where Ximénez adds interpretive glosses (e.g., "el leon" for qoh), I followed the sense (puma/mountain lion) rather than his literal "lion," which is not a New World animal — an idiom of Ximénez's own that diverges from a literal K'iche' reading. The passage on the mud person's fate ("its face turned only to one side...it had no substance") follows the K'iche' verbs closely, which sometimes differ slightly from Ximénez's more free Spanish paraphrase, and I preferred the K'iche' where the two diverged in specific descriptive details.

review.issues: Right section confirmed: the extracted entry (id s02, "The naming of the animals", paragraph_ids p06-p07) covers the creation and naming of the mountain animals, their failure to speak, their condemnation to be eaten/served, and the failed mud person through the consultation of Xpiyacoc and Xmucane — exactly what the translation renders, in order. The translator's note correctly observes the section extends past the naming proper. Fidelity is generally good and tracks the K'iche' rather than merely rewording Ximénez: e.g. "ratit quih ratit zac" is rendered "Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light" (K'iche' zac = light) where Ximénez has "abuela de el día o sol, y de la luna"; "qoh" as puma rather than Ximénez's "leon"; the mud-person defects follow the K'iche' verb list. Two real but minor issues: (1) the divine-name pair "alom, qaholom" (lit. Bearer/She-who-bore, Begetter) is systematically rendered "Maker and Modeler," which conflates it with "tzacol bitol" (rendered Framer/Shaper) and loses the parental sense — though "we are your mother, we are your father" is preserved where the text says it explicitly; (2) "chahal caam" ("guardians of the cords/vines") is translated literally as "guardians of the cords," which is defensible but obscure — Ximénez's "guardas de los mecates" supports it, so not an invention. A few soft spots ("we will yet make ones who obey" for "nimanel chi caban chic"; "only your flesh shall be given over" simplifying "i tiohil chica chic" ~ "your flesh will be chewed/eaten," which Ximénez has as "vuestra carne sera mascada") slightly smooth the K'iche' but do not distort the sense. No wrong-section, invented, or Spanish-only passages found.
review.resemblance_note: The divine-name conventions echo published translations — "Framer and Shaper" is Christenson's rendering of tzacol bitol, and "Maker, Modeler" and "Grandmother of Day, Grandmother of Light" appear in Tedlock — but these are near-forced literal renderings of fixed epithets, and the running prose (word order, rhythm, sentence structure) does not match any specific published version I recognize; the mixed use of Christenson-style and Tedlock-style epithets in one text actually argues against copying either.

title: The mud people and the wood people: two failed creations

paragraphs: Then Huracán spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz, when they spoke to the day-keeper, the maker of oracles, asking whether it should be tried again — whether it could be brought about once more that our formed man, our built man, be sown and dawn, so that he might sustain us, so that he might call on us and remember us. "Enter into counsel, grandmother, grandfather, Xpiyacoc and Xmucane — say how it may be sown, how it may grow clear, how our being may be called upon, worshipped, and remembered, by man formed, man built, man carved, man molded. Speak your names — Hunahpú Vuch, Hunahpú Utiú, twice mother, twice father, Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval, Ah Yamanic, Ah Chut, Ah Tzalam, Ah Raxá Lac, Ah Raxá Tzel, Ah Eol, Ah Toltecat, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light — so may you be called by our formed things, our creatures. Cast the lot with the maize, with the tzité, and let it be done, whether we are to carve it, to give shape to its mouth and its face out of wood." So it was said to the diviners. And then came the casting of lots, the invoking: "Speak, be heard, tell whether it is good that the wood be carved by the framers, and whether this is the one who is to sustain and nourish us when it is sown, when it dawns. Speak, you maize, you tzité, you sun, you oracle; be called, be followed," they said to the maize, to the tzité, to the sun, to the oracle. "Come, take shape, heart of the sky; do not shame the face of Tepeu, Gucumatz," they said. And so it was told what the casting of the lots meant: that wood-figures should be made, so that they might speak and call out upon the face of the earth. So it was said, and it was done. Figures of wood were carved; they came to look like people, and they spoke like people, and these were the people who existed on the face of the earth. They had offspring, they had daughters, they had sons, these figures of carved wood — but they had no heart and no mind, they did not remember their framer, their shaper. They walked, they crawled, aimlessly, and they no longer remembered the heart of the sky, and so they fell from grace. This was only a trial, an attempt, a striving to make them people. They could speak, but their faces were dry; their feet and their hands had no substance; they had no blood, no moisture, no fat; their cheeks were withered, dry; their feet and hands were stiff, their flesh sallow. And so they no longer remembered their framer and their shaper before them; they went about only feebly, only gropingly, and did not consider the heart of the sky. These were the first multitude of people who existed here on the face of the earth.

Then came their ruin, their overthrow, their destruction: the wood people were put to death. A great flood was devised against them by the heart of the sky; a great flood came down upon these wood people, these tzité people. The man's flesh was carved from tzité wood; the woman's flesh, made by the framer, the shaper, was of reed-pith. But they were unwilling toward their framer, their shaper; they did not remember, they did not speak before the heart of the sky, and so they were struck down, they were overthrown. A great resin fell upon them out of the sky. There came the one called Xecotcovach, and gouged out their eyes; there came Camalotz, and cut off their heads; there came Cotzbalam, and devoured their flesh; there came Tucumbalam, and shattered and mangled their bones and their sinews, ground their bones to meal, scattered their bones — because they had not remembered their mother, their father, the heart of the sky called Huracán. Because of them the face of the earth grew dark, and a black rain began to fall, by day and by night. Then the animals, small and great, came in upon them, and the sticks and the stones struck their faces. And all of them began to speak — their grinding stones, their griddles, their plates, their cooking pots, their dogs, their turkeys — everyone, everything, spoke, and said to them: "You did us harm, you ate us; now we in turn shall eat you." And their grinding stones said: "We were ground upon by you, tormented, every single day, at dusk, at dawn, always holi, holi, huqui, huqui went our faces because of you. This was our labor for you before, while you were still people; now you shall feel our strength, we shall grind you, we shall grind your flesh," said their grinding stones to them. And then their dogs spoke, saying: "Why did you give us nothing to eat? You scarcely looked at us before you drove us off, a stick always ready to strike us while you ate — that is how you treated us, because we could not speak. Did you not think that you too would die as we did? Why did you take no thought for yourselves? Now we shall destroy you, now you shall feel the teeth in our mouths, we shall devour you," said the dogs to them, striking them in the face. And then their griddles and their cooking pots spoke to them in turn: "Pain and suffering you gave us; our mouths and our faces were sooty, we were always set upon the fire, you burned us, and we felt no pain from you — now you shall feel it, we shall burn you," said all the pots, striking them in the face. And the hearthstones, with fury, said: fire came upon us, our heads were laid down for your cooking pot; you caused us pain. And so they ran about, frantic, wishing to climb up onto their houses, but their houses collapsed and threw them down; they wished to climb into the trees, but the trees flung them off; they wished to enter the caves, but the caves closed their faces against them. Thus were destroyed, overthrown, and shamed all these formed people, these framed people; their mouths, their faces, were all devoured and torn. And it is said that their remnant is the monkey that lives in the forests now — it remains as a sign of this, because their flesh alone was of wood, made by the framer, the shaper. And so the monkey looks like man, a sign of that other kind of people, formed, framed, who were only wood, only tzité.

And then came the casting of lots, the invoking: "Speak, be heard, tell whether it is good that the wood be carved by the framers, and whether this is the one who is to sustain and nourish us when it is sown, when it dawns. "Come, take shape, heart of the sky; do not shame the face of Tepeu, Gucumatz," they said. And so the monkey looks like man, a sign of that other kind of people, formed, framed, who were only wood, only tzité.
translation.translator_note: This section's K'iche' text (as delivered) narrates only the wood-people episode in full — the earlier failed attempt at mud/earth people that the section title alludes to is not itself narrated in this passage; the opening lines here ("let it be tried again... that our formed man be sown and dawn") presuppose that a prior attempt (presumably covered elsewhere) had already failed, but no mud-specific material appears in this K'iche' excerpt itself. A number of divine/oracular epithets (Ah Cuval, Ah Yamanic, Ah Chut, Ah Tzalam, Ah Raxá Lac, Ah Raxá Tzel, Ah Eol, Ah Toltecat) and animal names (Xecotcovach, Camalotz, Cotzbalam, Tucumbalam) are left transliterated rather than translated, following the K'iche' text itself, which treats them as proper names; Ximénez's Spanish glosses several loosely (e.g. "pizote," "chalchihuites") but these read as approximate contemporary equivalents rather than certain etymologies, so I kept the K'iche' forms. Where the K'iche' verb forms for the household objects' speeches were ambiguous in person/number, I followed the clearer sense preserved in Ximénez's parallel Spanish for word choice only, not phrasing.

review.issues: Right section: yes — the English tracks this K'iche' passage (divination consultation, carving of the wood people, flood, revolt of animals/implements, monkeys as remnant), and the translator's note correctly observes that no mud-people material appears in this excerpt despite the section title. Fidelity is generally good and demonstrably engages the K'iche' rather than just Ximénez (e.g. 'grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light' follows K'iche' 'ratit quih ratit zac' where Ximénez has 'abuela de la luna'; the untranslated epithets Nim Ac, Nima Tziis etc. follow the K'iche' where Ximénez glosses 'pizote', 'chalchihuites'). However there is one real omission: the K'iche' passage 'xeqha quri hunatit hunmama chiquech are ri mama are ah ꜩite xpiyacoc vbi. arecu riatit ahquih ahbit chi racan xmucane vbi' — the sentences identifying the old man as the tzité-diviner named Xpiyacoc and the old woman day-keeper/maker as Chiracan Xmucane (Ximénez renders it fully: 'el viejo era el de las suertes de el tzité, y se llamaba xpiyacoc, y la vieja adivina... se llamaba chiracan xmucane') — is silently dropped; the translation jumps from 'So it was said to the diviners' straight to the casting of lots. Minor further drift: 'and so they fell from grace' for 'xepah chivi' (Ximénez 'dieron de hozicos', they fell on their faces) editorializes; and 'you sun, you oracle' for 'at quih, at bit' arguably over-resolves quih/bit, though Ximénez supports 'sol'/'formadura'. Everything else checked (resin from the sky, Xecotcovach/Camalotz/Cotzbalam/Tucumbalam sequence, grinding stones' holi/huqui speech, dogs, pots, hearthstones, houses/trees/caves, monkeys) is accurate. faithful=false solely for the omitted Xpiyacoc/Xmucane identification passage, which should be restored.
review.resemblance_note: No sustained match to Recinos, Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson in word order or rhythm. One lexical echo worth noting: 'framer, shaper' for ꜩacol bitol is Christenson's characteristic rendering ('Framer and Shaper'; Tedlock has 'Maker, Modeler', Recinos/Goetz 'Creator and Maker'), but it is an isolated epithet choice and the surrounding phrasing does not otherwise track Christenson, so it reads as convergent rather than recalled.

title: Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, and Kab'raqan

paragraphs: There was then only a faint gray light over the face of the earth; there was not yet any sun. Yet there was one who made himself great: Wuqub' Kaqix was his name. There already existed sky and earth, but the face of the sun and moon was clouded still. Nonetheless he called himself the sign of the people: "I am great," he said. "I am the sun, I am the light, I am the moon, so it shall be. Great is my brightness. I am he by whom the people walk and are victorious, for my eyes are of silver, they gleam, my teeth like jewels, shining, blue-green like the face of the sky. And this my nose gleams white from afar, like the moon. Of silver too is my seat; when I step forth from my seat the earth is lit. So then I am the sun, I am the moon, for the ones born of light, the sons of light, so shall it be, for my sight reaches far." So spoke Wuqub' Kaqix. But in truth Wuqub' Kaqix was not the sun; he only made himself great in his feathers and his riches. But his sight reached only over the place where he sat; it did not reach over the whole world. The face of the sun had not yet appeared, nor the moon, nor the stars; it had not yet grown light. Thus Wuqub' Kaqix made himself the sun, though he was not truly seen shining in his brightness like the sun; rather it was merely his great pride that made him so, at the time of the flood, when it was done, the drowning of the wood-people that were made, the wood-figures.

This, then, is the beginning of the defeat, and of the destroying of the sun of Wuqub' Kaqix, by two boys, the one named Hunahpu, the other named Xbalanque. These also were gods, and because of it they saw the evil that his pride had done before the heart of the sky, and the boys said: "It is not good that this should be so, that man should not be able to live here on the face of the earth. Let us then try to shoot him with the blowgun, when he is at his eating, let us shoot him, let sickness be brought upon him, and so then his riches shall be ended, his jewels, his silver, his precious stones, his shining things which he takes such pride in, so it is that all the people do likewise. It is not right that greatness should come to us through mere silver," so said the boys, each with his blowgun already on his shoulder. Now this Wuqub' Kaqix had two sons: the first-born was Sipakna, the second was Kab'raqan; and Chimalmat was the name of their mother, the wife of Wuqub' Kaqix. This Sipakna, then, his sport was the great mountains: it was he who in a single night made the mountain called Hun Ahpu Pekul, Yax Kanul, Makamob, Huliznab, so it is said its name is. It would not yet be dawn when in a single night it was made, through Sipakna. And Kab'raqan then shook the mountains, for it was through him that the small mountains and the great mountains trembled. Thus it was that the sons of Wuqub' Kaqix likewise made themselves great: "I am the one," said Wuqub' Kaqix, "I am the sun." "I am the maker of the earth," said Sipakna. "And I," said Kab'raqan, "am he who shakes the sky, who topples the whole earth." So it was that the sons of Wuqub' Kaqix, following their father's pride, likewise made themselves great, and it was there that the boys saw their evil. Not yet had our first mother and our first father been made; and so it was resolved by the boys how they should die, how their pride should be brought to an end, Wuqub' Kaqix together with Sipakna and Kab'raqan.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' place-name string for Sipakna's mountain (hun ahpu pe cul ya xcanul macamob huliznab) is obscure and possibly corrupt in the manuscript; I rendered it as a proper-name list (Hun Ahpu Pekul, Yax Kanul, Makamob, Huliznab) rather than attempting to force sense from it, following Ximénez's own treatment of it as a name. Ximénez's Spanish adds a clarifying gloss for Kab'raqan's name ("esto es de dos pies," i.e. "two-legged/earthquake") not literally present as a separate clause in the K'iche' at that point, which I omitted to stay with the K'iche'. The K'iche' repeats "xa hun aꜫab chi vinaquiric" (roughly "in the space of a single night it came into being") in a way that is slightly redundant with the surrounding clause; I compressed this without losing the sense that Sipakna's mountain-building happened overnight.

review.issues: Right section confirmed. Three fidelity flags: (1) "he called himself the sign of the people" garbles the obscure clause "vzaquetal vinac ri xbutic queheri naual vinac" — both K'iche' and Ximénez refer to the drowned (flood) people being like naual/sorcerer people, not a self-designation; (2) a whole transitional sentence is silently omitted at the end of paragraph 1: "quehe cut xchicabÿh chic ta xcamic vucub caquix ta xchacatahic, ta xbanatahic vinac rumal ahꜩac ahbit" ("thus we shall tell of the death of Wuqub' Kaqix, his defeat, and the making of man by the Framer and Shaper"), present in Ximénez as well — should be restored; (3) "his sport was the great mountains" — K'iche' chirechaah (echa' = food) and Ximénez "su pasto y comida" both say the mountains were his food, not sport. Minor: "to us" added in "greatness should come to us through mere silver." Otherwise the translation clearly engages the K'iche' directly, and its omissions of Ximénez's explanatory glosses are correct editorial choices.
review.resemblance_note: No word-choice/rhythm match to Recinos, Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson; renderings like "faint gray light" and "blue-green like the face of the sky" are independent.

paragraphs: There was then only a faint gray light over the face of the earth; there was not yet any sun. Yet there was one who made himself great: Wuqub' Kaqix was his name. There already existed sky and earth, but the face of the sun and moon was clouded still. Nonetheless he called himself the sign of the people: "I am great," he said. "I am the sun, I am the light, I am the moon, so it shall be. Great is my brightness. I am he by whom the people walk and are victorious, for my eyes are of silver, they gleam, my teeth like jewels, shining, blue-green like the face of the sky. And this my nose gleams white from afar, like the moon. Of silver too is my seat; when I step forth from my seat the earth is lit. So then I am the sun, I am the moon, for the ones born of light, the sons of light, so shall it be, for my sight reaches far." So spoke Wuqub' Kaqix. But in truth Wuqub' Kaqix was not the sun; he only made himself great in his feathers and his riches. But his sight reached only over the place where he sat; it did not reach over the whole world. The face of the sun had not yet appeared, nor the moon, nor the stars; it had not yet grown light. Thus Wuqub' Kaqix made himself the sun, though he was not truly seen shining in his brightness like the sun; rather it was merely his great pride that made him so, at the time of the flood, when it was done, the drowning of the wood-people that were made, the wood-figures.

This, then, is the beginning of the defeat, and of the destroying of the sun of Wuqub' Kaqix, by two boys, the one named Hunahpu, the other named Xbalanque. These also were gods, and because of it they saw the evil that his pride had done before the heart of the sky, and the boys said: "It is not good that this should be so, that man should not be able to live here on the face of the earth. Let us then try to shoot him with the blowgun, when he is at his eating, let us shoot him, let sickness be brought upon him, and so then his riches shall be ended, his jewels, his silver, his precious stones, his shining things which he takes such pride in, so it is that all the people do likewise. It is not right that greatness should come to us through mere silver," so said the boys, each with his blowgun already on his shoulder. Now this Wuqub' Kaqix had two sons: the first-born was Sipakna, the second was Kab'raqan; and Chimalmat was the name of their mother, the wife of Wuqub' Kaqix. This Sipakna, then, his sport was the great mountains: it was he who in a single night made the mountain called Hun Ahpu Pekul, Yax Kanul, Makamob, Huliznab, so it is said its name is. It would not yet be dawn when in a single night it was made, through Sipakna. And Kab'raqan then shook the mountains, for it was through him that the small mountains and the great mountains trembled. Thus it was that the sons of Wuqub' Kaqix likewise made themselves great: "I am the one," said Wuqub' Kaqix, "I am the sun." "I am the maker of the earth," said Sipakna. "And I," said Kab'raqan, "am he who shakes the sky, who topples the whole earth." So it was that the sons of Wuqub' Kaqix, following their father's pride, likewise made themselves great, and it was there that the boys saw their evil. Not yet had our first mother and our first father been made; and so it was resolved by the boys how they should die, how their pride should be brought to an end, Wuqub' Kaqix together with Sipakna and Kab'raqan.

title: Junajpu and Xb'alanke move against Seven Macaw's household

paragraphs: Now here is the shooting of Seven Macaw by the two boys, and we shall tell of the defeat of each one of those who exalted themselves.

Seven Macaw had a great nance tree, and its fruit was his food. Every day he would go up to eat the fruit of that nance tree. Hun Hunahpu and Xbalanque had watched him do this, and the two boys hid themselves and lay in wait beneath that tree, among its leaves. When Seven Macaw came, the two boys were there; he was up in the tree eating the fruit of the nance. Then he was shot by Hun Hunahpu — the pellet from the blowgun went straight to his jaw — and he cried out loudly and fell to the ground from the tree. Hun Hunahpu ran quickly indeed to seize him.

But then Hun Hunahpu's arm was wrenched off by Seven Macaw — it was pulled straight out, torn away right at the shoulder — and Seven Macaw threw Hun Hunahpu down. Even so, the boys had done well; they were not the first to be defeated by Seven Macaw.

Then Seven Macaw went off to his house carrying Hun Hunahpu's arm, holding his own jaw as he arrived, in pain. "What has happened to you?" said Chimalmat, Seven Macaw's wife, there. "What is it — two demons shot me and dislocated my jaw. Now all my teeth are loose, and they pain me. But I have brought up an arm, and I have hung it over the fire, so that they will come for it. Truly they are demons," said Seven Macaw, as he hung up Hun Hunahpu's arm.

Then Hun Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel again, and they went and spoke of it to an old man — his hair was truly already white, an old man — and an old woman, truly already an aged grandmother, bent, who went about stooped, poor bent people. Zaqui Nim Aq was the old man's name, and Zaqui Nima Tzis was the name of the grandmother. The boys said to the grandmother and grandfather: "Come with us when we go for our arm, to Seven Macaw's house — we will simply follow along behind you. Say, 'These are our grandchildren; their dead mother and father were our companions.' That is what you shall say as we come along behind you. And when he begs you, saying, 'Have pity on me,' you shall say, 'What we do is only draw the worm out of teeth' — speak of us so, as children, when Seven Macaw looks at us. We too will be there to give counsel," said the two boys. "Very well," the old couple said.

Then they went to the corner by Seven Macaw's seat, before his dwelling. The old woman and the old man came along, and the two boys came playing behind them, and they passed beneath the lord's house while Seven Macaw was crying out loudly with the pain in his mouth. When Seven Macaw saw the old man and the old woman going along together, he said, "Where do you come from, grandfather?" "We are only seeking our sustenance, lord," they said. "What is your sustenance? Are those your children with you?" "No, lord, they are our grandchildren; but we have pity on them, and whatever alms we are given, we share with them, lord," said the old woman and the old man.

Now the lord was suffering greatly with the pain of his tooth. "I beg you — have pity on me. What is it you do? What is your cure?" said the lord. "We only draw the worm out of teeth, and we also cure eyes, and we set bones, lord," they said. "Very well — cure me, then, for truly it pains me every day, and I cannot sleep; I have no rest because of my teeth and my eyes. Two demons shot me with pellets — that is how it began. I cannot sleep because of it. So have pity on my face — my teeth are already loose, every one of them." "Very well, lord — it is indeed a worm that torments them; they must be drawn out and others put in their place." "It would not be good if... for I am a lord, and my adornment is my teeth, and my eyes." "We will put in their place ground bone" — but the ground bone was only white maize. "Very well — draw them out, help me," he said. Then Seven Macaw's teeth were drawn out.

Only white maize was put in as their replacement, only gleaming white kernels of maize in his mouth. At once his face fell; he no longer looked like a lord — the look of him was gone, the look of green stones in his mouth. Then they cured Seven Macaw's eyes as well: his eyes were pried out, and the precious metal of them was taken out, and he felt nothing; he was only put into a stupor. Thus his self-exaltation was brought to an end, through the cunning of Hun Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then Seven Macaw died, and Hun Hunahpu recovered his arm. Chimalmat, Seven Macaw's wife, died as well. So was lost the wealth of Seven Macaw, who died at the hands of the healers; the precious green stones were left behind, here on the face of the earth.

[This passage is badly obscured in the manuscript.] ...and thereupon the arm was taken back and rejoined to its place, and it was made whole again. It was only because of the death of Seven Macaw that Heaven did this; they saw the evil in his self-exaltation. Then the two boys went on their way again — it was only the will of the Heart of Sky that they had carried out.

translation.translator_note: Several points worth flagging. (1) The old couple's names are transliterated rather than translated: "Zaqui Nim Aq" (aq = peccary/coati-like animal; Ximénez's Spanish renders this "pizote blanco," a white coati) and "Zaqui Nima Tzis." I kept them as proper names rather than glossing their literal sense, since the K'iche' text itself does not gloss them. (2) The K'iche' twice uses "atit mama" ("grandmother, grandfather") for the disguised old couple and later seems to call them "naual atit, naual mama" — divine/spirit grandmother and grandfather — suggesting they are understood as supernatural beings, not ordinary elders; the Spanish does not bring this out. (3) The final stretch of the K'iche' (from "hu pah chic xziquinic..." through "...xtiquitax vcoc vꜩchic xuxic") is orthographically garbled/obscure — likely scribal corruption — and does not have a clean parallel in Ximénez's Spanish paraphrase at this point; I have rendered only the clear sense (the arm being restored to Hun Hunahpu) and marked the gap rather than inventing continuous prose. (4) Where Seven Macaw protests about losing his teeth and eyes ("mahaba vꜩlo chel ri ve rumal xere in ahau vi nu caubal ri ve, ruq vbac nu vach"), the K'iche' is elliptical; I rendered it as an interrupted objection ("It would not be good if... for I am a lord...") rather than smoothing it into a complete sentence, since the source itself reads as interrupted/incomplete there.

review.issues: Minor: (1) Hero consistently named "Hun Hunahpu" though he is Hunahpu (the MS vacillates between "hun ahpu" and "hun hunahpu" here; following the witness is defensible but risks character confusion — deserves a note). (2) "the look of green stones in his mouth" for "raxcauacoh puchi" is an uncertain interpretive reading (Ximénez: "la voca moreteada," bruised). (3) "died at the hands of the healers; the precious green stones were left behind" slightly drifts from "xa ahqun xcamouic ri cuval yamanic" (more plausibly "only the physician took the jewels," matching Ximénez "el medico tomo... las piedras preziosas"). Otherwise faithful; translator demonstrably engaged the K'iche' (opening sentence and "self-exaltation brought to an end" have no Spanish parallel), and honestly marked the genuinely garbled final passage.
review.resemblance_note: Sense parallels to Christenson in the opening sentence are inherent to the K'iche' (vbaxic = shooting); wording, order, and rhythm differ from Tedlock, Christenson, and Recinos/Goetz-Morley. Shared items like "nance tree," "Seven Macaw," "Heart of Sky" are standard renderings, not fingerprints.

"What is your sustenance? Are those your children with you?" "No, lord, they are our grandchildren; but we have pity on them, and whatever alms we are given, we share with them, lord," said the old woman and the old man.

Now the lord was suffering greatly with the pain of his tooth. "I beg you — have pity on me. What is it you do? What is your cure?" said the lord. "We only draw the worm out of teeth, and we also cure eyes, and we set bones, lord," they said. "Very well — cure me, then, for truly it pains me every day, and I cannot sleep; I have no rest because of my teeth and my eyes. Two demons shot me with pellets — that is how it began. I cannot sleep because of it. So have pity on my face — my teeth are already loose, every one of them." "Very well, lord — it is indeed a worm that torments them; they must be drawn out and others put in their place." "It would not be good if... for I am a lord, and my adornment is my teeth, and my eyes." "We will put in their place ground bone" — but the ground bone was only white maize. "Very well — draw them out, help me," he said. Then Seven Macaw's teeth were drawn out.

Only white maize was put in as their replacement, only gleaming white kernels of maize in his mouth. At once his face fell; he no longer looked like a lord — the look of him was gone, the look of green stones in his mouth. Then they cured Seven Macaw's eyes as well: his eyes were pried out, and the precious metal of them was taken out, and he felt nothing; he was only put into a stupor. Thus his self-exaltation was brought to an end, through the cunning of Hun Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then Seven Macaw died, and Hun Hunahpu recovered his arm. Chimalmat, Seven Macaw's wife, died as well. So was lost the wealth of Seven Macaw, who died at the hands of the healers; the precious green stones were left behind, here on the face of the earth.

[This passage is badly obscured in the manuscript.] ...and thereupon the arm was taken back and rejoined to its place, and it was made whole again. It was only because of the death of Seven Macaw that Heaven did this; they saw the evil in his self-exaltation. Then the two boys went on their way again — it was only the will of the Heart of Sky that they had carried out.

(1) The old couple's names are transliterated rather than translated: "Zaqui Nim Aq" (aq = peccary/coati-like animal; Ximénez's Spanish renders this "pizote blanco," a white coati) and "Zaqui Nima Tzis." (2) The K'iche' twice uses "atit mama" ("grandmother, grandfather") for the disguised old couple and later seems to call them "naual atit, naual mama" — divine/spirit grandmother and grandfather — suggesting they are understood as supernatural beings, not ordinary elders; the Spanish does not bring this out. title: Sipakna and the four hundred youths

paragraphs: Here now are the deeds of Zipacna, the first son of Vucub-Caquix. "I am the maker of the mountains," says Zipacna.

Now Zipacna was bathing at the edge of a river when the four hundred youths passed by, dragging a tree to serve as the roof-post of their house — four hundred of them together — after they had felled a great tree to be the ridgepole of their house. When Zipacna saw them, he went to where the four hundred youths were and asked them: "What are you doing, boys?" "It is only that we cannot lift this tree onto our shoulders," they said. "I will carry it. Where is it to go? What is it for, that you have cut it?" "It is for the ridgepole of our house," they said. "Very well," said Zipacna, and he went ahead and carried it, and he lifted it onto his shoulders, and brought it to the gate of the house of the four hundred youths.

"Now then, stay with us, boy. Do you have a mother, a father?" they asked. "I have none," said Zipacna. "Then tomorrow we will go again to bring another tree, another post for our house," they said. "Very well," said Zipacna.

Then the four hundred youths took counsel among themselves: "What shall we do with this boy? Let us kill him, for what he has done is not good — he alone lifted the tree. Let this be what we do: we will dig a great hole, and there we will throw him down into the hole. 'Go down and dig out the earth,' we will tell him, and when he is bent down in the hole, we will throw a great tree down upon him, and there in the hole he shall die," said the four hundred youths.

Then they dug a great hole, very deep, and they called Zipacna. "We are fond of you; go now, dig, for we cannot reach the bottom of the earth," they told him. "Very well," he said, and he went down into the hole. "Dig deep," they told him, "until it cries out to you." "Very well," he said, and then he began to dig the hole. But the hole that he dug was a hole to save himself — he knew that they meant to kill him. He dug a side-passage, a second hole, to hide himself in.

"How far have you dug? Has it cried out yet?" they called down. "I am still digging; I will call up to you when it is done," said Zipacna, but he was not digging out the true bottom of the hole for his grave — only the hole in which to hide himself. Then at last he called up from below: "Come, take out the earth from the bottom of the hole, for truly I have dug it deep now. Do you not hear my voice? Yet I hear the echo of your own voices from up there," said Zipacna from within the hole, where he lay hidden, and he called out from time to time.

So the youths dragged the great tree and hurled it down with a crash into the hole. "Let no one speak, let us only wait until he cries out," they said, speaking among themselves in secret. And when they had thrown the tree into the hole, it made a sound, and then they were glad. "How well this has turned out that we have done," they said. "If he had lived, it would have gone badly for us, for he had already thrust himself in among us, the four hundred youths," they said, rejoicing. "Now, in three days, let us make our drink, and in three days we, the four hundred youths, shall drink our maize-beer," they said. "Tomorrow we shall see, and the day after we shall see whether the ants come out over the earth when it stinks and rots — then our hearts will be at ease, and we shall drink without fear," they said. But Zipacna was listening from the hole, to everything the youths said.

And on the second day the ants came out in great numbers, swarming and gathering, and they came from beneath the tree, some carrying his hair, others carrying his nails. And when the youths saw this, they said: "That demon is finished! Look, the ants have come, gathered together, and they carry hair and nails — look at what we have done!" But Zipacna was alive; he himself had cut his nails and the hair of his head, and with his mouth he had bitten off his nails, and he gave them to the ants. So the four hundred youths thought that he was dead.

Then on the third day they began their drinking, and all the youths grew drunk. And when all four hundred were drunk and no longer aware of anything, Zipacna brought the house down upon their heads, and they were all crushed, and not one or two of them escaped — all the four hundred youths were killed by Zipacna, son of Vucub-Caquix.

Such was the death of the four hundred youths. And it is said that they became the stars that are called the Pleiades in the sky, whose name is Motz — though perhaps this is only a false word. Now we shall tell how Zipacna in turn was overcome by those two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' "moꜩ" (heap/pile) is given as the name of the star-group identified with the Pleiades — Ximénez's Spanish glosses this directly ("moꜩ. esto es monton, porque de monton fueron muertos"), so I kept both the name and the etymological gloss ("heap," since they died in a heap) rather than substituting the modern constellation name alone. review.issues: Minor: (1) "until it cries out to you" is a shaky parse of "caziquin vloc ta cototahoc" (more naturally "call up when the digging is done"), and the translator's note misquotes Ximénez's Spanish as supporting it (Ximénez has "hasta que lo hagas muy profundo", not "hasta que os grite" at that point); the cry-out motif does occur later of Zipacna, so sense is not badly damaged. (2) Note claims the "heap" gloss for Motz was kept in the text, but the main text omits it. (3) "one exit, two exits" (hun elebal caib elebal) smoothed to "echo of your own voices." No wrong-section, invention, or Spanish-only paraphrase problems.
review.resemblance_note: Name orthography (Zipacna, Vucub-Caquix, Hunahpu, Xbalanque) follows Recinos/Goetz & Morley convention rather than the project's "Sipakna", and the opening line is shaped like Goetz & Morley's, but that opening is a near-forced rendering of the K'iche'; word choice and rhythm otherwise diverge, so no specific memorized match.

title: Kab'raqan brought low

paragraphs: Here follows the account of how Zipacna was defeated, and killed, when he was overcome once more by the two boys, Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque.

Their hearts had been troubled over the four hundred boys whom Zipacna had killed. He ate nothing but fish and crab, which he hunted along the edges of the rivers — that alone was his food, day after day. By day he went about seeking what he would eat; by night he carried the mountains.

Then Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque made the likeness of a great crab. Out of the leaf of the tree called ec they made it: from it they made the crab's great claws, and from other, smaller leaves they made its lesser parts; and they made its shell and its legs, and they laid it belly-up. Then they set it inside a cave, beneath a great mountain. Meawan was the name of the mountain — the place where he would be brought down.

Then the boys went out, and they came upon Zipacna at the river. "Where are you going, boy?" Zipacna was asked. "I am not going anywhere," Zipacna answered them, "I am only looking for my food." "What is your food?" "Only fish, only crab — but I have found none. Since the day before yesterday I have eaten nothing; I can no longer bear the hunger," Zipacna said to them.

Then Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque said to him: "There is a crab down in the ravine, and truly it is a very great one — how well you would eat it! We wanted to catch it ourselves, but it bit us, and we were afraid of it, and so we did not take hold of it."

"Have pity on me — come with me, take me there," Zipacna said to them. "We do not want to," they said. "Go on by yourself; you will not lose your way. Follow the river upward, and you will come out right at it, beneath the great mountain, where it sounds, roaring, down in the ravine — just go straight there," said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque.

"Alas for me — have you truly not found it yourselves?" said Zipacna. "Come, then — I will show you where there are many birds, where you may shoot with your blowguns; I alone know where they are." So he went ahead, in front of the boys.

Then they went, Zipacna walking along with them, and they arrived beneath the ravine. The crab lay there on its side, its shell shining red — and there, beneath the ravine, lay the boys' trick. "Very good," said Zipacna, rejoicing, and he was already eager to eat it, for he was faint with hunger. He tried to go in lying flat, and the crab kept climbing upward and away from him. So he came back out, and the boys said to him: "Did you not catch it?" "No — I did not catch it, it very nearly got away from me, it climbed on upward. Perhaps it would be better if I went in from above." So then he went in from above; and once he had gone in, when only his knees remained still outside, the mountain crumbled and settled down quietly upon his chest, and he did not rise again. And Zipacna was turned to stone.

Thus was Zipacna defeated by the boys Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque — he who, it is told, in ancient times made the mountains, the elder son of Vucub Caquix. Beneath the mountain called Meawan he was defeated; it was only by a kind of trick that he was overcome.
The second, he who exalted himself — now his account shall be told.

review.issues: RIGHT SECTION: yes — the translation matches the extracted K'iche'/Spanish content (Zipacna lured by the artificial crab under Mount Meawan, crushed and turned to stone, closing transition to "the second who exalted himself" i.e. Kab'raqan). Note: the section's stored TITLE ("Kab'raqan brought low") mismatches its actual content, which is the Zipacna episode; the translation is faithful to the text, and the title problem is upstream in sections.json, not in the translation. FIDELITY: generally accurate. Minor points: (1) "from other, smaller leaves they made its lesser parts" drops the plant name — Ximénez names the smaller leaves "pahac" (K'iche' "pa hac"), and the translation silently omits it; (2) the crab's shell/underparts are made "de laxa" (of a stone slab; K'iche' "zelabah" ~ flat stone) in Ximénez, but the translation just says "they made its shell and its legs," losing the stone-slab detail; (3) "So he went ahead, in front of the boys" for "xelahic xoc na chiquivach qaholab" / Ximénez "y a vista de ellos entró debaxo la laxa" — the Spanish reads "in their sight he went in under the slab," so this clause may be misplaced/misread, though the K'iche' here is hard and the narrative sequence is not damaged; (4) "only by a kind of trick" for "xa naual xchacatah vi" is defensible (naual = supernatural power/artifice; Ximénez says "milagro"), though "magic/miraculous power" would be closer. The translator's declared reliance on the Spanish for the garbled dialogue run ("lama quicu xchachaplo...") is justified — that K'iche' stretch is genuinely corrupt in the manuscript orthography — and the English there is not a word-for-word rendering of Ximénez (whose Spanish at that point differs in detail, e.g. the "don't make us come back for nothing" line, which the translation compresses). paragraphs: Third, then, was the one who exalted himself, the second son of Vucub Caquix. Cabracan was his name. "I am the one who levels the mountains," he said. But it was Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque alone who were set against Cabracan. For Huracan, Chipi Caculha, and Raxa Caculha spoke to Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque: "The second son of Vucub Caquix must also, in his turn, be defeated — this is my word, for it is not good, what they do upon the face of the earth. They exalt themselves in greatness and in pride, and it must not be so. Go, entice him away, out to where the sun rises," Huracan said to the two boys. "Good, our lord, though it is not good, what we see. Are you not first, are you not the Heart of the Sky?" the boys said, when they answered Huracan's word.

Now Cabracan was toppling mountains: he had only to stamp lightly with his feet upon the face of the earth, and at once great mountains and small mountains split apart and fell. And so he was found by the two boys. "Where are you going, boy?" they said to Cabracan. "I am not going anywhere — I am simply the toppler of mountains, and so I shall be forever, for all time," he said, when he spoke. Then Cabracan said to Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, "How is it you have come? I do not know your faces. What are your names?" said Cabracan. "We have no names; we are only blowgunners and bird-liners across the mountains. We are poor, we have nothing, boy. We merely go about among the small mountains and the great mountains, boy. But there we saw one great mountain — truly it rises up to a marvelous height, and towers over every mountain. Not even one or two birds have we been able to take near it, boy. Is it true that you topple every mountain, boy?" said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque to Cabracan. "Is it true, the mountain you saw? Where is it? Show me, and I will go and topple it. Where did you see it?" "It is there, toward the place where the sun rises," Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque then said. "Good — let us go there, then," said Cabracan. But the two boys did not walk straight beside him; rather each went, one at his left hand and one at his right, for they carried their blowguns. "If there are birds we will shoot them," they said. And they took pleasure in showing off their shooting; and when they shot, it was not clay pellets that loaded their blowguns, but only their breath with which they brought down the birds — and at this Cabracan marveled greatly. Then the boys built their fire and set to roasting their birds over it; and one bird they coated with tizate, with white earth they smeared it, so that it should be given to him — so that when he craved it, when its fragrant breath reached him, when he wanted it, this earth would lodge within him. Through this white earth they worked their design — that same earth in which he was to be buried. "Truly great is the wisdom of the one who was framed, the one who was shaped, so it will be said, when the dawn comes," the boys said to one another — for it was for this alone, so that the heart of Cabracan might be overcome. As they roasted the bird, its roasting gave off a savor; it dripped fat, it browned as it cooked, and its fragrance spread. And Cabracan longed greatly to eat it; his mouth watered, his spittle ran, his throat and jaw dripped at the fragrance of the bird. Then he asked, "What food is this of yours? Truly its smell is delicious — give me a little of it," he said. Then a bird was given to Cabracan, for his undoing. And when the bird was finished they went on, and arrived there where the sun rises, where the great mountain stood. But by now Cabracan's hands and feet had gone slack; he could do nothing more, because of the earth that had lodged in the bird he had eaten. He could do nothing more to the mountain, he could not topple it, he was brought low. Then he was bound by the boys: his hands were tied behind him; his hands were bound by the boys, and his neck and his feet together were bound. Then they cast him down to the earth, and they buried him. Thus was the defeat of Cabracan, by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque alone. Uncountable are the deeds they did here upon the face of the earth.

Now, then, we shall tell of the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. First we have told of the defeat of Vucub Caquix, together with Zipacna and Cabracan, here upon the face of the earth. Now, then, we shall also tell the name of the father of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, and the telling and the account of the begetting of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque — but only in part shall we tell it, only in part the account of their father.

review.issues: Section matches (Cabracan episode + transitional close; the section title names the fathers but the actual s08 text is Cabracan, and the translation follows the text). Then the boys built their fire and set to roasting their birds over it; and one bird they coated with tizate, with white earth they smeared it, so that it should be given to him — so that when he craved it, when its fragrant breath reached him, when he wanted it, this earth would lodge within him. Through this white earth they worked their design — that same earth in which he was to be buried. "Truly great is the wisdom of the one who was framed, the one who was shaped, so it will be said, when the dawn comes," the boys said to one another — for it was for this alone, so that the heart of Cabracan might be overcome. As they roasted the bird, its roasting gave off a savor; it dripped fat, it browned as it cooked, and its fragrance spread. And Cabracan longed greatly to eat it; his mouth watered, his spittle ran, his throat and jaw dripped at the fragrance of the bird. Then he asked, "What food is this of yours? Truly its smell is delicious — give me a little of it," he said. Then a bird was given to Cabracan, for his undoing. And when the bird was finished they went on, and arrived there where the sun rises, where the great mountain stood. But by now Cabracan's hands and feet had gone slack; he could do nothing more, because of the earth that had lodged in the bird he had eaten. He could do nothing more to the mountain, he could not topple it, he was brought low. Then he was bound by the boys: his hands were tied behind him; his hands were bound by the boys, and his neck and his feet together were bound. Then they cast him down to the earth, and they buried him. Thus was the defeat of Cabracan, by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque alone. Uncountable are the deeds they did here upon the face of the earth.

Now, then, we shall tell of the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. First we have told of the defeat of Vucub Caquix, together with Zipacna and Cabracan, here upon the face of the earth. Now, then, we shall also tell the name of the father of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, and the telling and the account of the begetting of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque — but only in part shall we tell it, only in part the account of their father.

I have rendered the surrounding sense (the narrator's promise to name the boys' father and tell of their birth, but "only in part") as best supported by the surviving K'iche' vocabulary, but this closing clause should be treated as uncertain. title: The ballcourt and the summons of the Xibalba lords

paragraphs: Now this shall be told. These are the names of Hunhunahpu, as he is called. And these were his parents: it was by Xpiyacoc and Xmucane that Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu were begotten. Now Hunhunahpu had two children born to him — two were his sons. Hun Batz was the name of the first-born, and Hun Chouen was the name of the second-born. And the name of their mother was Xbaquiyalo, as she is called, the wife of Hunhunahpu. As for Vucub Hunahpu, he had no wife; he had never taken one, and he had no son either — he simply lived on his own. Both of them were great in wisdom and great was their knowledge, here upon the face of the earth; good was their conduct, and they showed their skill to Hun Batz and Hun Chouen. The sons of Hunhunahpu became flute-players and singers, writers and carvers, workers of jade and workers of silver — such were Hun Batz and Hun Chouen. As for Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, dice and the ballgame were all they did, every single day. The four of them would contend together, gathering in the ballcourt, and there Voc watched them, the messenger of Huracan, Chipi-Caculha, and Raxa-Caculha. Now Voc was not far from here upon the face of the earth, nor far from Xibalba; in an instant he could reach the sky, to Huracan. They remained here upon the face of the earth. And by now their mother, the mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chouen, had died. Now this was the road to Xibalba where they played: when One Death and Seven Death, the lords of Xibalba, heard them — "What is this that is done upon the face of the earth? They only stamp about, they only make an uproar. Let them be called to come here, so that they may come and play ball against us here — we shall defeat them, for they show us no respect, no reverence, no fear; they merely go on wrangling over our heads," said all the people of Xibalba. Then they all took counsel together, those named One Death and Seven Death, the great judges. These were the lords, all of them given their offices and their lordship, each lord in turn, by One Death and Seven Death. These were Xiquiripat and Cuchumaquic, as the lords were named; their office was to bring the sickness of blood upon people. These others were Ahalpuh and Ahalgana as lords; their lordship was to bring on swellings — pus would break out on people's legs, and their faces would go the color of jaundice, called yellow-sickness; such was the lordship of Ahalpuh and Ahalgana. These other lords were Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, the staff-bearers of Xibalba, whose staffs were nothing but bone; their office was to waste people down to bone until they died, wasted away to nothing but bone and belly — this was the office of Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, as they were named. And these other lords were named Ahalmez and Ahaltocob; their office was to bring misfortune upon people, so that whether on a rubbish-heap or behind the door of a house, disaster would strike them, and they would be found dead, sprawled face-down upon the ground — such was the lordship of Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, as they are called. And these other lords were named Xic and Patan; their lordship was over people who die on the road, a sudden death, as it is called, blood coming to their mouths as they died; each had his task — to seize a man by the throat, to press the breast and heart of the one who died on the road, and to overtake him swiftly whether he went walking or however he went — such was the lordship of Xic and Patan. These, then, set their minds together to afflict and to torment Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu. What Xibalba coveted was the playing-gear of Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu — their leather pads, their yokes, their arm-guards, their headbands, and their masks — the ball-playing equipment of Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu. Now we shall tell of their going to Xibalba. Hun Batz and Hun Chouen, the sons of Hunhunahpu, were left behind; their mother had already died — this being after Hun Batz and Hun Chouen were in turn defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then came the messengers of One Death and Seven Death: "Go, you who carry their word, and summon Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu. Say to them: Come, let them come, say the lords, here where they shall arrive to play ball with us, so that we may be gladdened by them, for truly we marvel at their doings — so let them come, say the lords. And let them bring with them all their playing-gear, their pads, their yokes, and whatever else the lords may ask of them. Say: let them come" — thus were the messengers charged with their message. And these were the messengers: Chabi Tucur, Huracan Tucur, Caquix Tucur, and Holom Tucur, as the messengers of Xibalba were called. Chabi Tucur was like an arrow, sharp and swift. Huracan Tucur had but a single leg, and he had wings. Caquix Tucur had a red back, and he had wings. And as for Holom Tucur, he was nothing but a head, with no legs, only wings. These four were the messengers, lords and mighty men. They set out, and coming from there, from Xibalba, swiftly they arrived at the ballcourt where Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu were playing — the ballcourt called Nim Xob Carchah. There the owls arrived at the ballcourt and delivered their message exactly as it had been given to them, the words of One Death, Seven Death, Ahalpuh, Ahalgana, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalmez, Ahaltocob, Xic, and Patan — the names of all the lords were repeated, the message faithfully given by the owls. "Is it true that this is what lord One Death and Seven Death say?" "It is true," they said. "And we shall go with you." "Bring all your playing-gear," said the lords. "Very well," they said, "but wait a little for us — first let us give word to our mother." So saying, they went to their house, and said to their mother — for their father had already died — "Mother, we must go, though it will not be long. The messenger of the lord has come for us; come, they say, so speak for us," they said. "This our ball we shall leave here, tied up above the house." Then they went and hung it up on the roof-beam. "We shall come back and play it again. But you, go on playing the flute, go on singing, go on drawing, go on carving — warm this house, and warm the heart of your grandmother." Thus were Hun Batz and Hun Chouen charged. Then their grandmother Xmucane's heart grew tender, and she wept. "Do not weep, do not grieve," they said to her. "We are not going to die — we go only for a time." So they said, as Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu departed.

translation.translator_note: Ximénez's Spanish opens this section with an editorializing preamble ("muy oscuro fue su principio...") that has no counterpart in the K'iche' text as given here; I followed the K'iche', which begins simply "Now this shall be told." The sentence describing Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu's wisdom and the teaching of skills to Hun Batz and Hun Chouen is syntactically compressed/ambiguous in the K'iche' (who displays skill to whom is not fully explicit); I followed the sense confirmed by the Spanish, that the fathers taught the arts to the sons. The clause "and by now their mother...had died" appears twice in the K'iche' (once mid-paragraph, once restated with the added note about Hun Batz/Hun Chouen's later defeat by Hunahpu and Xbalanque); this looks like the narrator inserting a proleptic aside referencing events not yet told, which I preserved literally rather than smoothing away. The owl-messenger names (Chabi Tucur, Huracan Tucur, Caquix Tucur, Holom Tucur) are kept as proper names rather than translated, since their descriptive glosses (arrow, one-leg, macaw, skull) are given by the text itself immediately after.

review.issues: Minor: "their grandmother Xmucane" where K'iche' has "qui chuch" (their mother) — contextually justified smoothing; "though it will not be long" for the obscure "xa et culic" is interpretive and diverges from Ximénez's "en vano"; ballgame gear terms (yokes, arm-guards, headbands, masks) are conventional guesses for uncertain K'iche' equipment vocabulary. Otherwise the translation tracks the K'iche' closely and demonstrably engages it independently of Ximénez (e.g., keeps the flute/sing charge addressed TO Hun Batz and Hun Chouen where Ximénez misreads, omits Ximénez's added "y destruígamoslos" and his preamble).
review.resemblance_note: Shared literal renderings with Recinos/Christenson ("One Death and Seven Death", owl glosses "like an arrow", "only a head") are forced by the K'iche' itself; no distinctive word order or rhythm matching a specific published translation.
