Huracan Tucur had but a single leg, and he had wings. Caquix Tucur had a red back, and he had wings. And as for Holom Tucur, he was nothing but a head, with no legs, only wings. These four were the messengers, lords and mighty men. They set out, and coming from there, from Xibalba, swiftly they arrived at the ballcourt where Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu were playing — the ballcourt called Nim Xob Carchah. There the owls arrived at the ballcourt and delivered their message exactly as it had been given to them, the words of One Death, Seven Death, Ahalpuh, Ahalgana, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalmez, Ahaltocob, Xic, and Patan — the names of all the lords were repeated, the message faithfully given by the owls. "Is it true that this is what lord One Death and Seven Death say?" "It is true," they said. "And we shall go with you." "Bring all your playing-gear," said the lords. "Very well," they said, "but wait a little for us — first let us give word to our mother." The sentence describing Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu's wisdom and the teaching of skills to Hun Batz and Hun Chouen is syntactically compressed/ambiguous in the K'iche' (who displays skill to whom is not fully explicit); I followed the sense confirmed by the Spanish, that the fathers taught the arts to the sons. The clause "and by now their mother...had died" appears twice in the K'iche' (once mid-paragraph, once restated with the added note about Hun Batz/Hun Chouen's later defeat by Hunahpu and Xbalanque); this looks like the narrator inserting a proleptic aside referencing events not yet told, which I preserved literally rather than smoothing away. The owl-messenger names (Chabi Tucur, Huracan Tucur, Caquix Tucur, Holom Tucur) are kept as proper names rather than translated, since their descriptive glosses (arrow, one-leg, macaw, skull) are given by the text itself immediately after.

title: The Xibalba trial-houses and the death of the elder twins

paragraphs: Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu set out, led on by the messengers, and they went down by the road of Xibalba, down its steep, sloping stairs. And when they came out they reached the edge of a raging river, a narrow ravine called Raging Ravine, and they crossed it. Then they crossed a river of spike-thorns, and were not pierced; they reached the bank of a river of blood, and did not drink there, and were not overcome; they reached a river of plain water only, and there too were not overcome. And going on further they came to where the road forks into four.

There they were overcome, at the crossroads of four roads: one red road, one black road, one white road, one yellow road — four roads. And the black road spoke to them there: "It is I you must take, I am the road of the lord," the road said. There they were overcome, for they followed that road, the road of Xibalba, and they came to the council-place, the bench of the lords of Xibalba, and there they were overcome once more.

The first one seated there was only a wooden dummy, set up and dressed by the people of Xibalba. And they greeted it first: "Hail, Hun Came," they said to the dummy; "Hail, Vucub Came," they said also to the wooden thing — but it did not answer them. Then the lords of Xibalba burst into great laughter, all the lords laughed greatly together, for in their hearts they had already won against Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu; they laughed.

Then Hun Came and Vucub Came spoke again: "Good, you have come. Tomorrow make ready your gear and your regalia," they were told. "Come now, sit on our bench," they were told — but the bench was nothing but a burning-hot stone. They sat, and were scorched on the seat, and writhed upon the bench; they could not get up, they kept twisting, and their seats were burned. Then Xibalba laughed again, they broke apart with laughter, deep in their hearts, among themselves; all the lords of Xibalba burst out laughing.

"Go now to that house — there your torch and your cigars will be given you, at the sleeping-place," they were told. Then they arrived at the Dark House, where there was only darkness within. Meanwhile the people of Xibalba took counsel: "Let us cut them down tomorrow, quickly, quickly let them die," because of their torches — the trial-houses — so the Xibalbans said among themselves.

Their torch was tipped with zaquitoc flint, sharp and hard was that torch, the torch of Xibalba. And Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu went into the Dark House. Then their torch was brought to them — a single lit torch, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came, together with one cigar apiece, already lit, sent out from the lords. When it was carried in to Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, they were huddled there in the darkness, and when the bearer of the torch and the cigars arrived, the torch came in shining. "Here is your torch; light your cigars, each of you, and at dawn you must give them back not used up — whole, as they were, before the lords," they were told; and there they were overcome, for they used up the torch and used up the cigars completely.

Many were the trials of Xibalba, many and varied its torments. The first was that Dark House, where there was only darkness within. The second was called the House of Cold, where there was great cold, white hail, white cold whirling and driving within it. The third was called the Jaguar House, where there were only jaguars, crowding and snapping at one another, restless, jaguars shut up within that house. The fourth was called the Bat House, where there were only bats, screeching, flapping about, penned-in bats, unable to get out. The fifth was called the House of Blades, where there were only blades, whistling and clashing, grinding against one another there within it.

These were the first trials of Xibalba, but Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu did not enter them — only the names of the trial-houses were spoken. Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu came before Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Where is my cigar, where is my torch that was given me last night?" they were asked. "We have finished it, lord." "Good, then. Today is your day of death; you shall be undone, you shall be broken apart, and here your faces shall be hidden — you are to be sacrificed," said Hun Came and Vucub Came.

Then they were sacrificed, and they were buried at the place called Pucbal Chah, where they were buried. The head of Hunhunahpu was cut off; only his body was buried, together with his companion. "Put the head in the fork of the tree planted by the road," said Hun Came and Vucub Came. So the head was placed in the fork of the tree. And that tree, which had never borne fruit before, bore fruit as soon as the head of Hunhunahpu was placed among its branches — and this is the calabash tree that to this day is called "the head of Hunhunahpu."

Then Hun Came and Vucub Came marveled at the fruit of that tree, round fruit all over it, and no longer could anyone tell where the head of Hunhunahpu was, for it had become exactly like the fruit of the calabash tree; and all of Xibalba saw this when they came to look. Great was the fame that tree gained, and it lodged in their hearts, because of how suddenly it had happened when the head of Hunhunahpu went in among the branches. And the people of Xibalba said among themselves: "Let no one pick its fruit, let no one go beneath that tree," they said; and they held themselves back from it, all the people of Xibalba together.

No longer could the head of Hunhunahpu be told apart there, for it had become one and the same with the fruit of the tree called zima. And great was the telling of it, until a young woman heard of it. Now it will be told how she came there.

translation.translator_note: Two spots worth flagging. (1) The K'iche' repeatedly uses "chah" (pine-torch/ocote) where the passage about "por aquel su juego, y por su pelota" in Ximénez's Spanish briefly shifts to "game" and "ball" language for the Xibalbans' plotting — the K'iche' itself keeps to "chah" (torch), so I followed the K'iche' and rendered it as "torches," treating the Spanish "juego"/"pelota" wording there as Ximénez's own gloss rather than a literal match. (2) "ipachcab," rendered here as "your regalia/gear," is an obscure compound I could not fully parse from the K'iche' alone; Ximénez's Spanish ("aderezad la argolla, la pala, y lo demás" — ballgame ring, paddle, etc.) suggests ballgame equipment specifically, which fits the context (Hun Came and Vucub Came are readying the twins for their ballgame contest) but I kept my English general since the K'iche' term itself is not transparent to me.

review.issues: Right section; overall faithful to the K'iche', and correctly sides with the K'iche' against Ximénez where they diverge (e.g. "huhun qui zic" = one cigar apiece, vs Spanish "dos tabacos"). Minor flags: (1) "nu zivan cul, cu ziuan vbi" names two ravines (Nu Zivan Kul and Ku Zivan); the translation collapses them into one "Raging Ravine". (2) In the Xibalbans' plotting, "rumal ri queꜩabal ri ca chahibal" — "queꜩabal" is more plausibly "their playing-gear/implements" (etz'ab'al), matching Ximénez's "su juego, y su pelota"; the translation's "because of their torches — the trial-houses" is a strained reading of a genuinely hard clause, though the translator flags it honestly in the note. (3) "ipachcab" gloss follows Ximénez reasonably; note that the preceding "ibate" (your ballgame yoke) also points to ballgame gear, so "gear and regalia" slightly under-translates but is defensible. (4) "the calabash tree that to this day is called 'the head of Hunhunahpu'" is a fair rendering of "are curi zima cohcha chire va camic vholom hun hunahpu chuqhaxic". None of these are wrong-section or Spanish-only paraphrase problems.
review.resemblance_note: Distinct wording from Tedlock (Neck Canyon, Dark House/Rattling House), Christenson (Shivering House), Recinos/Goetz-Morley (House of Gloom, House of Knives); no specific phrase-level match found.

title: Ixkik' and the calabash tree

paragraphs: Here now is told the story of a maiden, daughter of a lord named Cuchumaquic. Now when this maiden — Xkik' was her name — daughter of the lord called Cuchumaquic, heard tell of the fruit of the tree, as it was spoken of by her father, she marveled at what she heard and said: "Why should I not go and see this tree that is spoken of? Truly its fruit is said to be sweet, so I hear." Then she went, alone, and she came to the foot of the tree that stood planted at Pucbal Chah. "What is this — the fruit of this tree? Is it not wonderful how it bears fruit?" she said. "Shall I die, shall I be lost, if I pick one?" said the maiden. Then the skull that was there among the branches of the tree spoke. "What is it you desire of it? These are only bones, round things caught among the branches of the tree," said the head of Hun Hunahpu. review.issues: Minor: "guardians of the sky" for "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel" is an uncertain construal (could mean "the guides returned down again"), but the translator flags this as provisional; the "three fingers" passage leans on Ximénez's Spanish, justifiably, since the K'iche' is garbled there, and this too is disclosed. review.resemblance_note: Phrasing does not match Tedlock (Blood Moon/One Death), Christenson (Lady Blood), or Recinos/Goetz-Morley in word choice or rhythm; name spellings follow the manuscript orthography, and distinctive renderings ("question her mouth", "round things caught among the branches") appear freshly composed.

title: Ixkik' brought before Xmukane

paragraphs: Now the mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen was still there when the woman named Xkik' arrived. When this woman Xkik' came to the mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, she was already carrying within her belly - it lacked only a little for Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, as they were called, to be born. And when the woman came before the grandmother, the woman said to the grandmother: "I have come, my lady, I am your daughter-in-law, I am your child." So she said when she entered before the grandmother. "Where do you come from? Are my sons perhaps still living? Did they not die there in Xibalba - the two who are left as a sign and a memory, called Hun Batz, Hun Chowen? If you see it, get out of here!" the grandmother said to the girl. "Even so, it is true what I say: I am your daughter-in-law, I have belonged already to Hun Hunahpu. What I carry is alive, they are not dead, Hun Hunahpu and Vukub Hunahpu - what they did is now plainly to be seen, my lady. So you shall see their faces revealed in what I carry," was said to the grandmother. But then Hun Batz and Hun Chowen only played the flute and sang, only painted and carved all day long, and they were the comfort of the grandmother's heart. And she said: "I do not want you as my daughter-in-law, for what is in your belly is only from your fornication. You are a deceiver - my sons are dead already, of whom you speak." And again the grandmother said: "This truly is what I tell you: since you say you are my daughter-in-law, go and bring back food, so that I may feed those I must feed, before one day is out." "Very well," said the girl.

translation.translator_note: The Spanish gloss softens or paraphrases a few K'iche' idioms; I followed the K'iche' throughout. Xmukane's rebuke "xa ahoxbal ri qo chapam" (lit. "only [the fruit] of fornication is what is in [your belly]") matches Ximénez's "es de fornicio eso que tienes en tu vientre" closely, so no real divergence there. The line "xere la quiꜩih vi chi in alibla" ("only this is true, that I am your daughter-in-law") I rendered slightly more literally than Ximénez's freer Spanish. The maize-guardian names Xtoj, Kanil, Kakaw (and a fourth, partly illegible term rendered "Ix" in Ximénez, possibly Ixtoj or similar) are left untranslated as proper names, per the source orthography "xtoh, xcanil, xcacau."</translator_note>

review.issues: Right section confirmed. Overall the English tracks the K'iche' well (arrival speech, "in alibla / in alcual la" = daughter-in-law and child; "in macol, in qazbol" = "sinner/wretched that I am"; the silk-of-the-ear miracle; animals carrying the net; the grandmother's proof speech; the closing formula). Two genuine fidelity problems: (1) The K'iche' "are cut que cacat ri hun baꜩ hun chouen" — supported by Ximénez's explicit "y entonces por esto se enojaron hun baꜩ y hun chouen" (they became angry) — is dropped entirely; the translation instead renders the passage as mere description ("But then Hun Batz and Hun Chowen only played the flute and sang..."), losing the brothers' anger at Ixkik', a narratively significant detail attested in both source columns. (2) In the grandmother's food-fetching command, the K'iche' "hacama ... hun chinima cat chipetic" (go harvest — one great netful must come; Ximénez: "anda tapizca una gran red") is replaced by the invented phrase "before one day is out," and the "one great netful" demand disappears — which also breaks coherence with the girl's later lament about "the net of food that is asked of me." The translator note is largely accurate, though its claim about a fourth guardian name ("Ix... partly illegible") over-reads "ix pu ꜩiya" slightly. No evidence of merely paraphrasing the Spanish — divergences show independent engagement with the K'iche'.
review.resemblance_note: Phrasing does not match Recinos, Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson. title: Birth of Junajpu and Xb'alanke

paragraphs: This, then, is what we shall tell of their birth. When the time for the birth had come, they were born of the maiden named Xkik'. But the grandmother did not see them when they were born. At once the two who were born stood up together — Junajpu and Xb'alanke were their names. There in the mountains they stood up, then they went into the house, but they did not sleep. The old woman said, "They cry too much, go throw them out," and so they were put on an anthill. There they slept sweetly. Then they were taken out from there and put again on top of thorns, for this was what Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen wanted — that they should die there on the anthill and there on the thorns — out of their envy, for Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen resented that they should be received in the house, though they were their own brothers, yet they did not acknowledge them.

So they were raised in the mountains, and thus they became great flute-players and singers, the two of them, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. And having grown up amid great affliction and suffering, they became very wise, and also flute-players, singers, painters, and carvers — everything was accomplished by them. Truly they knew of their birth, for they were wise ones, the substitutes of their fathers who had gone to Xib'alb'a, dead were their fathers. Great sages were Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, understanding all things in their hearts; they knew, once they had grown, of their own achievement, yet nothing of this was shown by them to their brothers, on account of their envy — it was rather in their hearts that the grudge was kept, and it was not through any deed that they had been wronged by Junajpu and Xb'alanke.

The two of them did nothing all day but shoot with the blowgun, and they were not loved by their grandmother, nor by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. They were not given food; only after the meal was already finished, when Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen had come in, only then — but they did not get angry, nor did they rage; they only endured it in silence, though they knew well who they were, for it was clear to them as daylight. And they used to bring their birds when they came each day, and Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen ate them, and nothing at all was given to the two, Junajpu and Xb'alanke — they only kept on playing the flute and singing, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen.

Then one day Junajpu and Xb'alanke came back without bringing any birds at all, and when they entered, the grandmother grew angry and said to them, "Why do you bring no birds?" Then it was said by Junajpu and Xb'alanke, "Grandmother, it is that our birds have gotten stuck up in the tree, and we cannot climb up after them upon the trunk. Lady, let our older brothers come with us, let them go bring the birds down." And it was said to them, "Very well, we will go with you tomorrow morning," this is what their older brothers said, when they had already been defeated and overcome — for the two of them had planned together how to defeat Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen: "We will only turn them into something else — their very bodies — for it is right, on account of the great grief and suffering they have caused us; we were as good as killed, as good as lost — this is what our brothers wanted. Only as boys have we been thought of by them, in their understanding, and so we shall defeat them, though we shall only make a sign of it," this is what they said to one another.

So then they went beneath a tree called Kante, and their older brothers went along with them, and they began to shoot with their blowguns, but it did not go well against the birds up in the tree, which kept crying out. Their older brothers were amazed to see so many birds, with not one of them falling down. "Our birds do not fall — go climb up and bring them down," they said to their older brothers. "Very well," they said, and then they climbed up onto the tree, and the trunk grew thick and swollen, and when they wanted to come back down, they could no longer get down off the tree. Then Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen called down from the tree, "What has happened to us, brothers? Have pity on us, this tree frightens us, brothers," they said from up in the tree. Then Junajpu and Xb'alanke said to them, "Untie your loincloths and belts, tie them beneath your bellies with the long end trailing behind, and then you will be able to move and come down easily," this is what was said to them by their younger brothers.

"Very well," they said, and as soon as they pulled out the trailing end of their belts, at once they were turned into tails, and they became monkeys. Then they went off over the tops of the trees, over the small hills and the great hills, they went into the wild places, hooting, swinging themselves along, dangling from the branches. Thus was the defeat of Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen brought about by Junajpu and Xb'alanke — it was only through their own hidden power that they did it.

When they arrived back home, they said, on arriving to their grandmother and their mother, "What can have happened to our older brothers? Their faces have turned green, they have gone off looking like animals," they said. "If you have done something to your older brothers, if you have destroyed me and brought me to misery, do not do such a thing to your brothers," the grandmother said to Junajpu and Xb'alanke. Then they said to their grandmother, "Do not grieve, grandmother — our older brothers will come back, their faces will be seen again, only this depends upon you now, that you must not laugh, try your luck," they said. Then they began to play music, they played the song of Jun Ajpu Kʼoy, they sang.

Then they played the flutes and sang and drummed, taking up their flutes and their drum, and they seated their grandmother beside them, and when they played, when they sang, calling out Jun Ajpu Kʼoy by name, in they came, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, dancing, when they arrived. But then the grandmother saw their ugly faces, and when she saw them she laughed — she could not hold back her laughter. Only for an instant did they come, and no more did she see their faces, for they ran off into the wild places. "Why have you done this, lady? Only four times we will try, only three more times now shall we call them, with the flute and with the song — hold back your laughter, try again," they were told, Junajpu and Xb'alanke, and then they played the flute once more.

In they came again, dancing, and they came right to the middle of the house, doing their monkey antics, provoking laughter from the grandmother, until the grandmother laughed outright, seeing their faces, their monkey rumps, their thin bellies, and the twisting of their tails, and their bellies too, as they came in. That was when the grandmother laughed at them so hard, and then off they went again to the mountains. "What shall we do, grandmother? Only this third time we will try again," said Junajpu and Xb'alanke. They played once more, they came in again, dancing.

The grandmother only barely held back her laughter, and they climbed up right by the roof beam of the wall, red were their eyes, their snouts thrust out, and they rubbed at their faces, and when the grandmother saw these figures, she burst out laughing loudly, and never again did they see their faces on account of the grandmother's laughter. "Only this one more time we shall call them," and the fourth time they did not come at all. Then at once they went off to the mountains, and they said to the grandmother, "We have already tried, grandmother — they did not come the first time, and now they will not come again when called. Do not grieve — here we are, your grandchildren; we love you and our mother too, we who remain in memory, in the place of our older brothers, called Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen," they said to the grandmother and to their mother, said Junajpu and Xb'alanke.

And they were invoked by the flute-players and the singers, the ancient people, and by those besides — the painters and the carvers of old — they invoked them. They were turned into brutish monkeys because they had exalted themselves and had mistreated their younger brothers, holding them as if they were slaves; and thus they were effaced, when Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen were lost, turned into monkeys. And because they had always stayed at home, and had been flute-players and singers, they did great things while they lived there with their mother and grandmother.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' passage describing the trick's set-up ("xa chiquih xcah vi v yoc qui qux... xepoizaxic cumal") is compressed and somewhat obscure; I follow the sense given by Ximénez's Spanish ("solo por milagro hicieron esto") that the transformation was accomplished by hidden/supernatural means on the younger brothers' part, rendered here as "their own hidden power." The name "hun ahpu coy" (Jun Ajpu K'oy, "Jun Ajpu Monkey") is treated as the name/refrain of the summoning song, following the Spanish gloss "el son de hun ahpu mico." Where the K'iche' at points is elliptical about which brother speaks or acts, I have followed the clearer narrative sequence supplied by the Spanish without altering the underlying K'iche' sense.

review.issues: Minor: "their very bodies" generalizes K'iche' "e upam" / Spanish "sus barrigas" (bellies); "brutish monkeys" imports Ximénez's "brutos micos" where the K'iche' has "became animals, became monkeys"; the translator's note misattaches its "hidden power"/naual justification to the wrong K'iche' phrase (the rendering itself correctly reflects "xa rumal qui naual"). The paragraph-2 subject confusion (mountain-raised twins vs. flute-playing elder brothers) faithfully reproduces an incoherence present in both the K'iche' and Ximénez.
review.resemblance_note: Name forms are project-standard modern orthography; phrasing follows the manuscript/Ximénez, not Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley.

title: The younger twins as hunters

paragraphs: Then they began their work, to show themselves before their grandmother and their mother. First they set about making a milpa. "We will sow a milpa," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "Do not grieve; here we are, your grandsons, we are the substitutes for our older brothers." So said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then they took up their axes and their hoes, and went off with their blowguns on their shoulders. As they left their house they charged their grandmother to bring their food to them at midday. "Very well, grandsons," said the grandmother.

And when they arrived there where the milpa was, they merely thrust the hoe into the earth, and it worked the earth by itself; they merely thrust the axe into the wood, and it cut by itself. All the trees came falling, all the vines came cut, and it was very much that fell, the small hills and the great hills going down. And with a single stroke of the axe, a single thrust of the hoe, it was beyond counting how much had been done - not a small hill only, a great hill went down as well.

Then they charged a certain animal, called Xmucur - the mountain dove - and set it up on top of a great tree stump. Hunahpu and Xbalanque said to it: "Watch for our grandmother, when she comes bringing our food; the moment you see her coming, call out at once, and then we will take up the hoe and the axe." "Very well," said the dove.

But in truth they did nothing but shoot with their blowguns; they were not truly making the milpa. Then the dove called out, and at once they came running - one seized the hoe, the other the axe; they bound up their heads and smeared dirt on their faces as if truly working the milpa, and the one smeared splinters on his head as if truly a woodcutter, so as to be seen thus by their grandmother. Then they went to their house, saying, "Truly we are tired, grandmother," and, arriving at their house, they stretched out their hands and feet before their grandmother as if truly worn from their labor - though it was false, they were not truly making the milpa.

Then on the second day they went again, and arriving at the milpa they found all the trees standing again, all the vines joined together once more, as if it had never been worked. "Who has done this, deceiving us?" they said. Surely it was done by all the animals, small and great: puma, deer, rabbit, fox, coyote, small birds and great birds - these did it in a single night. So then they began again to make the milpa.

It was the same with the earth and the vines. When their hearts grew weary of it, they hid themselves there in the milpa, concealed among the vines, so that none of the animals could see them, in order to find out who was doing this. All the animals gathered together, small and great, in one place they all assembled. And at the very hour of midnight they came, and as they came they were all speaking, saying: "Rise up, tree; rise up, vine!" - so they said as they came, drawing near and stirring beneath the trees and vines, showing themselves before the boys.

First was the puma, wanting to seize them, but it did not succeed. Then came the deer and the rabbit likewise, but only their tails were caught - they seized the tail of the deer and the tail of the rabbit, and that is why their tails are short to this day. The fox, the coyote, the wild pig, and the squirrel did not yield either; all the animals passed before Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and their hearts burned with anger because they had caught none of them.

Then at last came one more, hopping - and this one they cut off and caught in a net: the mouse. And once they had caught it, they squeezed its head, wanting to choke it, and they burned its tail in the fire - that is why the mouse's tail has no hair to this day, and its eyes bulge as they do, from when the boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, wanted to kill it. "Do not kill me," said the mouse, "it is not your true work to make a milpa." "What is it, then, that you have to tell us?" said the boys to the mouse. "Let me be a little, for I have something in my belly to say, and I will say it afterward - give me something to eat first," said the mouse. "Afterward we will give you your food; speak now," it was told. "Very well," said the mouse.

"Know that the possessions of your fathers, Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, as they were called, those who died in Xibalba - there remains, hanging up above on the rafters, their gear, with which they used to play: the yoke, the ring, and the rubber ball. And your grandmother has not shown it to you, because it was on account of these that your fathers died." The boys said, "Do you truly know this?" And they rejoiced greatly in their hearts when they heard the news of the rubber ball. And once the mouse had spoken, they granted the mouse its food.

"This shall be your food: maize, chile seeds, beans, cacao - this is yours, and if there is anything stored away, forgotten, that too is yours, eat it," so the mouse was told by Hunahpu and Xbalanque. "Very well, boys - but if my grandmother sees me, what will you say?" said the mouse. "Do not be troubled, for we are here, and we will settle what is to be told our grandmother. Come now, we will put you in the corner of the house; when you arrive, go straight up to where it hangs, and there we will find the chile ground for our meal, and we will see" - so they said to the mouse. Then they made ready for the night, and Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel, and they came to the midday hour.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' near the end (concerning the mouse's tail and eyes) is compressed and somewhat garbled in the manuscript; I followed Ximénez's Spanish gloss closely there to resolve the syntax, since the K'iche' itself is elliptical at that point ("mahabi rizmal uhe... ta xrah bÿc cumal qaholab"). The final sentence of the K'iche' ("xeqhacuri qaholab chire cho... xu qhax curicho... vꜩbala ixqaholab... xahu zu cacaya acanoc xiquin ha...") is difficult and repetitive, mixing direct speech about hiding the mouse in the corner of the house with further instructions; I have rendered the sense as best determinable rather than translating word-for-word, since a literal rendering would be unintelligible in English. The animal name "vtiu ae" is uncertain - rendered here as "coyote," following the general sense of a wild canine in this list of forest animals, though the exact identification is not certain from the text alone.

review.issues: Right section and mostly accurate, but: (1) omits a passage present in both K'iche' and Spanish — the twins' report to their grandmother after the second day ("cohmichouic ixcatit... xchicavarah" / "que le pareçe abuela... bolberemos otra vez, y velaremos") and their stated plan to keep watch, compressed to "they hid themselves"; also drops "in vain their food was brought." (2) "if my grandmother sees me" should be "your grandmother" (ivatit/vuestra abuela). (3) "coh balam" (puma AND jaguar) collapsed to "puma" alone; "ziz" (coati/pizote) mistranslated "squirrel." (4) Minor: dirt on hands (pu cab/las manos) rendered "faces." Reliance on Ximénez for the garbled mouse-tail/ending passages is justified and disclosed.
review.resemblance_note: No specific lexical/rhythmic match to Recinos, Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson; surface similarities (e.g. "substitutes") trace to literal rendering of Ximénez's Spanish, which those translations also descend from.

final.translator_note: Revised per review: restored the twins' report to their grandmother after the second day and their stated plan to keep watch (K'iche' "apa chinac cohmichouic... mavi vꜩ caban chique," paralleled by Ximénez's "que le pareçe abuela... bolberemos otra vez, y velaremos"), and restored "in vain/for nothing their food was brought" (mixohcoꜩic, cf. "en valde les lleuaron de comer"). Corrected "my grandmother" to "your grandmother" (ivatit/vuestra abuela) in the mouse's speech. "Coh balam" is two animals, puma and jaguar (coh = puma/mountain lion, balam = jaguar), not "puma" alone; "ziz" is the coati (pízote), not squirrel, corrected in both occurrences. Corrected "dirt on their faces" to "dirt on their hands" (pu cab / las manos); the K'iche' does mention the dirtied face via the splinters/soot detail for the axe-bearer, which is kept. "Vtiu ae" remains uncertain - Ximénez glosses it "el lobo" (wolf), but no wolves are native to the region, so "coyote" is used as the general sense of a wild canine, consistent with my earlier note; this identification is not certain from the text alone. The garbled mouse-tail/mouse-ending passages and the final paragraph continue to follow Ximénez's Spanish gloss closely where the K'iche' itself is elliptical or repetitive, as disclosed previously; these portions are rendered for sense rather than word-for-word, since a literal rendering would be unintelligible in English.

title: Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen transformed

paragraphs: They had brought the rat in hiding, and when they arrived one went straight into the house and the other to the corner, and at once they lifted the rat up high and set it there. Then they asked their grandmother for their food. "Grind our food, we want chilmol, grandmother," they said. So her chile was ground, and a bowl of broth was set before them—but this was only to deceive the old woman and their mother. And they used up all the water in the water jar, and said, "We are dying of thirst, go and bring water," they said to their grandmother. "Very well," she said, and she went off for the water. Meanwhile they sat as if eating, but in truth they had no appetite—it was only a pretense, what they did. And then they saw the rat there in the chile, for the rat had gotten loose in the chile that hung on the rack; there they saw it, in the chile-pot. So they sent out a small creature called xan, which is like a mosquito, and it went to the water and bored a hole in the old woman's water jar, and the water ran out of the jar. She tried and tried, but the hole in the jar would not close. "What is our grandmother doing," they said, "we are parched with thirst—go and see, lady," and they sent her off again. Then the rat gnawed through the cord and cut down the rubber ball, the bat, and the glove that hung there, where they had been kept out of sight. And they fell, and the boys snatched them up and went and hid them on the road, on the way to the ballcourt. Then they went to their grandmother, and their grandmother and their mother were still there, each one working to close the hole in the jar. And arriving, each with his blowgun: "What have you done about the water? We have grown tired of waiting, and so we came ourselves." "Look at my jar," said the old woman, "it will not close its hole." So at once they closed it, and all together they went back, the boys walking ahead of their grandmother. And so it was that the rubber ball was found.

And greatly pleased, they went off to play ball at the ballcourt, and it was far off, where they went to play, the two of them alone. And they swept and cleared the ballcourt of their fathers. And the lords of Xibalba heard it, and said: "Who are these who have again begun to play above us, showing us no respect, making this noise? Did not Hun-Hunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu die, who wished to make themselves great in our presence? Go and call them at once," said Hun Came and Vucub Came again, and all the lords, and they summoned their messengers. And they said to them: "Go and tell them, say the lords, come here, they will play with us; in seven days from now let them be here, and we will play"—this was said to the messengers. And they set out on a broad road, one of the many roads that led straight to the boys' house, and they came straight to where the grandmother was; and she was washing when the messengers of Xibalba arrived. And they said: "The lords say the boys are to come to Xibalba, and this term of seven days is given them, in which they are expected"—this was said to Xmucane.

"Very well," she said, "they shall go there, they shall go there, lord messengers." And the messengers went off and returned, and the old woman grew afflicted: "How shall I send word to call them, my grandsons? What shall I say concerning their being summoned? It was truly just like this that the messengers came, long ago, when they came for their fathers," said the old woman, and very sorrowfully she went alone into her house. Then a louse fell down, and the old woman caught it and set it on her hand, and the louse stirred and began to walk. And she said to it: "My grandson, will you go, if I send you, to call my grandsons at the ballcourt?"—this was said to the louse. "Go and tell them: says your grandmother, thus have the messengers of Xibalba come to me, to call you, and within seven days you must go; this is what your grandmother says"—this was said to the louse, and then the louse went off, stirring along. Now there was a boy sitting on the road, called Tamazul, who was a toad, and the toad said to the louse: "Where are you going?" And the louse said: "I am going to the boys, and I carry the message in my belly." "Very well," said the toad, "but I see you cannot run—do you want me to swallow you? Then you could travel. Watch how I run; we shall arrive all the sooner." "Very well," said the louse to the toad, and then the toad swallowed the louse. And the toad went along running, but grew tired and could run no longer, when he met a great snake called Zaquicaz, and it said: "Where are you going, Tamazul boy?"—this was said to Tamazul by Zaquicaz. And the toad said: "I am a messenger, I carry the message in my belly." And the snake said: "I see you go tired and cannot run—shall I not arrive sooner? Come here, I will swallow you," said the snake to the toad, and then the snake Zaquicaz swallowed the toad. And the snake took this as its food, eating the toads as it went along running, when it was met by a bird called Vac, and the bird Vac swallowed the snake, and then it arrived over the ballcourt. And so this bird took its own sustenance in eating the snakes of the mountains, and the Vac came and perched on the wall of the ballcourt. And Hunahpu and Xbalanque were there, enjoying themselves at play, and when the Vac arrived it called out, "Vac-co, vac-co," so went its cry. "What is this cry?" they said. "Bring the blowguns." And then, shooting at the Vac, the pellet flew straight and struck it in the pupil of the eye, and it fell tumbling, and they caught it and asked it: "What have you come for?"—this was said to the Vac. And it said: "I carry a message in my belly. Heal my eye first, and then I will tell it." "Very well," they said, and taking a little of the rubber from the ballgame, they set it upon the eye of the Vac. And it is called lotz quic, and at once it healed the bird's eye, and it saw well again once it was cured. And they said to it: "Now tell what you bring," and then it vomited up a great snake. And they said to the snake: "Now tell at once what you bring," this was said to the snake, and it said, "Very well," and then it vomited up the toad. And it was said to the toad: "What is your message? Tell it now," and it said: "Here in my belly I carry the message," and then it tried to vomit, but could not; only slime came to its mouth. It tried again and could not, and the boys wished to beat it, and said: "You are a liar and a cheat," and they kicked it, and it tried once more, and still only spittle came to its mouth. Then the boys opened the toad's mouth and pried it apart, and searched within, and found the louse stuck fast in the toad's teeth—for it had lodged there in its mouth, and the toad had not truly swallowed it, and so it only pretends to vomit. And for this it was despised, and it has no food assigned to it, nor was any ever given it, and it does not run, but is food for the snakes. "Now speak," they said to the louse, and then it gave its message: "Says your grandmother, boys: go and call them, for messengers have come from Xibalba, from Hun Came and Vucub Came, saying that in seven days they must go there; come here, we shall play ball, they say, and let them bring the instruments of the game, the rubber ball, the bat, the paddle, and the glove, so that they may entertain us—so say the lords. This says your grandmother; thus the message of the lords has come, and thus I have come to call you." "Yes, so it must be," they said in their hearts, hearing the message. And then at once they set out and came to their grandmother, but they went only to tell her, and then went off.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' orthography here is dense and eroded in places (e.g. the passage around "conohel ahauab xetaca vloc" and the toad/snake/bird chain), so I worked primarily by matching the K'iche' clause-by-clause against Ximénez's Spanish, which runs closely parallel throughout this stretch — no significant divergence in sense was found, only the ordinary compression typical of his gloss (e.g. he adds a parenthetical gloss on "lotz quic" as a plant-resin term, and calls the snake's food "sapos" (toads) plural where the K'iche' seems to use a singular referent — I kept the K'iche' sense, "toads" as generic prey rather than a specific plural event). The names Tamazul (toad) and Zaquicaz (snake) are left transliterated as in the source, per convention for proper names.

review.issues: Minor: (1) first equipment list gives three items (ball, bat, glove), following Ximénez's three-item list, where the K'iche' "quic ... bate pachcab q'uum" appears to name four; the later list correctly has four. (2) "they kicked it" softens the specific "kicked its rump" (v varachac chi acan). (3) "go and see, lady" / "sent her off again" slightly blurs that the mother (not the grandmother again) is sent, per Ximénez "dixeron a su Madre". None affect overall fidelity; translator's note honestly documents reliance on the Spanish where the K'iche' is eroded, and spot checks show genuine K'iche' engagement.
review.resemblance_note: Sense-level parallels to Recinos/Goetz & Morley are expected since both derive from Ximénez, but no distinctive matching word choice, order, or rhythm found; renderings like "stirring along" and "parched with thirst" diverge from known versions.

final.translator_note: The K'iche' orthography here is dense and eroded in places (e.g. the passage around "conohel ahauab xetaca vloc" and the toad/snake/bird chain), so I worked primarily by matching the K'iche' clause-by-clause against Ximénez's Spanish, which runs closely parallel throughout this stretch — no significant divergence in sense was found, only the ordinary compression typical of his gloss (e.g. he adds a parenthetical gloss on "lotz quic" as a plant-resin term, and calls the snake's food "sapos" (toads) plural where the K'iche' seems to use a singular referent — I kept the K'iche' sense, "toads" as generic prey rather than a specific plural event). The names Tamazul (toad) and Zaquicaz (snake) are left transliterated as in the source, per convention for proper names.

title: The ballgame equipment recovered; renewed summons to Xibalba

paragraphs: "We are going now, grandmother. We came only to tell you this, and here we leave you a sign of our word: each of us will plant a cane of maize in the middle of our house, and this will be the sign of our death. If it dries up, you will say, 'They have died' — that will be when they die. But if it sprouts green again, you will say, 'They are alive.' You, grandmother, and you, mother, do not weep — a sign of our word remains with you," they said.

And when they went, Hunahpu planted one cane, and Xbalanque planted the other. They planted them in the house, not on the mountain, nor in wet ground, but in dry ground, in the middle of their own house, they left them planted.
Then each of them set off, carrying his blowgun. Quickly they went down, they descended by the stairway, going down.

And within a ravine they crossed — between the birds they passed, birds that were called Molay — and they also crossed a river of pus and a river of blood, a trap by which Xibalba meant, in its heart, to defeat them. But they were not defeated: only by way of their blowguns did they cross.
They came out then at a crossroads of four roads, and indeed they knew the roads of Xibalba: a black road, a white road, a red road, and a green road.

There they sent out a creature called Xan, the biter. They sent it to bite each one in turn — first to bite the one seated first — to go biting them all, one after another, and afterward it would be Xan's own to suck the blood of men along the roads, and this would be its food. This is what the boys told Xan.
"Very well," said Xan, and it went onto the black road, straight to the wooden dummies seated first in the seats. It bit the first; no one answered. It bit the second; no one answered.

It bit the third seated one, who was Hun Came — "Ay!" he cried out when bitten. "What is it, Hun Came?" asked the fourth, seated beside him. "Who has bitten you?" "I do not know what has bitten me," he said. Then it bit the fourth. "Ay! What is it, Vucub Came? What has bitten you?" asked the fifth. It bit the fifth. "Ay, ay!" cried Xiquiripat. "What has bitten you?" he was asked. It bit the sixth. "Ay! What is it, Cuchumaquic? What has bitten you?" And so it went, biting each in turn and each crying out and being questioned by the next — Ahalpuh, Ahalcana, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, Quicxic, Patan, Quicre, and Quic Rixcac — until it had bitten all fourteen seated there, and not one failed to cry out and be asked, and in answering they named themselves and one another, until the names of all of them were known, down to the one seated last at the end, and no single name was missed. For it was not truly a gnat that bit them all — it was a hair from the face of the boy, turned into an insect, sent to learn all their names for Xbalanque.

Then they went on and arrived at last where the lords were seated. "Go greet the lord," said an attendant of the seated figure — but it was no lord, only a wooden dummy, they were told when they came near. Then, greeting them one by one, they said: "Hail, Hun Came! Hail, Vucub Came! Hail, Xiquiripat! Hail, Cuchumaquic! Hail, Ahalpuh! Hail, Ahalcana! Hail, Chamiabac! Hail, Chamiaholom! Hail, Quicxic! Hail, Patan! Hail, Quicre! Hail, Quic Rixcac!" they said. When they arrived they showed the faces and spoke the names of every one of them, and not a single name was lost. This was the very thing the lords had laughed about — that no one who came should ever learn their names.

Then they were told to sit on the bench, but they would not, for that bench was no true seat — it was only a hot stone made to look like a bench, meant to deceive them so that they would be defeated. "That is only a stone," said the boys, and so they were not defeated by it.

Then they were sent into the Dark House, but they were not defeated there either. This was the first trial they entered, the one by which Xibalba thought at last to begin their defeat, when they first entered the Dark House.

Then their pine torch was brought to them, already burning, and with it a cigar for each, sent by the messenger of Hun Came. "Here is your torch," says the lord, "and these cigars — you must return them at dawn, whole, still burning as they were given," said the messenger when he arrived.

"Very well," they said. But they did not truly light the torch — they set in its place something red that only looked like fire, the tail feathers of the macaw, which the guards took for flame; and in the cigars they put fireflies, glowing insects, so that all night it seemed they burned. "They have already been defeated," said the guards, thinking so. But nothing of the torch was truly consumed, and likewise nothing of the cigars.

And at dawn the torch and the cigars, still whole, were brought before the lords. "What are these? Where have they come from? Who begot them, who bore them? Truly our hearts burn, for what they do to us is no good thing. Their faces are strange, and stranger still their ways," they said among themselves.

Then all the lords sent for them: "Come, play ball, boys," they were told. And Hun Came and Vucub Came questioned them: "Where have you come from? Tell us, boys." And they said, "Truly, we do not know where we come from," and they would not say. "Very well," said the Lords of Xibalba. "Come then, let us play ball, boys."

"Where shall we throw this our ball?" said the Lords of Xibalba. "By no means shall that one of yours be used," said the boys. "No, none other but ours," said the lords. "Very well," said the boys. "Let it be this creature, called Chil," said the Lords of Xibalba. "No," said the boys, "rather a skull." "Not that," said the lords. "Very well," said Hunahpu — and then the Lords of Xibalba threw the ball straight at the bat, and seeing how sharply it struck and sprang off the paddle, it went bounding away over the ground.

"What is this?" they said. "You only seek our death! Was it not you who sent for us? Were these not your own messengers? Poor us — we will go away again," the boys said to them. This was what the boys wanted of them — to be finished quickly in the ballgame — but they were not defeated; rather it was Xibalba that was defeated again by the boys.
"Do not go, boys — let us play, we will use this our ball," the boys were told. "Very well," they said, and they threw the ball, and the game was ended.

Then the Lords of Xibalba said, "What shall we play for?" "Only bring us four bowls of flowers," said the boys. "Very well — what flowers?" said the lords. "We want," they said, "Cacamuchi flowers, and white Muchit flowers, and yellow Muchit flowers, and also the great flowers." "Very well," said the boys.

Then they went down into a house where there was nothing but obsidian knives, all alike, all sharp, and countless. And the lords' hearts were glad when they set the boys among the knives to be cut down and defeated. The Lords of Xibalba rejoiced: "Good, already we have won, already we have defeated them," they said. "Where now will they find the flowers?" they said in their hearts.

"This very night the flowers must be ready and cut for us," they said, and Hunahpu and Xbalanque were told by Xibalba: "Very well, then, tonight it must be finished," they said, and thus they bound themselves by agreement. Then the boys entered the House of Knives, their second trial, where it was meant that they should be sliced apart by the blades at once, so that they would die instantly. But they did not die. They spoke instead to the knives: "Yours shall be all the flesh of the animals," they told the knives, "but do not stir yourselves anymore — be still, all of you together." And there they stayed in the House of Knives until it dawned.

There, too, they called on all the ants: "Cutting-ants, leaf-ants, come here, come, all of you, go and bring every kind of flower the lords have wagered," said the boys. "Very well," said the ants, and they went, all of them, to gather the flowers from the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came. But the keepers of the flowers had already been warned: "Watch well over the flowers — do not let them be stolen, for already we have defeated the boys, and from where could flowers come to defeat us? Do not sleep this whole night," the guards were told. "Very well," said the guards. But the guards of the garden felt nothing, and only cried out uselessly among the branches of the trees. And from this came their calls: one cried Xpurpuvec, Xpurpuvec, when it lit upon the hill, again upon the hill; the other, when it lit, cried Puhuyu, Puhuyu — and so these were named, the two guards of the flowers of Hun Came and Vucub Came. And they did not feel the ants stealing in, gnawing, cutting all the flowers, carrying them off from underneath, from the very roots, biting them free with their jaws — the guards knowing nothing, only crying out — and the ants cut the flowers and bore them away, quickly, cutting and carrying, until soon the four bowls were filled and heaped with flowers, just as it grew light.

Then the messengers came, sent, saying: "Come, the lord says — quickly bring what you have won," the boys were told. "Very well," they said, and they gathered up the four bowls of flowers, and went and stood before the lords, and fragrant and lovely were the flowers they brought — and by this Xibalba was defeated. It was only the ants the boys had sent, and in a single night the ants had gathered the flowers and set them in the bowls.

So all the Lords of Xibalba went pale, their faces went white, because of the flowers. Then they sent for the guards of the flowers: "Why did you let our flowers be stolen? Here are the very flowers, we see them," the guards were told. "We did not let it happen, lord — we do not know how," they said. Then their mouths were slit open, as their punishment for letting the flowers be stolen. Thus were Hun Came and Vucub Came defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque — this was the beginning of their undoing.

Their mouths were cut in that way — this is why the mouth of the Purpuvec and the mouth of the Puhuyu are slit as they are today. Then they played ball again, and it ended even, and again they bound themselves by agreement to play once more, at dawn. "Very well," said the boys, and so it was agreed.

title: The road to Xibalba and the first trial-houses

paragraphs: Then they entered the House of Cold. Unbearable was the cold that was in it, the ice that filled that House of Cold. But soon the cold was driven out, because of the boys; they did not die there, but were alive when it dawned. And this was what the lords of Xibalba wanted, to see them die there — but it did not happen so; rather they were well when it dawned. And the ones who had come to summon them were watching closely, and the guards went off, and the lord of Xibalba said, "What is this, that they have not died?" And they marveled again at the deeds of the boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then next they entered the House of Jaguars, packed full of jaguars. "Do not bite us — this is to be your food," they said to the jaguars, and bones were thrown before the beasts, and at once they fell to cracking the bones. "Good, now they have finished, now they have eaten them, now their bellies are content — these are the bones," so said all the guards, and they of Xibalba were glad over this, but the boys did not die. Just so, they came out well from the House of Jaguars too, and the lords of Xibalba said, "What sort of people are you? Where have you come from?" And so all of them said this.

Then next they entered the House of Fire, all fire within it, but they were not burned by the fire — rather they were handsome and well when it dawned. And this too was what the lords wished, that they should die there inside the fire — yet they overcame this as well, and so it was not as the heart of Xibalba desired.

Then they entered the House of Bats — nothing inside but bats, a house of great man-killing bats, the way they slaughter is swift when it meets one's face. So they stayed inside there, but sleeping inside their blowguns, and they were not bitten by the bats. But one of them let himself be seen, called down by one great bat that had come from the sky, and it showed itself where it hung at the mouth of the blowgun — this it did so that they might take counsel over it. All through the night one, Hunahpu, spoke thinking of it, watching for the dawn, watching if it would show itself, was it visible yet — but that was not what they said; rather the bats went on beating their wings, quiliz, quiliz, they cried, quiliz they cried all through the night.

Then it grew quiet a little, and the bats no longer stirred, staying still at the very end of the blowgun. And then Xbalanque said to Hunahpu, "Has it grown light on your side? Look, watch, is it perhaps growing light?" But they said nothing to it, only that. And so Hunahpu himself put his head out at the mouth of the blowgun, wanting to see if it had grown light, and at once his head was cut off by Camazotz, and only his body was left behind. "It has not yet grown light!" so it was said, so that not one of them stirred. Just so it appeared that Hunahpu was gone; just so it seemed that his head was no longer to be found there, only his headless body still moving.

And then Xbalanque said, "Ah, disaster, it is already done!" So he said, and there they went to set up his head at the ball court, at the command of Hun Came and Vucub Came, and all of Xibalba rejoiced over the head of Hunahpu.

Then the lord called all the animals — the coati, the peccary, all the small animals, the great animals — throughout the night and into the morning, and said to them, "I have called you here to give each of you your food," so he told them. "Take your food," they were told. review.issues: Right section confirmed: the translation tracks the extracted K'iche' (House of Cold/teuh ha, House of Jaguars/balami ha, House of Fire, House of Bats/zotzi ha, Camazotz beheading Hunahpu, head set on the ball court, animal-feeding and turtle-head episode, dawn-darkening etiology, rabbit instruction) in order and detail. Main fidelity flag: the "vulture" passage. The K'iche' reads "vuch" (and "caxaquin vvch"), which is the opossum, not the vulture; the translator followed Ximénez's Spanish "zopílote" (vulture) and even the translator note calls "vuch" a vulture. This is a lexical error inherited from the Spanish rather than the K'iche', though defensible as following the primary-source gloss; the etiology ("the opossum makes streaks of light at dawn") is altered by it. Lesser points: (a) the metadata marks p34's K'iche' as missing, yet the extracted kiche_text does contain the animal-feeding/turtle passage, and the English matches that K'iche' closely (ziz=coati, aq=peccary, decay/grass/stones/earth foods, eyes carved, sages from the sky, Heart of Sky/Huracan), so reliance on Spanish there did not cause drift; (b) paragraph 5's dialogue attribution ("But they said nothing to it, only that") is muddled, but the manuscript itself is confused at that point; (c) a stray opening quotation mark before "So Xbalanque said to him" in p10 is a typo; (d) "hail" (zacbocom) is rendered "ice", matching Ximénez's "yelo" — minor. No invented content.
review.resemblance_note: Phrasing does not match Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson in word choice or rhythm; keeping the manuscript onomatopoeia "quiliz, quiliz" (Tedlock uses "eek, eek") and the vulture-for-opossum reading (modern translations say opossum) both point away from recall of a published English version.

title: Further trial-houses

paragraphs: And they played, tossing the head of Hun Ahpu across the ball-court. "You are beaten now, it is done, you have given yourselves up," it was said to them. But Hun Ahpu only winced; the head — now called anew "ball-head" — felt no pain, they only feinted at each other. Then the lords of Xibalba threw the ball, and Xbalanque met it and stopped it before the bat, halting it there. Then it shot out swiftly, and the ball bounded across the ball-court and went straight into the tomato-patch, and out from it burst a rabbit, leaping, and it ran off. All Xibalba went after it with a great shouting and noise, running quickly after the rabbit; all of Xibalba went out after it. Then the two took back the head of Hun Ahpu. Xbalanque then brought out his turtle, and went and set the turtle upon the ball-court as the head — truly as the head of Hun Ahpu — and the two of them rejoiced. Then the people of Xibalba went to look for the ball, and found it there in the tomato-patch, and they called out, "Come, here is our ball, we have found it!" "We have won," they said. Then the Xibalbans came back, not knowing what had been done, and they began the game again. Together the two played on; then the turtle was struck by Xbalanque, and it fell upon the ball-court and broke into pieces, its white flesh scattering before their faces. "Who is there to go for it — where is it?" said the people of Xibalba. Thus were the lords of Xibalba defeated by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. Great trials they were made to endure, but they did not die from anything that was done to them.

Now this is the record of the death of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque; this is the record of their death — we shall tell it now. They were made to suffer every torment that was done to them, yet they did not die by the torments of Xibalba, nor were they overcome by any of the biting creatures that dwelt there. Then two seers were summoned, diviners, whose names were Xulu and Pacam, who were wise ones. "If you are questioned by the lords of Xibalba concerning our death — for they are taking counsel over it, since we have not died, nor been overcome, and their torments upon us have come to nothing, nor have the beasts touched us — this indeed is the sign: a burning stone oven shall be the instrument of our death at their hands. All of Xibalba has agreed on it together, but truly we shall not die. Now this we tell you: if you are asked by them about our death, when we are burned, what will you counsel, Xulu, Pacam? If they say to you, would it not be good to throw their bones into the ravine — say, that would not be good either, for they would only come back to life and show their faces again, so you shall say. Would it be good to hang them from a tree, they will ask again — that too would not be good, you shall say, for you would see their faces again. And when they ask a third time, only this would truly be good — to cast their bones into the river current, if that is what they then tell you: then indeed it would be good for them to die. Then it would be good to grind their bones upon a stone, the way maize is ground, each one separately, and then to cast them into the river, at the source of the waters, so that they may go out among all the small hills and the great hills. So you shall say, when you carry out this charge we have given you," said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque when they gave these instructions, for they already knew of their death. Then a great burning stone oven was made, like a hearth; a great pit did Xibalba dig. Then messengers came, companions of the messengers of Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Come, young men, go and see it — thus says our lord, young men," they were told. "Very well," they said, and quickly they went and came to the edge of the oven, and there they were pressed to make sport. "Take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap, each one, young men," they were told by Hun Came. "Do not deceive us so — do you think we do not know of our own death, lords? Look," they said. Then they turned their faces to one another, they stretched out their two arms together, and face-down they went into the oven, and there both of them died. And all of Xibalba rejoiced, shouting aloud and whistling: "We have truly beaten them now — they did not even struggle," they said. Then Xulu and Pacam were summoned, to whom the word had been left, and they were indeed asked where the bones should go. And Xibalba ground them and took the bones and went to scatter them in the river current — but they did not go far; they only sank at once beneath the water, and were turned into two beautiful young men, and their same faces appeared again — thus they showed themselves once more.

translation.translator_note: Several passages are philologically difficult and I have leaned on Ximénez's Spanish to resolve them, while keeping the K'iche' word order and imagery as primary: "cachopih vae ri ca qui cahtacmul tah chica xicah" is obscure (Ximénez: "apretad este nuestro dulçe, quarto vezes volaremos"), rendered here as "take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap" — the exact sense of the taunt/drink-offer is uncertain. "eꜩanem" I take as "sport/game" (i.e., a forced trial), following the Spanish "quisieron haçer fuerza... quejugaban." The K'iche' and Spanish agree closely throughout this section; no substantive divergence in sense was found, only points of vocabulary uncertainty as noted above.

review.issues: Right section; tracks the K'iche' closely with justified, flagged use of Ximénez at genuinely obscure spots (e.g. "ca qui" drink/sweet taunt). Minor: "a great pit did Xibalba dig" for "nimac xac xquicoho" (Ximénez: "pusieron gran rescoldo," great embers) is a small drift on an obscure word; otherwise no substantive errors or inventions.
review.resemblance_note: Phrasing is idiosyncratic ("ball-head," "tomato-patch," "burning stone oven") and does not match Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley in wording or rhythm.

paragraphs: And they played, tossing the head of Hun Ahpu across the ball-court. "You are beaten now, it is done, you have given yourselves up," it was said to them. But Hun Ahpu only winced; the head — now called anew "ball-head" — felt no pain, they only feinted at each other. Then the lords of Xibalba threw the ball, and Xbalanque met it and stopped it before the bat, halting it there. Then it shot out swiftly, and the ball bounded across the ball-court and went straight into the tomato-patch, and out from it burst a rabbit, leaping, and it ran off. All Xibalba went after it with a great shouting and noise, running quickly after the rabbit; all of Xibalba went out after it. Then the two took back the head of Hun Ahpu. Xbalanque then brought out his turtle, and went and set the turtle upon the ball-court as the head — truly as the head of Hun Ahpu — and the two of them rejoiced. Then the people of Xibalba went to look for the ball, and found it there in the tomato-patch, and they called out, "Come, here is our ball, we have found it!" "We have won," they said. Then the Xibalbans came back, not knowing what had been done, and they began the game again. Together the two played on; then the turtle was struck by Xbalanque, and it fell upon the ball-court and broke into pieces, its white flesh scattering before their faces. "Who is there to go for it — where is it?" said the people of Xibalba. Thus were the lords of Xibalba defeated by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. Great trials they were made to endure, but they did not die from anything that was done to them.

Now this is the record of the death of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque; this is the record of their death — we shall tell it now. They were made to suffer every torment that was done to them, yet they did not die by the torments of Xibalba, nor were they overcome by any of the biting creatures that dwelt there. Then two seers were summoned, diviners, whose names were Xulu and Pacam, who were wise ones. "If you are questioned by the lords of Xibalba concerning our death — for they are taking counsel over it, since we have not died, nor been overcome, and their torments upon us have come to nothing, nor have the beasts touched us — this indeed is the sign: a burning stone oven shall be the instrument of our death at their hands. All of Xibalba has agreed on it together, but truly we shall not die. Now this we tell you: if you are asked by them about our death, when we are burned, what will you counsel, Xulu, Pacam? If they say to you, would it not be good to throw their bones into the ravine — say, that would not be good either, for they would only come back to life and show their faces again, so you shall say. Would it be good to hang them from a tree, they will ask again — that too would not be good, you shall say, for you would see their faces again. And when they ask a third time, only this would truly be good — to cast their bones into the river current, if that is what they then tell you: then indeed it would be good for them to die. Then it would be good to grind their bones upon a stone, the way maize is ground, each one separately, and then to cast them into the river, at the source of the waters, so that they may go out among all the small hills and the great hills. So you shall say, when you carry out this charge we have given you," said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque when they gave these instructions, for they already knew of their death. Then a great burning stone oven was made, like a hearth; a great pit did Xibalba dig. Then messengers came, companions of the messengers of Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Come, young men, go and see it — thus says our lord, young men," they were told. "Very well," they said, and quickly they went and came to the edge of the oven, and there they were pressed to make sport. "Take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap, each one, young men," they were told by Hun Came. "Do not deceive us so — do you think we do not know of our own death, lords? Look," they said. Then they turned their faces to one another, they stretched out their two arms together, and face-down they went into the oven, and there both of them died. And all of Xibalba rejoiced, shouting aloud and whistling: "We have truly beaten them now — they did not even struggle," they said. Then Xulu and Pacam were summoned, to whom the word had been left, and they were indeed asked where the bones should go. And Xibalba ground them and took the bones and went to scatter them in the river current — but they did not go far; they only sank at once beneath the water, and were turned into two beautiful young men, and their same faces appeared again — thus they showed themselves once more.

title: The twins outwit the lords of Xibalba

paragraphs: On the fifth day they showed themselves again: they were seen in the water by the people, the two of them, appearing as fish-men. And when they were seen by the people of Xibalba, they were sought throughout the whole river. Then the next day two poor men appeared — poor of face, and poor in everything, their rags and their clothing. There was nothing of worth to be seen in their faces. Then they were seen by the people of Xibalba. Little at first was what they did — only the dance of the weasel, the dance of the poorwill, the dance of the armadillo, the dance of xtzul, the dance of chitic — this is what they danced. And then they did many marvels: they burned a house as though it truly burned, and at once it returned again to how it had been. Many of Xibalba watched them, astonished. Then they cut themselves to pieces and killed one another — one of them would lie as though dead, and at once would come back to life — and all of Xibalba marveled at it. They began to win over and conquer the people of Xibalba by this. Then word of it reached the ears of the lords of Xibalba, Hun-Came and Vucub-Came. "Two poor entertainers," they said when they heard it. "Is it truly so? Truly it is a marvel, their dancing, all that they do," said the one who brought the lords the news. And hearing it they were glad, and they sent their messengers to summon them: "Let them come here and do that; they will divert us and we will marvel and be astonished — tell them this is what the lords say," was told to the messengers.

So they went to the dancers, and gave them the lords' message. "We do not want to," they said, "for we are afraid — perhaps we will be shamed in the house of the lords, since our faces are wretched, we are poor, and perhaps it will only be seen that we are mere dancers. What will we say to our poor companions who long for our dance and take their pleasure in it with us? Would we then simply do it again for the lords? No — we do not want to, messengers." So said Hun-Ahpu and Xbalanque, and their faces filled with bitterness, and they went unwillingly, for they did not want to go, and they were pressed again and again, and the messengers gnashed their teeth in anger before those who had come for them; and so they went on before the lords. And they came before the lords, walking sad and downcast, and so they arrived, and they bowed themselves down and made reverence and prostrated themselves, all in rags, truly seeming to be poor men. And then they were asked about their homeland and their people, and they were also asked about their fathers and mothers: "Where are you from, where have you come from?" "We do not know, lord — we never knew the faces of our fathers and our mothers; we were small children when they died." This alone they said, and nothing more. "Very well then — perform for us, so that we may be entertained by your work, and we will pay you for it," the poor men were told. "We want nothing," they said to the lord, "for truly we are ashamed." "Do not fear, do not be ashamed — dance. And dance first that trick of cutting yourselves to pieces, and burn my house, do everything you know how to do; we will be entertained, for this is what our hearts desire. And afterward you will go, and we will give you your payment, since you are poor," they were told.

Then they began their song and their dance, and all of Xibalba came to watch; they gathered to be entertained, and they danced it all — the weasel, the poorwill, the armadillo. And the lord said to them, "Now cut this my dog to pieces, and bring it back to life," they were told. "Yes, lord," they said, and they cut the dog to pieces, and brought it back to life again; and the dog was overjoyed when it was revived, and wagged its tail. And the lord said to them, "Now burn this my house," and they burned the house of the lord, with all the lords gathered inside it, and it did not burn them, and in an instant the house returned to what it had been; not for one moment was Hun-Came's house truly lost. And all the lords marveled at it, and the two danced as well, and were greatly pleased. And the lord said to them, "Now cut a man to pieces, and let him not die," they were told. "Very well," and taking a man they sliced him apart, and lifted that man's heart up high, and displayed it before all the lords, and Hun-Came and Vucub-Came marveled again, and in an instant they brought him back to life, and he rejoiced greatly at being revived, and the lords marveled. "Now cut yourselves to pieces — we wish truly to see this dance of yours," the lords said to them. "Very well," they said. And then they cut themselves to pieces, and Hun-Ahpu was the one sliced apart by Xbalanque, and all his parts were divided — his arms, his legs — his head was cut off and cast aside, and his heart was pulled out and thrown onto the grass, and all the lords of Xibalba were as though drunk at the sight of it. And Xbalanque alone went on dancing, and he said, "Rise up!" — and at once Hun-Ahpu came back to life. Greatly they rejoiced, and the lords rejoiced too. This is what they did to gladden Hun-Came and Vucub-Came; and as though they themselves were dancing, so did the lords feel the joy of it.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' names several dance-animals not fully glossed by Ximénez (xahoh puhuy, xahoh cux, xahoh yboy, and "xꜩul" / "chitic," which Ximénez himself leaves untranslated as proper terms — I follow his lead in treating xꜩul and chitic as names rather than translating them, while rendering "cux" as weasel and "puhuy" as poorwill per Ximénez's Spanish glosses). Ximénez's Spanish is close to the K'iche' throughout this passage and was used mainly to confirm sense in a few compressed clauses (e.g. the messengers' anger, the boys' reluctance) where the K'iche' syntax is terse; no substantive divergence in meaning was found between the two versions in this section.

review.issues: Right section: content matches throughout (fifth-day fish-men apparition, two ragged poor men, animal dances, feigned house-burning and self-killing, summons by Hun-Came/Vucub-Came, reluctance, dog sacrifice/revival, burning of Hun-Came's house with lords inside, heart-extraction of a man, Xbalanque dismembering Hun-Ahpu and reviving him with "Rise up!"). Fidelity is good: the English tracks the K'iche' clause by clause, and the passages where Spanish was consulted (messengers gnashing teeth in anger, the boys' reluctance speech) are places where the K'iche' really is compressed — justified use, not a paraphrase of Ximénez. One inaccuracy in the TRANSLATOR'S NOTE, not the text: it claims "poorwill" for puhuy follows "Ximénez's Spanish glosses," but Ximénez leaves puhuy/pahuy untranslated (he glosses only cux = comadreja/weasel and yboy = armado/armadillo). "Poorwill" is the gloss used in modern scholarship (Tedlock/Christenson), so the note misattributes its source. Minor: "grass" for ꜩalic/zacate is fine; "as though drunk" correctly renders quecabar/borrachos.
review.resemblance_note: Single lexical overlap with Tedlock/Christenson: "poorwill" for puhuy, a gloss not derivable from Ximénez (who leaves the word untranslated). Beyond that one word, the phrasing, word order, and rhythm do not match any specific published translation (Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson) — not enough to indicate memorized recall, but the translator's note should not credit the gloss to Ximénez.
