What will we say to our poor companions who long for our dance and take their pleasure in it with us? Would we then simply do it again for the lords? No — we do not want to, messengers." So said Hun-Ahpu and Xbalanque, and their faces filled with bitterness, and they went unwillingly, for they did not want to go, and they were pressed again and again, and the messengers gnashed their teeth in anger before those who had come for them; and so they went on before the lords. And they came before the lords, walking sad and downcast, and so they arrived, and they bowed themselves down and made reverence and prostrated themselves, all in rags, truly seeming to be poor men. And then they were asked about their homeland and their people, and they were also asked about their fathers and mothers: "Where are you from, where have you come from?" "We do not know, lord — we never knew the faces of our fathers and our mothers; we were small children when they died." This alone they said, and nothing more. "Very well then — perform for us, so that we may be entertained by your work, and we will pay you for it," the poor men were told. "We want nothing," they said to the lord, "for truly we are ashamed." "Do not fear, do not be ashamed — dance. And dance first that trick of cutting yourselves to pieces, and burn my house, do everything you know how to do; we will be entertained, for this is what our hearts desire. And afterward you will go, and we will give you your payment, since you are poor," they were told.

Then they began their song and their dance, and all of Xibalba came to watch; they gathered to be entertained, and they danced it all — the weasel, the poorwill, the armadillo. And the lord said to them, "Now cut this my dog to pieces, and bring it back to life," they were told. "Yes, lord," they said, and they cut the dog to pieces, and brought it back to life again; and the dog was overjoyed when it was revived, and wagged its tail. And the lord said to them, "Now burn this my house," and they burned the house of the lord, with all the lords gathered inside it, and it did not burn them, and in an instant the house returned to what it had been; not for one moment was Hun-Came's house truly lost. And all the lords marveled at it, and the two danced as well, and were greatly pleased. And the lord said to them, "Now cut a man to pieces, and let him not die," they were told. "Very well," and taking a man they sliced him apart, and lifted that man's heart up high, and displayed it before all the lords, and Hun-Came and Vucub-Came marveled again, and in an instant they brought him back to life, and he rejoiced greatly at being revived, and the lords marveled. "Now cut yourselves to pieces — we wish truly to see this dance of yours," the lords said to them. "Very well," they said. And Xbalanque alone went on dancing, and he said, "Rise up!" — and at once Hun-Ahpu came back to life. Greatly they rejoiced, and the lords rejoiced too. Ximénez's Spanish is close to the K'iche' throughout this passage and was used mainly to confirm sense in a few compressed clauses (e.g. the messengers' anger, the boys' reluctance) where the K'iche' syntax is terse; no substantive divergence in meaning was found between the two versions in this section.

title: Defeat of Jun Kame' and Wuqub' Kame'

paragraphs: Then desire and despair grew in the hearts of the lords over how they had been shown up by Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke. And so the order went out from Jun Kame' and Wuqub' Kame': "Do that to us too — tear us to pieces, tear us apart one by one," said Jun Kame' and Wuqub' Kame' to Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke. "Very well — be glad, then; it was not to make us glad that you were brought here, you who are lords over your own vassals," they were told. And the first to be torn apart was the one who was head and lord of Xibalba, named Jun Kame'. And once Jun Kame' was dead, Wuqub' Kame' was seized next, and neither of them was raised up again, their faces were not restored. Then the people of Xibalba fled out in terror when they saw their lords dead, scattered and broken open, both of them — it was done for a punishment. In an instant the lord died and did not come back. And one lord who had escaped ran in among the dancers; he was not caught, and begged for mercy when he was recognized. And all of them, every vassal, fled to a great ravine, and all crowded down into a great pit, and there they all lay crammed together when countless ants came and went to sting them in the ravine, and so drove them out, and coming out they all gave themselves up, since their lord of Xibalba was already defeated — and it was only as a marvel and a wonder that they changed shape as they did this. Then they spoke their names and boasted of themselves before all of Xibalba. "Hear us — we will say our names, and we will say also our fathers' names to you. We are Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke, so we are called. And our fathers are those you killed, who were named Jun Junajpu and Wuqub' Junajpu. We are the avengers of the pain and suffering of our fathers, and of all the wrongs you did to them. So we will finish you all off, we will kill you, not one of you shall escape," they were told. Then all of them fell down weeping: "Have mercy on us, Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke — truly we sinned greatly against your fathers, of whom you speak, who lie buried in the ash-heap," they said. "Very well," they answered. "Now hear, all of you people of Xibalba, what we tell you: because your fortune shall not be great, and your portion shall not be great, small shall your headship be, and none of you shall have noble blood — only broken pottery and griddle-stones and cords shall be yours, and you shall be mothers only to what rots away, and only the children of straw and the children of weeds shall belong to you, not the shining vassals — they shall perish only in your presence. You shall be the wrongdoers, the sinners, the sorrowful and wretched ones, the ones who bring on guilt; let the seizing of men not be sudden — hear this and attend to it, this sickness of blood," they were told, all of Xibalba. And so began their being lost and going astray, and their being invoked. Their power was never great in the old days — they were only enemies and adversaries of men in the old days, and they were not gods, nor were they so called in the old days, but rather they were the terror in evil things, the faces of these enemies were owls, and they were deceivers, inciters to fault and sin, and they were also two-faced, traitors, full of envy, oppressors — that is what they were called, and they showed cruel faces and made war. And so they were brought low, and their greatness fell, and their dominion ceased to be great. This is what Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke did.

And this is what their grandmother wept and mourned over, before those canes which had been left planted, which sprouted, and then withered when the boys were burned in the oven, and which sprouted again a second time — and then that grandmother burned copal before the canes, in memory of her grandsons. And her heart rejoiced greatly when the canes sprouted that second time. And from this began the reverence paid by their grandmother, and then it was named "the middle of the house" and "the middle of the courtyard, the whirlwind place." Chatam Uleu, "earth made into a bed," it was called; and so it was named the middle of the house and of the courtyard by them, because it was in the middle of the house that the canes were planted. And it was also named Chatam Uleu because the canes were set upon this earth made like a resting-frame, the place where the canes are planted. And it was likewise named Kazam Ah, "the planted canes," because they had sprouted; and this name was given to it by her, Ixmukane, because Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke had left the canes planted there, as a memorial of themselves for their grandmother.

These, then, were our first fathers of old, Jun Junajpu and Wuqub' Junajpu, who went to their deaths, who were killed; and the twins saw again the faces of their fathers there in Xibalba, and their fathers spoke again to their sons once Xibalba was defeated. And so their fathers were gathered up by them; they went to bring Wuqub' Junajpu together there, they went to gather him at the ash-heap place. They found him there in the ash-heap — there they went to find him, where the ash had been scattered — and they sought to raise up his face as well; his name was asked of him, his mouth and his nose and his eyes, and his name was found first, though little did he speak. Only his name went unspoken, Junal Puil his mouth — only this much was told. And so their father's heart was greatly comforted, and the ash-heap remained, so that there your invocation shall be made, the sons told him, consoling him. And you shall be the first invoked, the first greeted, by all the shining sons and vassals, and your name shall not be lost when the light dawns, they told their father, consoling him. And we are the avengers of your death, of the pains that were done to you. And so it was, their charge left behind, once all of Xibalba was overcome. Then they rose up here to the earth's surface, and in an instant they rose up into the sky. And one of them was made the sun, and the other the moon, when the sky grew bright. And the four hundred boys whom Sipakna had killed rose up also; and these became their companions, and were made into the stars of the sky.

translation.translator_note: This section's K'iche' transcription is unusually corrupt/garbled in places (likely OCR or copying errors in the source file), especially the passage describing the finding of Jun Junajpu's remains at the ash-heap and the naming episode ("catecut xcaton ricatit xucat ri pom..."). Where the K'iche' word-order and word-breaks could not be confidently parsed, I leaned more heavily on Ximénez's Spanish for sense while still rendering my own English (not his wording). Two name/place items are of note: "hunalpuil" (K'iche') appears as the fragmentary "name of his mouth" that goes unspoken — rendered literally as "Junal Puil his mouth" per the text, since its exact sense is unclear even to Ximénez, who transliterates rather than translates it. The place name "Chatam Uleu" (K'iche' "earth made into a bed/frame") and "Kazam Ah" ("planted canes") are given both in K'iche' and with their glossed meanings, following the text's own explanatory structure. No substantive divergence in overall sense was found between the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish beyond this legibility issue.

review.issues: Minor: opening drops the K'iche' "chire qui xahoh" (at their dance), paraphrasing as "shown up"; "the whirlwind place" follows Ximénez's "remolino" gloss of "nicah bichoc" rather than the K'iche' itself. The heavier reliance on Spanish in the ash-heap/naming passage is justified — that K'iche' transcription is genuinely garbled, and the translator disclosed it.
review.resemblance_note: Distinctive renderings (e.g. "children of straw and the children of weeds," "griddle-stones," "Junal Puil his mouth") do not match Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, Goetz-Morley, or Edmonson in wording or rhythm.

Two name/place items are of note: "hunalpuil" (K'iche') appears as the fragmentary "name of his mouth" that goes unspoken — rendered literally as "Junal Puil his mouth" per the text, since its exact sense is unclear even to Ximénez, who transliterates rather than translates it. The place name "Chatam Uleu" (K'iche' "earth made into a bed/frame") and "Kazam Ah" ("planted canes") are given both in K'iche' and with their glossed meanings, following the text's own explanatory structure. No substantive divergence in overall sense was found between the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish beyond this legibility issue.

title: Paxil and K'ayala': discovery of maize; the first four men and women

paragraphs: Here now begins when it was thought out how man should be made, and the search for what would become the flesh of man. So spoke the Bearer, the Begetter, the Framer and the Shaper, called Tepeu and Gucumatz: "The time of dawn draws near, that the work be finished, that the provider, the nourisher, be brought forth, the bright children, the bright offspring, humankind, on the face of the earth," they said. They gathered, they came, they went into council in the darkness of night; there they sought and pondered, there they deliberated and grew troubled. And thus their thinking came out into the light: they found and recognized what was to become the flesh of man, while it yet lacked little for the sun, moon, and stars to appear over the Framers, the Shapers.

In Paxil, in Cayala' as it is called, the yellow ears, the white ears, came. These are the names of the animals that brought the food: Yac, Utiw, Quel, and Hoh — four animals that revealed the yellow ears, the white ears, to them, coming from Paxil; they showed the way to Paxil. This, then, was what they found to be food, and this became the flesh of formed man, of shaped man; this became the blood, the blood of man — this the maize became, by the Bearer, the Begetter.

So they rejoiced at having found that beautiful mountain, filled with sweetness, abundant with yellow ears, white ears, abundant too with pataxte and cacao, with countless zapotes, anonas, jocotes, nances, sapodillas, honey — abundant food was there within that town called Paxil, Cayala'; there was food of every kind, small food and great food, small plantings and great plantings, and the way to it had been shown by the animals. Then, when they had ground the yellow ears, the white ears, Xmucane made nine drinks/grindings, and food entered in, and from it came strength, fatness, and the muscle and vigor of man arose, when this was done by the Bearer, the Begetter, Tepeu, Gucumatz, so it is told. Then they put into practice the making, the shaping, of our first mother, our first father: only yellow ears, white ears were their flesh; only this was the food of the arms and legs of man, of the four men who were made; only this entered as their flesh.

These are the names of the first men who were formed and shaped. The first man was Balam Ki'tze'. The second was Balam Aqab. The third was Mahukutah. The fourth was Iq'i Balam. These are the names of our first mother, our first father.

It is said they were only made, only shaped: they had no mother, they had no father. We simply call them men, but they were not born of woman, nor were they begotten by the Framer and the Shaper — only by a wonder, by sorcery, were they made and shaped, by the Framer, the Shaper, the Bearer, the Begetter, Tepeu, Gucumatz.

And when they came to be men, they were made as men, they spoke, they reasoned; they saw and they understood; they moved about and they grasped things — good men were they, handsome, of fine appearance, and their look had life in it. They came to know, and at once their sight reached out; their knowledge became great; their gaze passed over everything, they knew the whole extent of the sky and the face of the earth, without having first to move in order to see what lay at the foot of the sky; wherever they were, they simply saw it. Great was their knowing; their sight passed over the trees, the stones, the lakes, the seas, the mountains, the plains. Truly precious men were they, Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aqab, Mahukutah, and Iq'i Balam.

Then they were questioned by the Framer, the Shaper: "What is your being now? Do you not see? Do you not hear? Is your speech not good, and your walk? Look, then, at the foundation of the sky, the mountains and the plains, look upon them," they were told. And so they looked upon the whole foundation of the sky, and upon the earth, and then they gave thanks to the Framer, the Shaper, truly twice, thrice giving thanks, saying: "Truly we are given being, mouths, faces; we speak, we hear, we think, we move, we feel; we have come to know what is far and what is near; we have seen the great and the small of all that is in the sky and on the earth. And so we give thanks to you, that we were made, that we were given being and were shaped — you our grandmother, you our grandfather," they said, giving thanks for their creation and their shaping. They finished knowing everything, and they beheld the four corners, the four sides, of the sky and of the earth. But this did not please the Framer, the Shaper, who heard it: "Not good is what our formed ones, our shaped ones, say — they know everything, great and small," they said.

So then this was once more the thought of the Bearer, the Begetter: "What more shall we do with them? Their sight reaches everywhere, they know everything, they behold the whole face of the earth. Not good is what they say. Are they to be merely formed, merely shaped, and become like gods themselves? But if they do not increase, if they do not multiply, when it is to dawn, when it is to grow light — how shall it be? It is only a trial, a further attempt, that they exist; it is not good, let us undo this a little." Thus they took counsel among themselves once more — the Heart of Sky, Hurricane, Chipi-Kaqulha, Raxa-Kaqulha, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Bearer, Begetter, Xpiyacoc, Xmucane, Framer, Shaper — so they said among themselves; and then they set about the changing of their formed ones, their shaped ones.

translation.translator_note: The four animals' K'iche' names (yac, vtiu, quel, hoh) are kept transliterated (Yac, Utiw, Quel, Hoh) rather than translated as "mountain cat, coyote/wolf, small parrot, crow," since Ximénez himself glosses them loosely and inconsistently in Spanish ("el gato de monte, el lobo, el chocoy, y el cuervo") and the exact species are debated; the K'iche' terms are given as proper names of the animals as the text itself treats them. "xmucane echa xoquic ruqha ropenal" (Xmucane's nine preparations/drinks made from the ground maize) is a compressed, somewhat obscure clause — rendered as "nine drinks/grindings" to keep both readings open, following Ximénez's "nueve bebidas." One clear divergence from Ximénez: where the Spanish has the newly-made men praise their creators and only afterward, in a separate declaration, complain of their own excessive knowledge as reported speech by the gods ("no esta bien esto que dizen nuestras criaturas"), the K'iche' more starkly attributes the judgment "not good" directly and immediately to the divine council itself upon hearing the men's thanksgiving — the translation follows the K'iche' structure here, keeping the gods' private deliberation distinct from the men's speech of gratitude.

review.issues: Right section confirmed. Overall faithful to the K'iche', with independent engagement (e.g. "beautiful mountain" for "vtzilah huyub" where Ximénez has "tierra"; "town" for "tinamit"; following the K'iche' attribution of the "not good" judgment, as the translator note explains). Minor issues: (1) In the final divine deliberation, the K'iche' "xata nacah chopon vi qui mucubal xata zcaquin v vach vleu chiquilo" is a proposal ("let their sight reach only nearby, let them see only a little of the face of the earth" — cf. Ximénez "que solo lo que esta cerca vean... un poco de la haz de la tierra"); the translation flattens this into the complaint "Their sight reaches everywhere... they behold the whole face of the earth," losing the explicit proposal to narrow their vision, keeping only "let us undo this a little." (2) "xapa xchihunamatah quibanoh cuq ri naht copon vi quetamabal quilon ronohel" ("shall their deeds be equal to ours, whose knowledge reaches far, who see everything?") is dropped/absorbed into the "become like gods" clause. (3) "It is only a trial, a further attempt, that they exist" is a loose paraphrase of "xa cayoho chi zcaquin chic qo chi carah" ("let us hold back a little; there is still more they need/lack" — cf. Ximénez "todavía les falta que hazer"). These are compressions/omissions in one paragraph, not wholesale invention; the rest tracks the K'iche' closely.
review.resemblance_note: Epithet renderings "Bearer, Begetter" and "Heart of Sky" coincide with Tedlock's standard equivalents, and "Framer, Shaper" with Christenson's — but these are near-conventional glosses of alom/qaholom, u k'ux kaj, tz'aqol/b'itol. Sentence structure, rhythm, and distinctive phrasing (e.g. "nine drinks/grindings," "their look had life in it," "the foundation of the sky") do not match Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos/Goetz-Morley in any sustained way; no passage reads as recalled from a published translation.

title: The K'iche' lineages and their patron gods Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz

paragraphs: Then breath was blown upon their eyes by the Heart of Sky, and they were clouded, as when breath is blown upon the face of a mirror and it fogs. Their eyes were blinded, so that only what was close could be seen, only that was clear to them. In this way the knowledge and all the wisdom of the four men was lost — the root, the beginning of them, in the same way that our first grandfathers, our fathers, had been shaped and formed by the Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth.

Then their companions came to exist; their wives came to be. Our god deliberated again, and thus, as if in a dream, they received — they received their wives. Beautiful women were there with Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. They already had their wives when they awoke from that sleep, and their hearts rejoiced greatly on account of their companions. These, then, were the names of their wives: Caha Paluna was the name of the wife of Balam Quitze; Chomiha was the name of the wife of Balam Acab; Tzununiha was the name of the wife of Mahucutah; and Caquixaha was the name of the wife of Iqui Balam. These, then, were the names of the wives who became the mothers of the small lineages and the great lineages. These are the root of us, the K'iche' people.

Many became priests and sacrificers, yet it was not that many fathers came to be — only four were the mothers of us K'iche' people. Their names differed, each one, when they multiplied there at the rising of the sun. The names of the peoples that came to be were Tepeu, Oloman, Cohah, Quenech, Ahau — such were the names of the peoples called there at the sunrise where they multiplied. Known too is the origin of the Tamub and of the Ilocab: together they came from there, from the sunrise.

Balam Quitze was the grandfather and father of the nine great houses of Cavec; likewise Balam Acab was the grandfather and father of the nine great houses of Nihaibab; Mahucutah was the grandfather and father of the four great houses of Ahau K'iche'. Three branches of lineages there were, and the names of their grandfathers and fathers were not lost; these multiplied there at the sunrise. There too came the Tamub and the Ilocab, with thirteen branches of peoples — thirteen of Tecpan, together with the Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, the Ah Quinquinaha, and also the Zacahib, and the Lamaquib, Cumatz, Tuhalha, the Uchabaha, the Ah Chumilaha together with the Ahquibaha, the Ah Batenab, Acul Vinac, Balamiha, Canchahel, and Balam Colob. These, then, were the great branches of the peoples, of the many branches, that we speak of here; we have named only the greatest of them.

Many more came forth besides these, small lineages in the towns whose names we have not written, and who likewise multiplied there, coming from the sunrise. Many were the people, and it happened to them that they came into being before the sun was born, before there was light; all of them together, many as they were, existed there, moving about at the place of the sunrise. There was as yet nothing to sustain them; they only lifted their faces to the sky, not knowing where they were to go, nor how to travel far. And there in that place there existed black people, white people, people of different appearance, people of different speech — the two-eared ones — for there are different peoples in the world. And there were mountain-dwelling people whose faces had never been seen, who had no houses, but wandered like monkeys among the small hills and the great hills. translation.translator_note: Several passages posed genuine difficulty. (1) "mana xa e cahib chic xuxic xere cahib ri qui chuch" is slightly elliptical in the K'iche'; Ximénez's Spanish ("no solo fueron quarto; sino quesolo quarto fueron los padres") confirms the sense that many descendant lineages arose but the founding four mothers/fathers remained singular — I followed that reading over a more literal but contradictory rendering. review.issues: Right section; overall faithful with genuine engagement with the K'iche'. Minor problems: (1) "e chuh" means "madmen" (Ximénez: "locos"), not "monkeys" — the translator's note asserting "monkeys" is the literal sense is incorrect, making "wandered like monkeys" an unjustified rendering. (2) "xquitao vtzihol hun tinamit xebevi" likely means "they heard news of a town and went"; "a town heeded their word" follows Ximénez against the more natural K'iche' syntax. (3) "che abah" (wood [and] stone idols) rendered twice as "stone" only, dropping "wood." (4) Reliance on Ximénez at "mana xa e cahib chic xuxic" is justified — the K'iche' is elliptical there.
review.resemblance_note: Shared elements (Seven Caves, Seven Canyons; deity epithets; the mirror-breath image) are dictated by the source; distinctive diction does not match Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley.

title: Departure from Tulan; the long migration

paragraphs: They arrived then at Tulan, all of them — the people who came were not few in number, and many were they who came, all in order. Their coming forth was with their gods: first Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and rejoicing they said, 'Now we have found what we sought.' And it was Tohil, their god, who came out first, carried, borne along by Balam Quitze. Next came forth Avilix, the god carried by Balam Acab; next Hacavitz, carried by Mahucutah; and Nicahtacah was the name of the god that Iqui Balam brought out. These were the ones who accompanied only the Quiché people. And it belonged also to Tamub — it is the same god Tohil that the grandfathers and fathers of the lords of Tamub took up, and they bear that name still today. And third were the Ilocab, whose god likewise was named Tohil, taken up by their grandfathers and fathers, the lords, and this too they know still today. Thus were named the three branches of Quiché people, and they were not divided nor did they forsake one another, because the name of their god was one and the same: Tohil to the Quiché, Tohil to Tamub, Tohil to Ilocab — only one was the name of their god. So it was that the three great branches of the Quiché did not separate from one another; truly great was their being, of Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz. Then all the tribes entered as well: the people of Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, the people of Tziquinaha, and the Yaqui people, as they are named today. And there the speech of the tribes was changed; different their speech became, and it was no longer clear how they spoke to one another when they came out from Tulan. There they broke apart from one another; some went toward the rising of the sun, and many came here.

They had no fine things yet, nothing good with which to clothe themselves; only the skins of animals were their garments, and they were poor — they possessed nothing of their own, though they were beings of wonder in their nature. When they came from Tulan Zuyva, the Seven Caves, the Seven Canyons, as the old accounts say, it was a long journey before they reached Tulan. And they had no fire — only the god Tohil, first among the gods of the tribes, was the one who made fire; but it is not known how it came to be, for already it was blazing when Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam beheld it. 'Alas, we have no fire yet, we shall die of cold,' they said. Then Tohil spoke to them: 'Do not grieve. That fire of which you speak — the one that will be lost to you — shall still be yours,' Tohil said to them. 'Is it truly so? You are our god, our sustenance, our provider — you are the one,' they said to him, when they gave him thanks for what he had spoken. And Tohil said, 'It is well. Truly I am your god; so let it be — I shall be your lord.' Thus it was told to the diviners, the sacrificers, on account of Tohil. So then the tribes warmed themselves and rejoiced because of the fire.

Then a great rain began; hail came down, putting out the fire of the tribes — heavy indeed fell the hail upon the heads of all the tribes, and their fire was quenched by the hail, so that they no longer had fire. Then Balam Quitze and Balam Acab again asked for fire: 'O god, truly we are perishing of cold,' they said to Tohil. 'Do not grieve,' said Tohil, and then he brought forth fire, twirling it within his sandal. Then Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced, and then they warmed themselves. Meanwhile the fire of the other tribes had already gone out, and they were dying of cold. So then they came again to beg fire of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; they could no longer bear it, for they were shuddering from the hail, their teeth chattering, trembling; they had lost the feeling in their feet and hands, and could grasp nothing in them when they arrived. 'We are not ashamed before you to ask for fire — give us a little of your fire,' they said when they came. But they were given no answer, and then the tribes grew angry. Different now was the speech of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And they said, 'What is this — that they have abandoned our speech? How did this happen to us? We are lost. Where were we deceived? For we had only one speech when we came from Tulan, and one place of our origin and our raising — it is not good, what has become of us,' said all the tribes, beneath the trees, beneath the vines. Then a man showed himself before Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and the messenger of Xibalba spoke to them: 'Truly this is your god, this is the one who sustains you; this too is the likeness, the substitute, the remembrance of your Creator, your Maker. Do not give your fire to the tribes until they have begged it of Tohil — he it is who will tell you whence you are to give the fire they beg,' said that one from Xibalba. He had wings like the wings of a bat. 'I am the messenger of your Creator, your Maker,' said that one from Xibalba. Then they rejoiced, and their hearts were greatly lifted up over Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz, when he said this to them. And then swiftly he vanished from before them. Still the tribes kept arriving without ceasing, for they were perishing of cold, from the great hail and the black rain and the mist; unbearable was the cold. And all the tribes arrived, huddled and trembling with cold, when they came to where Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were. Greatly troubled were their hearts; they twisted their mouths and their faces.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish agree closely throughout this section; no major divergence in sense was found. A few notes on interpretive choices: (1) "vzamahel xibal ba" is rendered "the messenger of Xibalba" (the K'iche' underworld) rather than Ximénez's gloss "mensajero del infierno" (messenger of hell) — Xibalba is a proper place-name in the K'iche' text, not a generalized "hell," though the being is clearly cast as a deceiver from that realm, consistent with Ximénez's own marginal note "Demonium loquens." (2) "Tulan zu" / "tulan zuyva" is kept as the place-name "Tulan Zuyva," following the compound as it appears in the K'iche'. (3) "ruq yaquivinac" was rendered "the Yaqui people" — the term for a non-Quiché group named alongside Rabinal, Cakchiquel, and Tziquinaha; the exact referent is uncertain in the source but the sense of "another named tribal group" is clear from both K'iche' and Spanish. (4) A few short K'iche' clauses (e.g. around "roxichal queche" and the string of tribe names) are compressed slightly for readable English syntax while preserving all named content.

review.issues: Minor only: (1) "ta chuxoc" in Tohil's speech may mean "when it dawns" (so Ximénez, "quando amanezca"); rendered "so let it be," losing a possible dawn reference — K'iche' genuinely ambiguous. (2) "ahquixb ahcah" better "bloodletters and sacrificers" than "diviners, sacrificers." (3) "chiquecal hab" rendered "black rain"; more likely "downpouring/continuous rain" (Ximénez: "garua continua"). None of these affect overall fidelity; the translation demonstrably engages the K'iche' rather than merely rewording Ximénez.
review.resemblance_note: Shared phrases with published versions ("Seven Caves, Seven Canyons," "give us a little of your fire") are dictated by the source; no specific match in diction or rhythm to Recinos, Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson.

title: Multiplication of languages, separation of the peoples

paragraphs: Then the peoples came again before Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and said: "Have mercy on us — we ask only for a little fire. We did not all come from the same place; we are not all one household, we are only one nation. Have mercy on us, now that you have been formed and made." And they answered: "What shall we give you, that we might show you mercy?" They said: "Very well, we will give you silver." But the peoples said: "We do not want silver." Then the peoples said to Balam Quitze and Balam Acab: "What is it you want, then? We will ask for it." "Very well," said the peoples, "we will ask Tohil for it, and then we will tell you." And so it was said. Then they asked Tohil: "What shall we give the peoples, O Tohil, who come asking for your fire?" said Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. "Very well — let them join themselves to me, let them give their side and their armpit, let them embrace me, for I am Tohil, if their hearts truly desire it. If not, I will not give them my fire," said Tohil. "Tell them: not now, wait a little." It was told to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and when they had spoken Tohil's word, the peoples said: "Very well, we will let our side be pierced; we will embrace him." And when they heard this and accepted Tohil's word, they did not delay, but at once agreed, and then they received their fire and were warmed by it. But one clan stole fire in secret, by stealth — these were the people of the House of Bats, whose god was named Chamalcan; and in the shape of a bat they passed through the smoke silently, and came and took the fire without asking for it. These, the Cakchiquel, did not ask for the fire, and would not let themselves be won over as the rest were; only the other peoples let themselves be conquered, all of them who gave their side and their armpit to be pierced, for this was what Tohil had demanded. And when all the peoples were sacrificed before him, when their hearts were torn out through the side and the armpit — a thing not yet done before — greatness and dominion came to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam.

From there, from Tulan Zuyva, they set out. They did not eat; they only fasted continually, watching only for the dawn, watching for the rising of the sun, gathering together to look at the great star called Icoquih, which goes before the face of the sun when the sun is born — bright Icoquih, whose face was always turned there, toward the place where the sun rises. There in Tulan Zuyva, whence their god had come, they took their greatness and their lordship; and there too the great peoples and the small peoples were subdued, when they were sacrificed before Tohil and gave their blood, their side, their armpit — all the people. At once, in Tulan, their greatness and their great wisdom came to them; they had it in the darkness, and it was by night that it was done. Then they set out, they tore themselves away from that place, and left behind the place where the sun rises. "This is not our home," they said. "Let us go and see where we are to settle." So spoke Tohil in truth to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam: "Give thanks before you go — pierce the tips of your ears, and scrape your elbows; this shall be your thanksgiving before the god." "Very well," they said, and they pierced their ears, and it entered into the song of their leaving Tulan, and their hearts wept as they came away. "Alas! It is not here that we shall see the dawn, when the sun is born, the light that brightens the face of the earth," they said, when they set out. On the road some of the people stayed behind and slept, and each nation rose up again, always watching for the star, the sign of the sun, which was the sign of dawn in their hearts as they came from the place of sunrise; and with one likeness of face they passed on together through a great distance, so it is told now. Then they came to the top of a hill, and there all the Quiché people gathered together with the other nations, and there all of them assembled, and there they counseled together. "Place of Counsel" is the name of that hill still, for "Counsel" is what its name means. There they gathered themselves and there they exalted one another: "I am — I am the Quiché people; and you, you are Tamub, this shall be your name," it was said to those who became Tamub. And they said to Ilocab: "You are Ilocab, this shall be your name." "The three branches of the Quiché shall not be lost; we are of one heart alike," they said, when they took their names. Then the Cakchiquel too were named; "Cakchiquel" became their name, and likewise the Rabinal; this became their name, and it has not been lost to this day; and there too were the Ah Quikinaha, which is their name today. These are the names they gave themselves. There, where they had gathered, they only waited, watching for the dawn, watching for the rising of the star that goes first before the face of the sun when it is born. "From there we came, we who have been scattered," they said among themselves, and their hearts suffered great anguish on the journey, for they had no food, nothing to eat; they only smelled the tip of their staffs and imagined it was as if they were eating, though they were not eating at all. And as they came, it is not clear whether they crossed over the sea; they crossed as if there were no sea — they crossed merely over stones, stones scattered along the way. "Lined-up stones, scattered sand" they named it, by which they crossed over the sea, the water parting itself as they crossed. Their hearts suffered anguish there when they took counsel together, for they had no food, only a single grain of maize to sustain them. There they remained, atop the hill called "Counsel," as it is named. They carried with them there Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz. Great was the penance and fasting that Balam Quitze did there with his wife, named Caha Paluna. So too did Balam Acab, with his wife named Chomiha; and Mahucutah likewise fasted greatly with his wife, named Tzununiha; and Iqui Balam with his wife, named Caquixaha. These were the ones who fasted, in the darkness, with great grief in their hearts, as they stayed atop the hill called "Counsel" to this day. So spoke their god there.

review.issues: Right section: the translation tracks the K'iche' content closely and completely — fire petition, silver refused, Tohil's demand of side and armpit, the Cakchiquel/House of Bats (Chamalcan) stealing fire through the smoke in bat form, sacrifice and heart extraction, departure from Tulan Zuyva, the star Icoquih, ear-piercing and the song of leaving Tulan, gathering at the hill Chi Pixab, naming of Tamub, Ilocab, Cakchiquel, Rabinal, Ah Q'iquinaha, smelling staff-tips for food, crossing the sea on stones ("cholochic abah bocotahinac zanaieb" = "lined-up stones, scattered sand"), the single grain of maize, the four wives' names, and fasting on Chi Pixab. Minor problems, none disqualifying: (1) the opening speech's negatives ("maui xuculu mapu xurico, mapu xa hun cochoch, xa pu hun cahuyubal") are rendered "We did not all come from the same place; we are not all one household, we are only one nation" — the K'iche' more plausibly reads as rhetorical questions asserting shared origin ("are we not of one home, one mountain-place?"); Ximénez himself is inconsistent here, and the translation follows his negatives, so this is arguable rather than invented, but the sense may be inverted. (2) Speaker attribution in the silver exchange is muddled (both the offer of silver and its refusal are given to "the peoples"), though the muddle exists in Ximénez too and the K'iche' lacks clear speech-tags. (3) "chicaꜩonoh tucoc zcaquin i ꜫaꜫ" mid-speech order is smoothed but preserved. The translator's note honestly flags the genuinely obscure spots (vcomahil, the staff-smelling line, the stone-crossing), and the renderings there are defensible readings of the K'iche', not just rewordings of Ximénez — e.g. the crossing passage keeps K'iche' details (water dividing itself, "vhachon rib ha") that Ximénez omits.
review.resemblance_note: Sense necessarily overlaps with all published versions, but wording, rhythm, and epithets do not match Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson specifically; e.g. "Lined-up stones, scattered sand" differs from Christenson's "Lined-up Stones, Piled-up Sand" and Tedlock's "rock rows, sand banks".

If not, I will not give them my fire," said Tohil. "Tell them: not now, wait a little." It was told to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and when they had spoken Tohil's word, the peoples said: "Very well, we will let our side be pierced; we will embrace him." And when they heard this and accepted Tohil's word, they did not delay, but at once agreed, and then they received their fire and were warmed by it. title: The wait for the dawn

paragraphs: Then Tohil, Awilix, and Hacavitz spoke to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam: "Let us go, let us rise up from here, we must not remain here — put us in a hidden, secret place, for the dawn draws near. Perhaps it will be your misfortune if we are seized and taken captive by enemies here, in this place where you now keep us, you who are honored — so scatter us and hide us," they said when they spoke. "Very well," all of them answered, "we shall be uprooted from here; we shall go seek out the mountains," they all said. Then each of them took up his god and carried him. Awilix entered a ravine, called the Ravine of Hiding, so it was named, in the great ravine — a place in the mountains now called Awilix — and there he remained; he stayed hidden in the ravine, by Balam Acab. In order they were left in hiding: the first to remain was Hacavitz, above a great river; Hacavitz is the name of that mountain now. There was his dwelling, and there indeed the god Hacavitz stayed — that was his name. Likewise Mahucutah remained with his god, the second to be hidden by them; Hacavitz did not stay upon a wooded mountain but on a bare, open hill — that is where Hacavitz was hidden. Then Balam Quitze came and arrived at a great mountain, to hide Tohil; Tohil was hidden there by Balam Quitze, and that mountain is now called Patohil. They honored the hiding place in the ravine, the guardian of Tohil; many are the serpents there, and many the jaguars, vipers, and rattlesnakes, there in the ravine and the mountain where they were hidden by those lords.

Together, as one, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam remained; together they waited for the dawn there atop the mountain called Hacavitz. There was but little distance to where the gods of the Tamub and the Ilocab stayed — Amactan was the name of the place where the god of the Tamub remained, and there the dawn broke for that people; and the place where it dawned for the Ilocab, where their god remained, was but a short way off among the mountains. And there too were all the Rabinal people, the Cakchiquel, the Tziquinaha, and all the tribes, small and great; together, as one, they stood, waiting as one for the dawn and for the rising of the great star Icoquih, the one who comes out first, before the face of the sun, when day breaks. So they said. As one, Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam remained together; they had no rest, no sleep. Great was the weeping of their hearts, of their bellies, for the dawn and the appearing of light. And there too they were made ashamed; great sorrow and lamentation overtook them, and they were undone by anguish. There they remained, and they said: "Alas for us, bitterly have we come; alas, though we have come to see the dawn, it does not break. What are we to do — all of us share the same fate. Our faces were one, in our homeland, and now we have been abandoned." So they spoke to one another, in that sorrow and lament and weeping, and they said, "our hearts find no rest concerning the dawning of the sun. And now our gods are put away in ravines, in the mountains, among the grass and the undergrowth — they were not set in a worthy place," they said. And yet that Tohil, Awilix, and Hacavitz are great, of great power beyond all the gods of the peoples; great and many are their wonders, in journeying, in wet and in cold, and their very being strikes fear into the hearts of the peoples.

Yet the hearts of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were at peace, and their trust did not fail concerning the god they had carried and borne when they came from Tulan Zuyva, there from the place where the sun rises; and so they remained upon the mountain now called and named: the Dawning-place of Tohil, of Awilix, of Hacavitz, as it is still called today. And now we shall tell of when our grandfathers and our fathers were established and given light, and we shall speak further of the dawning and the appearing of the face of the sun, the moon, and the stars. This, then, is the dawning and the appearing of the sun, the moon, and the stars.

translation.translator_note: The record notes the K'iche' text for paragraph p58 is marked as missing in the source data, though a continuous K'iche' text was in fact supplied for the whole section and used throughout as primary source; Ximénez's Spanish was consulted alongside it for confirmation, especially for a few opaque items (e.g. "nima caeha," rendered here simply as "a great river," and the place-name "Vquin cat" for the Ilocab's dawning-place, left transliterated since neither text glosses it clearly). The passage "xa e qovi vloc mavi quz mi xohpe vi aca roc ohtah xcohilouic ralaxic quih..." is partly obscure in the K'iche'; the rendering follows the sense confirmed by the parallel Spanish lament rather than a strict word-for-word parse. No divergence in substance was found between the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish in this section — the Spanish tracks the K'iche' closely throughout.

review.issues: Minor: (1) place-name "Vquin cat" (Ilocab's dawning-place) is omitted from the English even though the translator note claims it was left transliterated; (2) "nima caeha" rendered "a great river," dropping Ximénez's gloss "agua colorada" (acknowledged in note); (3) "ixahquixb ah cahb" rendered "you who are honored"/"those lords" following Ximénez's Spanish rather than the K'iche' sense "bloodletters/sacrificers" — a softening of an archaic title. The Spanish text includes earlier p58 material (sea crossing, wives, fasting) absent from the K'iche'; the translation rightly covers only the extant K'iche'. Translation shows genuine K'iche' engagement (e.g. follows the K'iche' negative "trust did not fail" against Ximénez's contradictory "estan desesperados").
review.resemblance_note: No specific word-choice or rhythm match to Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, Christenson, or other known translations; diction appears independently composed.

title: Events preceding first light

paragraphs: Great then was the joy of Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam when they saw the morning star. It came out first, glittering, its face appeared first, before the face of the sun. Then they untied their copal, which had come from there, from the place where the sun rises — this was the task in their hearts when they untied the three gifts that they had resolved upon in their hearts.

Mixtam Pom was the name of the copal that Balam Quiꜩe carried. Cauizton Pom, in turn, was the name of the one that Balam Acab carried. Cabavil Pom was the name of the one that Mahucutah carried. The three of them had this copal, and this they burned when they went dancing toward the place where the sun rises. Sweetly they wept as they danced, and they burned their copal, their beloved, their precious copal. And then they wept, because they had not yet seen, had not yet witnessed, the birth of the sun.

Then, when the sun came forth, the small animals and the great animals rejoiced. All of them rose up out of the waters and the ravines where they had been, and stood at the edges of the hills; together they turned their faces to where the sun was coming out. Then the puma and the jaguar cried out; the first to sing was the bird called Queletzu. Truly all the animals rejoiced — they spread their wings, the eagle, the white vulture, the small birds and the great birds. And the lords knelt down, Rah Quixb, Rah Cahb, greatly rejoicing together with the vassals of Tamub, Ilocab, and Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, the Ah Quiinaha, and Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Quibaha, Ah Batena, together with the Yaqui Tepeu — however many the peoples were, even those who exist now and cannot be counted, all the people together: for all of them, dawn broke as one.

Then the face of the earth was dried by the sun. The sun was like a man when it showed itself, and its face was hot, and thus it dried the face of the earth. Before the sun, the face of the earth had been all mud and dampness; before the sun, it had only just been lifted up. The sun was like one man, but its heat was not yet strongly felt — only its likeness was shown when it was born; only its mirror-image remained. It is not truly this sun that shines now, so it is said, in the true account.

Then at once Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz turned to stone, together with the gods of the puma, the jaguar, the rattlesnake, and the Zaquicoxol — they only clung fast to the trees and the rocks when the sun, moon, and stars appeared. Everywhere they became stone. Perhaps we would not be alive today because of those ravenous animals, the puma, the jaguar, the rattlesnake, the Zaquicoxol — perhaps the first animals would not have turned to stone, were it not for the sun. When the sun rose, great joy filled the hearts of Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; greatly they rejoiced when dawn broke.

They were not yet many people where they dwelt; they were still few when they were there atop the mountain of Hacavitz. There dawn broke upon them, and there they burned copal and danced, facing toward the place where the sun rises. From there they had come — that was their mountain, their home; from there came Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, for these were their names. There they grew and multiplied atop the mountain; this became their citadel, and there they were when the sun, moon, and stars appeared. Dawn broke, the face of the whole earth was lit, and they were there. Then began their song, called Camucu, which they sang with grief in their hearts and their bellies, and this is what they said within their song:

"Alas, we were lost at Tulan; we were scattered there, and our elder and younger brothers were left behind there. Have you truly seen the sun? Where are you now?" — so, when dawn broke, they said to Rah Quixb and Rah Cahb of the Yaqui people. And likewise Tohil was the name of the god of the Yaqui people; Yolcuat Quiꜩalcuat was his name. "We parted there at Tulan Zuyva; that is where we set out from together, and that is the completeness of our being, when we came," they said to one another, as they remembered their elder brothers, the works of the Yaqui people, whose dawn broke there in what is now called Mexico, and who still exist.

And also the Chahcar people were left there in the east — Tepeu and Oliman were their names, and they remained behind there. They said: great was the sorrow of their hearts there atop Hacavitz. And so too did those of Tamub and Ilocab; and there likewise, in that same land, are the people called Dan. Dawn broke there for the vassals of Tamub together with their god, and it too was Tohil — for it was but one name, the name of the god of the three branches of the Quiché people. And likewise still was the name of the god of the Rabinaleb, only slightly changed — Hun Toh, in turn, was the name of the god of the Rabinaleb; and for this reason their speech is nearly the same as that of the Quiché.

But the speech of the Cakchiquel became different, because different was the name of their god when they came from there, from Tulan Zuyva — Tzotziha Chimalcan was the name of their god; and so their speech became different, as it is now. And from the name of their god they also took the name of their lineage, called Ah Pozotzil, Ah Poxa. And for the god as well, the speech was changed, when the god was given to them there at Tulan; behind the rock their speech was changed, when they came from Tulan, in the darkness. Yet it was one and the same, and thus dawn broke for all the tribes, each having its own name for its god, according to its own group.

Now we shall tell of their stay and their waiting there atop the mountain, the four of them together — Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were their names — their hearts weeping for Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz, who remained there among the grasses and the brush, on their behalf.

translation.translator_note: Several passages are genuinely obscure and rendered as best sense from context, checked against Ximénez's Spanish: "xucuxuxinac" (rendered "knelt down") is uncertain in root; "ah quixb, ah cahb" and the string of ethnonyms (Ah Quiinaha, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Quibaha, Ah Batena, Yaqui Tepeu, Chahcar, Dan) are left as proper names/tribal designations rather than translated, following the Spanish's own transliteration practice. "vꜩacat ca vach" (rendered "the completeness of our being") is a difficult idiom; the K'iche' and Spanish agree closely in overall sense throughout this section, with no major divergence in meaning, only in idiom.

review.issues: Minor: the five-item animal-god list (coh, balam, zochoh, canti, zaquicoxol; Ximénez: leon, tigre, vibora, canti, duende) is collapsed to four, merging the two snakes into one "rattlesnake" in both occurrences. "Clung fast to the trees and the rocks" adds "rocks" not in K'iche' or Spanish (trees/sticks only). "Ah quixb, ah cahb" is left as proper names rather than translated ("penitents/sacrificers"), but this is disclosed in the translator's note and follows Ximénez. Otherwise faithful, with genuine engagement with the K'iche' beyond the Spanish.
review.resemblance_note: No specific match to Recinos, Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson; distinctive renderings and retained manuscript-era name spellings diverge from all standard published versions.

When the sun rose, great joy filled the hearts of Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; greatly they rejoiced when dawn broke.

They were not yet many people where they dwelt; they were still few when they were there atop the mountain of Hacavitz. There dawn broke upon them, and there they burned copal and danced, facing toward the place where the sun rises. From there they had come — that was their mountain, their home; from there came Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, for these were their names. There they grew and multiplied atop the mountain; this became their citadel, and there they were when the sun, moon, and stars appeared. Dawn broke, the face of the whole earth was lit, and they were there. Then began their song, called Camucu, which they sang with grief in their hearts and their bellies, and this is what they said within their song:

"Alas, we were lost at Tulan; we were scattered there, and our elder and younger brothers were left behind there. Have you truly seen the sun? Where are you now?" — so, when dawn broke, they said to Rah Quixb and Rah Cahb of the Yaqui people. And likewise Tohil was the name of the god of the Yaqui people; Yolcuat Quiꜩalcuat was his name. "We parted there at Tulan Zuyva; that is where we set out from together, and that is the completeness of our being, when we came," they said to one another, as they remembered their elder brothers, the works of the Yaqui people, whose dawn broke there in what is now called Mexico, and who still exist.

And also the Chahcar people were left there in the east — Tepeu and Oliman were their names, and they remained behind there. They said: great was the sorrow of their hearts there atop Hacavitz. And so too did those of Tamub and Ilocab; and there likewise, in that same land, are the people called Dan. Dawn broke there for the vassals of Tamub together with their god, and it too was Tohil — for it was but one name, the name of the god of the three branches of the Quiché people. And likewise still was the name of the god of the Rabinaleb, only slightly changed — Hun Toh, in turn, was the name of the god of the Rabinaleb; and for this reason their speech is nearly the same as that of the Quiché.

But the speech of the Cakchiquel became different, because different was the name of their god when they came from there, from Tulan Zuyva — Tzotziha Chimalcan was the name of their god; and so their speech became different, as it is now. And from the name of their god they also took the name of their lineage, called Ah Pozotzil, Ah Poxa. And for the god as well, the speech was changed, when the god was given to them there at Tulan; behind the rock their speech was changed, when they came from Tulan, in the darkness. Yet it was one and the same, and thus dawn broke for all the tribes, each having its own name for its god, according to its own group.

Now we shall tell of their stay and their waiting there atop the mountain, the four of them together — Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were their names — their hearts weeping for Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz, who remained there among the grasses and the brush, on their behalf.
final.translator_note: Several passages are genuinely obscure and rendered as best sense from context, checked against Ximénez's Spanish: "xucuxuxinac" (rendered "knelt down") is uncertain in root; "ah quixb, ah cahb" and the string of ethnonyms (Ah Quiinaha, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Quibaha, Ah Batena, Yaqui Tepeu, Chahcar, Dan) are left as proper names/tribal designations rather than translated, following the Spanish's own transliteration practice. "vꜩacat ca vach" (rendered "the completeness of our being") is a difficult idiom; the K'iche' and Spanish agree closely in overall sense throughout this section, with no major divergence in meaning, only in idiom.

title: First dawn; the hardening of the stone gods

paragraphs: This was the beginning of the founding, the setting of the seat of Tohil. Then they went before Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz to visit them, to greet them and give thanks for the dawning. Now the stone was already split open, out in the wilderness, and it spoke only in a marvelous, spirit-way. When the lords, the Ahquixb and Ahcahb, came before Tohil, they carried nothing of great worth — only resin, and rachacnoh, together with pericón, which they burned before their god. Then Tohil spoke, only in that marvelous, spirit-way, and gave his counsel to the Ahquixb and Ahcahb.

They said, speaking thus: 'Here shall be our mountain-place, our valley-place. You are ours now — it has dawned; great is our sun, and great too is our lineage, because of all the people who are ours, all the nations. And we too shall be your companions; wherever the towns may be, give us your counsel as well — do not show yourselves before the people; be patient, for it is true that they exist, that they will be there, but do not let yourselves be caught in a snare because of it. Only give them the discarded husk, the worthless straw. Only let them bring you the doe, the hen-bird, a little of their blood — give that to them. Turn away your faces, hide the hide of the deer that is left over — that shall stand for the deer, and it shall also be shown before the people; wherever Tohil is spoken of, this deer shall be shown to them. And it will not be wrong for you to do this, for it will only increase your greatness, working upon all the peoples, receiving their blood, their fat, before you, wolf.' So Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz said. They appeared as young men when they were seen, when the offering was brought before them. Then began the hunting of the young of the birds and of the deer, sought out by the lords Ahquixb and Ahcahb. And when they found the young birds and fawns, they went and took their blood and set it upon the mouth of the stone of Tohil and Awilix. And indeed the stone spoke as soon as it was given blood, whenever the lords Ahquixb and Ahcahb arrived to bring their thanks. So too they did before the deer, burning resin and pericón and holom ocox, for the deer, each in its own place where it gathered, up on the mountain. They no longer stayed in their houses; they remained only on the heights of the mountains, wandering. They ate only the grubs of wasps, the grubs of bees, and of ants, seeking such food, and there was no good food or drink for them, and no one knew where their homes were, nor was it known where their wives were. And from this many peoples went on founding themselves, each of the tribes gathering together, and they settled themselves near the roads, and their roads lay open and visible. But as for Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, it was not known where they were.

And when the people saw them passing along the road, they would go into the passes of the mountains, and only the track of a coyote, or the track of a wildcat, would be seen there — they went about making only the track of a puma, only the track of a jaguar. And when the people saw the tracks, they said it was only a coyote that had entered, or a wildcat, or only a puma, only a jaguar. The people said: 'These surely are not men at heart, all these people — this is a mere trick of theirs; when they do this their hearts truly want it, they feel no shame doing it, they clearly desire to enter as puma, to enter as jaguar.' Yet when the people found one track or two, they said, they lost the trail and could go no further. Then the four would go home to their wives, bringing only the grubs of wasps and of bees, which they carried and gave to their wives each day. Then they went before Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz, and said in their hearts: 'To Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz we shall give only the blood of deer and birds; we shall only pierce our own ears and our elbows, and ask that strength and power be given us by Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz — will this not put an end to the killing of the people, who are being killed one by one?' So they said among themselves. And they went before Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz, and pierced their ears and their elbows before the god, and smeared on their blood and set it into the mouth of the stone. And truly they were not stones — they looked like mere boys when seen. And the lords rejoiced then over the blood of the Ahquixb and Ahcahb. Then came the sign of what they had done: 'Take their skins — this shall be your deliverance. From there it came, from Tulan, when you brought it here,' they were told. And then was given to them the hide called Qum Pa Zilizib, along with the smearing of the blood — it was blood from their own backs that was given, the gift of Tohil, together with Awilix and Hacawitz.

This, now, was the beginning of the stealing of the people, of the nations, by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. Then followed the killing of the people — those who died, whether one was taken or two were taken, could not be counted. Then they would go and sacrifice them before Tohil and Awilix, and then they would leave their blood spilled along the road and roll their heads down the road. And the people said, 'It is the jaguar that has eaten them' — so they said, because the tracks made looked just like a jaguar's; and so the four did not show themselves. Great was the number of people they stole, and the people were slow to notice it. 'Perhaps it is Tohil, Awilix, that comes here and hunts only for our chiefs. Where might their houses be? Let us follow the tracks,' said all the people. Then they took counsel among themselves, and began to follow the tracks of the lords Ahquixb and Ahcahb, but no true track could be found — only the tracks of deer could they see, and the tracks of jaguar; no track could be found, for none remained where the first tracks had been, since they were only scattered and undone; the road could not be followed. Only mist rose, only black rain came, only yellow mist rose, only dark rain came before the eyes of the people, and so their hearts grew weary of the search, and they gave it up, because great was the being of Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz. Far off, up on the mountain, this is what they did. As for the people they killed — this was when the theft of people first began, being carried off along the road and sacrificed before Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz; and their children were saved there, up on the mountain. Now Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz, before their children, in their own likeness, walked about only in the spirit-form of the stone; they stayed beside a river. There they used to bathe, at the water's edge — this alone was their manifestation, and it was named their bathing-place; Tohil-Water became the name of that place. Many times the people saw them, and quickly they would vanish when the people caught sight of them. And so it came to be known where Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were. And this, then, is what put it into the minds of the people to kill them.

translation.translator_note: Several words resisted certain identification: "ahquixb ahcahb" is a title for the priest-lords (nawal-holders) that I left transliterated, following the Spanish's implicit treatment of it as a proper title rather than translating; "vrachac noh" (Sp. "ra chac noh," glossed as also a kind of resin) I left as-is since neither text defines it further. "Holom ocox" is glossed by Ximénez as "an herb," left untranslated. "Zilizib"/"Pazilizib," the name of the hide/garment given to the founders, is treated by Ximénez as a proper name ("pazilizib") and I have kept it as such (Qum Pa Zilizib), though the exact referent (a specific skin/garment associated with the Tohil cult) is uncertain. The animal-track passage ("xaroquibal vtiu... roquibal yac... roquibal coh, roquibal balam") lists four animals (fox/coyote, wildcat, puma, jaguar) whose Spanish glosses (lobo, gato de monte, leon, tigre) reflect colonial usage (leon=puma, tigre=jaguar in Mesoamerican Spanish); I have rendered these as coyote, wildcat, puma, and jaguar to match the actual fauna referenced. The clause describing what the founders eat while in hiding ("qui a mul... torob... xnam queh xnam qiquin") was genuinely difficult; I followed the Spanish's sense of "grubs of wasps and bees, honeycomb" for the parallel passage about the founders living wild, but for the earlier clause about what they must not give the people ("ralquim ral torob") I likewise render as grubs/insects, consistent with Ximénez, though the precise entomological terms are uncertain. Where the K'iche' and Spanish diverge slightly — e.g., the Spanish reads the closing scene as the people "finding out" where the four were, while the K'iche' more literally says knowledge of their location "came" (xpe chicut retal) — I have followed the K'iche' sense throughout, translating fresh rather than adopting Ximénez's phrasing.

review.issues: Minor: "before you, wolf" for "chul vi coh" — coh is puma, not wolf, and the clause is garbled in both witnesses; "Take their skins" for "chichaconisah quihe" — quihe means "their tails" (Ximénez: "ganaldes las colas"); the rendering "discarded husk, worthless straw" for "ralquim ral torob" follows Ximénez and is defensible, but contradicts the translator's own note claiming grubs/insects there. Otherwise the English tracks the K'iche' closely, including places where it rightly departs from Ximénez's paraphrase (the animal-track passage, the closing "retal" clause).
review.resemblance_note: No specific lexical/rhythmic match to Recinos, Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson; shared phrases (e.g. "like boys", Tohil's bath) are the obvious literal renderings of the K'iche'.

And from this many peoples went on founding themselves, each of the tribes gathering together, and they settled themselves near the roads, and their roads lay open and visible. But as for Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, it was not known where they were.

And when the people saw them passing along the road, they would go into the passes of the mountains, and only the track of a coyote, or the track of a wildcat, would be seen there — they went about making only the track of a puma, only the track of a jaguar. And when the people saw the tracks, they said it was only a coyote that had entered, or a wildcat, or only a puma, only a jaguar. The people said: 'These surely are not men at heart, all these people — this is a mere trick of theirs; when they do this their hearts truly want it, they feel no shame doing it, they clearly desire to enter as puma, to enter as jaguar.' Yet when the people found one track or two, they said, they lost the trail and could go no further. Then the four would go home to their wives, bringing only the grubs of wasps and of bees, which they carried and gave to their wives each day. Then they went before Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz, and said in their hearts: 'To Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz we shall give only the blood of deer and birds; we shall only pierce our own ears and our elbows, and ask that strength and power be given us by Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz — will this not put an end to the killing of the people, who are being killed one by one?' So they said among themselves. And they went before Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz, and pierced their ears and their elbows before the god, and smeared on their blood and set it into the mouth of the stone. And truly they were not stones — they looked like mere boys when seen. And the lords rejoiced then over the blood of the Ahquixb and Ahcahb. Then came the sign of what they had done: 'Take their skins — this shall be your deliverance. From there it came, from Tulan, when you brought it here,' they were told. And then was given to them the hide called Qum Pa Zilizib, along with the smearing of the blood — it was blood from their own backs that was given, the gift of Tohil, together with Awilix and Hacawitz.

This, now, was the beginning of the stealing of the people, of the nations, by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. Then followed the killing of the people — those who died, whether one was taken or two were taken, could not be counted. Then they would go and sacrifice them before Tohil and Awilix, and then they would leave their blood spilled along the road and roll their heads down the road. And the people said, 'It is the jaguar that has eaten them' — so they said, because the tracks made looked just like a jaguar's; and so the four did not show themselves. Great was the number of people they stole, and the people were slow to notice it. 'Perhaps it is Tohil, Awilix, that comes here and hunts only for our chiefs. Where might their houses be? Let us follow the tracks,' said all the people. Then they took counsel among themselves, and began to follow the tracks of the lords Ahquixb and Ahcahb, but no true track could be found — only the tracks of deer could they see, and the tracks of jaguar; no track could be found, for none remained where the first tracks had been, since they were only scattered and undone; the road could not be followed. Only mist rose, only black rain came, only yellow mist rose, only dark rain came before the eyes of the people, and so their hearts grew weary of the search, and they gave it up, because great was the being of Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz. Far off, up on the mountain, this is what they did. As for the people they killed — this was when the theft of people first began, being carried off along the road and sacrificed before Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz; and their children were saved there, up on the mountain. Now Tohil, Awilix, and Hacawitz, before their children, in their own likeness, walked about only in the spirit-form of the stone; they stayed beside a river. There they used to bathe, at the water's edge — this alone was their manifestation, and it was named their bathing-place; Tohil-Water became the name of that place. Many times the people saw them, and quickly they would vanish when the people caught sight of them. And so it came to be known where Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were. And this, then, is what put it into the minds of the people to kill them.
final.translator_note: Several words resisted certain identification: "ahquixb ahcahb" is a title for the priest-lords (nawal-holders) that I left transliterated, following the Spanish's implicit treatment of it as a proper title rather than translating; "vrachac noh" (Sp. "ra chac noh," glossed as also a kind of resin) I left as-is since neither text defines it further. "Holom ocox" is glossed by Ximénez as "an herb," left untranslated. "Zilizib"/"Pazilizib," the name of the hide/garment given to the founders, is treated by Ximénez as a proper name ("pazilizib") and I have kept it as such (Qum Pa Zilizib), though the exact referent (a specific skin/garment associated with the Tohil cult) is uncertain. The animal-track passage ("xaroquibal vtiu... roquibal yac... roquibal coh, roquibal balam") lists four animals (fox/coyote, wildcat, puma, jaguar) whose Spanish glosses (lobo, gato de monte, leon, tigre) reflect colonial usage (leon=puma, tigre=jaguar in Mesoamerican Spanish); I have rendered these as coyote, wildcat, puma, and jaguar to match the actual fauna referenced. The clause describing what the founders eat while in hiding ("qui a mul... torob... xnam queh xnam qiquin") was genuinely difficult; I followed the Spanish's sense of "grubs of wasps and bees, honeycomb" for the parallel passage about the founders living wild, but for the earlier clause about what they must not give the people ("ralquim ral torob") I likewise render as grubs/insects, consistent with Ximénez, though the precise entomological terms are uncertain. Where the K'iche' and Spanish diverge slightly — e.g., the Spanish reads the closing scene as the people "finding out" where the four were, while the K'iche' more literally says knowledge of their location "came" (xpe chicut retal) — I have followed the K'iche' sense throughout, translating fresh rather than adopting Ximénez's phrasing.

title: Balam Ki'tze' and the first patriarchs

paragraphs: First the peoples wanted to take counsel on how to overcome Tohil, Awilix, and Hakawitz. This the lords proposed before the peoples. And all were called and summoned, and not one tribe, not two, held back — all of them gathered and called to one another. And then they took counsel, and said, asking one another: What shall we do to overcome these additions to the Quiché, for our vassals are being finished off, for it is not clear how the people are being lost — whether we ourselves are the cause of it, through theft that has been done, or whether this is great anger on the part of Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz. And if this Tohil is to be our god in bondage, it will not be possible for us to overcome them — are we not many men, after all, while this addition of ours is few? This they said when they had all gathered.

And one part of the peoples spoke and said: where has anyone seen him bathe in the river, every day? And if this is Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz, we shall conquer them there first, and that is where the conquering of the great ones will begin. This said the one half when it spoke. And they said: and with what shall we conquer them? said the rest. This is how we shall conquer them, they said, for they are young men when they show themselves at the river. Let two maidens go, and let them be very beautiful, very fair maidens, and let their desire go out to them. Very well, said all of them. Let us seek two beautiful maidens, they said. And then they sought among their own daughters, and indeed they were very fair young women.

And they gave them their orders, and said: Daughters, go wash clothes at the river, and if three young men should see you, strip yourselves before them, and if they desire you, say to them: we will come to where you are, if they say that to you. Tell them yes, and when you are asked from where you have come, and whose daughters you are, tell them: we are daughters of the lords. And tell them to give you a sign, and bring back whatever sign they give you. And if they wish to lie with you, give yourselves to them; and mark this — if you do not give yourselves, we will put you to death. And if you bring back a sign, then our hearts will be glad toward you. This they ordered the two maidens, who were named, one Xtah, and the other Xpuch. This was the whole counsel of the peoples.

Then they went off, they went to adorn themselves, when they went there to bathe where Tohil bathed, and Awilix, and Hakawitz. And the lords rejoiced over their two daughters whom they had sent. And when they arrived at the water, they began to wash, and the two of them undressed, and each stood at her stone working, when Tohil, Awilix, and Hakawitz came. They arrived at the river, and for a little they only glimpsed the faces of the two maidens as they washed; the maidens felt no shame at first, but when Tohil came, they were ashamed — and yet Tohil did not desire the two maidens at all.

And they were asked: from where have you come? the two maidens were asked. What is it you want, that you have come here to our water? And they were told: we were sent here by the lords, and they said to us, go, look upon the face of Tohil — this was said to us. And when they had spoken their errand, this is what the peoples wanted: that the maidens should be violated by the naguals of Tohil. So said Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz. And they said again to Xtah and Xpuch, for so the maidens were called: very well, a sign of our word shall go with you — wait a little, it shall be given, to be carried to the lords.

And then the patriarchs took counsel among themselves, and it was said again to them, to Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam: paint the sign — the mark of what you are — so that it may come before the lords, before the peoples, when the two maidens who are washing carry it and give it to them. This was said, this was they were told, to Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab, and Mahucutah.
