translation.translator_note: Several points of note: (1) The K'iche' text near the end says "oxib cul" ("three cloths/garments") to be painted with the sign, and its closing line names only three patriarchs (Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab, Mahucutah), while Ximénez's Spanish adds a fourth, Iqui Balam, in both places. I have followed the K'iche' order of naming (four named when the instruction is first given, matching "oxib cul" only loosely) but preserved the K'iche's own omission of Iqui Balam from the final repetition rather than silently harmonizing to the Spanish's tidier four-name list — this is a genuine inconsistency in the source, not a translation choice. (2) "Naguals" (K'iche' "naual") is left untranslated as a technical term (the animal/spirit co-essence or supernatural aspect of Tohil) since "spirit-double" or similar would narrow a concept broader than any single English word; Ximénez glosses it the same way in Spanish. (3) The passage describing the maidens' reaction to Tohil is compressed and slightly ambiguous in the K'iche' ("xa cu zcaquin xrocoibeh qui vach... xa huzu xequixbic ta xeopon"); I read it as: Tohil and the other two gods only briefly glimpsed the maidens washing, the maidens were at first unashamed, then grew ashamed once Tohil arrived — but Tohil felt no desire for them at all, which is the pivot of the episode (the ruse of sending beautiful women fails). (4) "Vꜫaꜫal"/"vꜩinic" type constructions around slavery/bondage of the god are rendered "in bondage" / "to enslave," following Ximénez's "en esclauítud," since the K'iche' root here is unusual and the Spanish gloss is the clearest guide to sense.

review.issues: Right section confirmed. Main issue: the K'iche' "oxib cul" (three cloths to be painted with the sign) is omitted from the translated body text ("paint the sign — the mark of what you are"), though the translator's note discusses it — the cloths are plot-critical and should appear in the text. Also "great anger" follows Ximénez's "grande enojo" where the K'iche' "nim vꜫaꜫal" (q'aq'al) more plausibly means "great glory/power" — a spot where the Spanish was reworded without the K'iche' clearly supporting it. The maidens' reported errand is slightly compressed (K'iche' also has "speak with them" and mention of the sign). Otherwise faithful; four-vs-three patriarch inconsistency correctly preserved from the K'iche' and documented. Minor typo: "this was they were told."
review.resemblance_note: No specific match to Recinos, Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson in word choice, name forms, or rhythm; reads as freshly composed from the manuscript.

title: Wives obtained; further wanderings

paragraphs: Then the three of them painted. First Balam Quiꜩe painted; the image of a jaguar he painted on the cloth. And Balam Acab painted his image, which was an eagle, on the cloth. And when Mahucutah painted, he painted wasps and hornets, all over covered with wasps was his painting on the cloth. The three of them finished their paintings; in three folds they painted. Then they went to give the cloths to the ones called Xtah and Xpuch. Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah said to them: "This is the token of your word; truly go and carry it before the lords and the judges. Truly Tohil has spoken to us, and this is the token we bring — this you shall tell them. And give them the mantles, that they may put them on." This was told to the maidens when they were sent off.

So they went, and they carried the painted cloths. When they arrived, the lords rejoiced greatly when they saw them, and the maidens came bearing what they had gone to seek hanging from their hands. "Did you perhaps see Tohil's face?" they were asked. "We saw him," said the maidens, Xtah and Xpuch. "And what token did you bring? Is it truly so?" the lords said. They thought it was the token of their having sinned with him. Then the maidens spread out the painted cloths before the lords, and there were jaguars all over, eagles all over, and wasps and hornets all over, painted within the cloth, gleaming to look at. And they desired to put them on. The first one put his on, and the jaguar that was painted on the cloth did nothing to him. Then the second lord put his on, in which was the eagle, and it did nothing to him either, and he went about before everyone, for they had asked that he put it on. Then the third put his on, painted with wasps and hornets, and at once the wasps and hornets began to sting his whole body. He could not bear it, he could not endure the stings of the painted creatures, and the lord cried out because of the creatures Mahucutah had painted in the third cloth.

So the lords were defeated, and the maidens Xtah and Xpuch were shamed by them: "What cloths are these you have brought? Where did you go to get them, demons?" the maidens were told when they were disgraced — and their defeat became known to all the tribes, because of Tohil. For what the lords had wanted was for Tohil to go after the two maidens, Xtah and Xpuch, and for the maidens to have made themselves whores at the will of the peoples, and to have become a temptation for Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah. But it did not come to pass; they were not deceived through their nagual spirits.

Then all the peoples took counsel again: "What are we to do to these men? Truly great is their being, now that it has come to this," they said again when they gathered in council. "What we shall do is overcome them, defeat them, and kill them. We shall arm ourselves with our bows and our shields. Are we not many? Let there not remain even one, not a single one of them," they said when they took their decision. Then all the peoples armed themselves, and a great many killers of all the peoples gathered together.

And Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were then upon the summit of the hill called Hacaviꜩ; there they sheltered their sons upon the hill, and they were few, not like the multitude that were the sons of the peoples — only small was the summit of the hill on which they had fortified themselves. Nor had it yet been resolved how they would be killed by the peoples, when all had armed themselves, when all had gathered, when all had assembled together. translation.translator_note: Title of the section ("Wives obtained") does not clearly match this passage's content, which concerns the painted cloths sent to test the lords' claim to have seen Tohil, and the subsequent war of the peoples against Balam Quiꜩe and his companions on Hacaviꜩ — no wife-taking occurs here; this may simply be a mislabeled/boilerplate section title carried over from the sections list rather than a translation issue. review.issues: Right section confirmed: the translation tracks the K'iche' paragraph by paragraph (painted cloths, Xtah/Xpuch, stinging of the third lord, war council, Hacavitz, night plucking of the sleeping warriors, effigies on the rampart, four gourds of wasps). Minor points: (1) "before the lords and the judges" — the K'iche' has only "chiquivach ahauab" (before the lords); "and the judges" is a small unwarranted addition (Ximénez likewise has only "ante los Señores"). (2) Tohil's speech "this here is for you" softens "are cut chicoh va chiquech" (Ximénez: "esto les meterís a ellos"), better "this you shall use against them" — slight drift. (3) "as their humiliation it was made a sign" compresses "xa pu michbal quech xbanic retal vnimal queche vinac" reasonably. The oddly literal renderings (e.g. "together with their jade beads and their necks and their staffs", mirroring the source's own awkward "ruq puch qui chachal... vcul quichami") show genuine engagement with the K'iche', with the Spanish used for confirmation, as the translator's note claims. The translator correctly flags that the section title does not match the content — that is a sections-list labeling issue, not a translation fault.
review.resemblance_note: Phrasing is literal and idiosyncratic (e.g. "eyebrows/eyelashes", "spies were made of the town", "in three folds they painted") and does not match the diction or rhythm of Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson.

title: Ajpatan, Makujutaj, and the patriarchs' sons

paragraphs: And there they were — Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — all together on the mountain, with their wives and their children, when all the warriors, the killers, came. They did not come as one or two bands only; the tribes surrounded the citadel entirely, howling as they came, armed with arrows and shields. They shrieked, they whistled, they beat their hands together as they closed in to attack, coming to the foot of the citadel. But the lords were not afraid; calmly they watched from the wall, all in order, with their wives and their children, and they waited, poised, for what was to come. The tribes rejoiced as they climbed the mountain — it was very near now, the point where they would fling themselves against the citadel — and then the four lords opened the gourds, all four of them, there in the citadel, and out came the hornets and the wasps, like smoke pouring from the gourds as they were opened. And so the tribes perished, on account of the animals: straight for their eyes the insects went, and for their noses, their mouths, their legs, their arms. Who could catch them, who could gather up all these hornets and wasps that were loosed? Straight into the eyes they went, biting, and the little animals swarmed, piling up on every warrior. The warriors reeled as if drunk from the hornets and wasps, and could no longer grip their arrows and their shields; these fell to the ground and lay scattered, and the warriors sprawled over the mountainside, no longer feeling the arrows shot at them nor the blows of the axes struck against them, for their faces were covered over, hidden beneath the swarm of little animals. And so it happened to every one of the tribesmen: they died because of the hornets and wasps; it was not that the men fought them with weapons, for the tribesmen could no longer take up their arrows or their shields — they were routed, sprawling helplessly across the ground, spreading out, falling down over the face of the mountain. As for the ones who were left, they could no longer rise up; they scattered, fleeing everywhere, once it was seen that Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, and their wives too, had turned into killers. And so, indeed, only a remnant of them was left, and the whole tribe fled from before Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah. "Have mercy on us, do not kill us!" they cried out. "Very well," they were told, "though you deserve to die, you shall only become our tributaries, from this day forward." Thus it was that the whole tribe was defeated, by our first mothers and fathers there, and this happened on the mountain called Hacavitz — its name was earned by this defeat. This was the first place where they were settled, where they arrived, where they multiplied, where they had daughters and sons, on Hacavitz. And they rejoiced greatly when they had defeated every tribe there, when the defeating was accomplished on the mountain; thus they accomplished the defeat of the tribes, of all the tribes.

After this their hearts grew calm, and they spoke to their sons, for they knew their death and their end were drawing near, and they wished to tell them before they died. And so it is again that we shall tell of the death of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. Knowing that their death, their vanishing, was at hand, they gave counsel to their sons. They were not sick, nor were they in agony, nor were they dying in pain, when they gave their instruction to their sons. These are the names of their sons: Balam Quitzé had two sons — Qocaib was named the first, Qocavib the name of his second son, sons of Balam Quitzé, ancestors and forefathers of the Cavek. And Balam Acab likewise had two sons — these were their names: Qoacul was the name of his first son, Qoacutec the name of his second son, sons of Balam Acab, of the Nihaib. And Mahucutah begot only one son, Qoahau by name. These three had sons; Iqui Balam had no sons. These, then, were the names of their sons, the true lords. Then they gave their instruction, all four of them together, and they sang, and their hearts grieved as they sang, and the song they sang was called "Kamucu" — that was the name of the song they sang. And then they gave their instruction to their sons: "O our sons, we are going, we are returning; a wise and clear word we leave with you as instruction, and we too, when we came from yonder, from across the sea, from that our homeland — that is what we told our wives, we spoke to each of them." "We are going, our task is done, our days are fulfilled. Remember us well, do not forget us; you shall yet see your homeland and your mountain-place — settle it, and there let it be, as it was from the beginning." "Go, then, and you shall see again the place we came from," thus they said when they gave their farewell instruction. And then Balam Quitzé left the sign of his being, saying: "This is a remembrance which I leave with you; this shall be your greatness, for I now take my leave, having given you my counsel, and I am sorrowful," he said as he left them the sign of his being, called the Pizom Qaqal, the Sacred Bundle — whose form was not seen, for it was wrapped up and could not be untied, nor was its stitching visible, for no one saw when it was wrapped. Thus it was that they gave their counsel, and then they vanished there on the mountain of Hacavitz, and they were not buried by their wives or their children, for their disappearance was not seen — the leave-taking alone was seen, and thereafter the Bundle was precious to them, kept in remembrance of their fathers. And so it was that they wept before that remembrance of their fathers, for it was there before their eyes, before their remembrance of their fathers. When the people were born, multiplied by these lords, the descendants of Balam Quitzé began there — this was the origin of the grandfathers and fathers of the Cavek. And so it was that the sons did not lose their inheritance: only these two, Qocaib and Qocavib, remained of the four, our first fathers and grandfathers, when they vanished. Thus it was they left their sons there on the mountain of Hacavitz, who then took root as their sons there. And now that the tribes were humbled and had no more greatness of their own, the tribes only served and carried burdens, all their days. They remembered their fathers, and the Bundle was a great thing to them, though they did not open it, for it remained wrapped, kept together with them, called by them the Wrapped Greatness. And so it was celebrated, and its name was given, that which their father left them in trust, only as a remembrance of who they had been, when they did it. Thus it was when Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam vanished and were lost. They were the first men who came from the other side of the sea, from where the sun rises; long ago they came here, and they died being already very old, and they are called the Venerable Ones, the Revered Ones.

translation.translator_note: The section title mentions "Ajpatan" and "Makujutaj" but these do not appear as distinct terms in this K'iche' passage as given (the text names "ahquixb ahcahb" — priests/lords of sacrifice — and "Mahucutah," one of the four original patriarchs; "Ajpatan" may reflect an editorial title label not directly reflected in this excerpt's wording, or a variant reading I could not independently verify against the transcription provided). I have translated "cocob"/"gourds" containing hornets and wasps as literally as the K'iche' supports (this matches Ximénez's "calabazas" — calabashes/gourds). The "Pizom Qaqal" (K'iche' "pizom ꜫaꜫal") is left partly untranslated as a proper term, glossed as "Sacred Bundle" / "Wrapped Greatness," following the sense both texts converge on (Spanish: "la magestad, y grandeza embuelta" — "the wrapped majesty and greatness"). Some short phrases in the K'iche' (e.g., a garbled sequence near "vꜩbala xa xix vi camel...ix ahpatan chibe quih chibe zac") were difficult to parse with full confidence due to apparent transcription corruption; I relied more heavily on the parallel Spanish there to establish general sense (mercy/tribute plea before the "ahpatan" — tribute-payers/subjects), while keeping wording my own rather than copying Ximénez's phrasing.

review.issues: RIGHT SECTION: yes — the extracted entry (id s30, title matching) covers exactly what the translation renders: the wasp/hornet gourd defeat of the tribes on Hacavitz, their submission as tributaries, the naming of the patriarchs' sons (Qocaib/Qocavib of the Cavek, Qoacul/Qoacutec of the Nihaib, Qoahau of Mahucutah, Iqui Balam sonless), the Kamucu song, the farewell, the Pizom Q'aq'al bundle, and the patriarchs' disappearance. FIDELITY: largely accurate and clearly worked from the K'iche' (e.g. correctly restores 'Kamucu' where Ximénez garbles it to 'qamaqu', and keeps K'iche' details Ximénez alters), but three real problems: (1) OMISSION — the K'iche' 'xechoi chi icah xa bolah che xquicoh chic balam quiꜩe balam acab' (they were hacked with axes; only bare staves/sticks did Balam Quitzé and Balam Acab wield) loses its second half: the striking detail that the patriarchs finished the rout with mere bare sticks (Ximénez: 'solo palos mondos sacaron') is dropped entirely. (2) OMISSION — in the farewell speech the K'iche' 'cholan chic cahaual queh leman chicah' (our Lord of the Deer is set in order, manifest in the sky — kept by Ximénez as 'ya queda en orden el Señor de los venados, manifiesto está en el cielo') is silently replaced by the generic 'our task is done, our days are fulfilled'; a mythologically significant clause vanishes. (3) MISTRANSLATION — 'xecaton chuvach qui nababal' means they burned (incense/offerings) before the memorial of their fathers; Ximénez reads 'cantaron' (sang); the translation's 'they wept before that remembrance' matches neither source and is invented. Minor drifts: 'ri chahcar' (the half of them; Ximénez 'la mitad') softened to 'a remnant'; final 'e ahquixb ahcahb' rendered 'Venerable Ones, Revered Ones' following Ximénez's 'respetados y acatados' rather than the K'iche' term (sacrificers/offerers) — defensible given the archaic term, and the translator's note honestly flags reliance on the Spanish around the garbled 'ahpatan' passage, which is justified there. MEMORIZATION: no specific match to Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson in wording, order, or rhythm; phrasing reads freshly composed.
review.resemblance_note: No distinctive word-choice or rhythm overlap with Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley; shared items are proper names and unavoidable content words.

title: K'oka'ib', K'o'akutek, K'o'ajaw and the journey to Nakxit

paragraphs: Then they took counsel among themselves there, at the place of the rising sun. This was their thought concerning the command of their fathers, which they had not forgotten — though already long since their fathers had died. They had married and taken parents-in-law; they had taken three wives. And when they had taken wives they said, "Let us go, let us go there to the place of the rising sun, from where our fathers came," they said, when they set out on their road, the three sons: K'oka'ib' was the name of the one, son of Balam Ki'tze', of all the Kaweq; K'o'akutek was the name of the son of Balam Aq'ab, of the Nija'ib'; K'o'ajaw was the name of the other son, of Majukutaj, of the lords of the Kiche'.

These, then, are the names of the ones who went there across the sea, the three of them. They went knowing what they were doing; they were not common men. They gave their charge to all their brothers when they left; joyfully they went. "We shall not die; we shall return," they said when the three set out. So they crossed over the sea, and they arrived there at the place of the rising sun, and they went to receive their lordship. And this was the name of the lord, the ruler of the place of the rising sun, before whom they arrived.

When they came before the lord named Nakxit, a great lord, the sole judge over much, over the greatness of the lordship, he then gave them the emblem of lordship, together with all its likenesses. There came the emblem of the Ajpop, of the Ajpop Kamja; there came the emblem of the greatness of the lordship, and of the Ajpop and the Ajpop Kamja. Nakxit finished giving them all the likenesses of the lordship.

These are their names: the canopy, the throne, the flute, the drum, the small drum, tatil, kanabaj, tzikwil-kotzikwil, the jaguar, the head, the feathers, the deer, makutax, tot, tatam, kuz, buz, kaxkon, chiyom, aztapulul — all of these they carried away when they came. And they crossed back over the sea with the writing of Tulan, the writing, as they called it, in which their entering into things, into their own history, was set down.

Then they arrived there at their citadel called Jakawitz. There all the Tamub and the Ilokab' gathered themselves; all the peoples gathered, and they rejoiced. When K'oka'ib', K'o'akutek, and K'o'ajaw arrived, there they took up the lordship once more, and the peoples rejoiced — the Rabinaleb', the Kaqchikeleb', the Ajkikinaja. They assembled and showed before them the greatness of the lordship. Great indeed was their standing before the peoples; the showing of the lordship was not soon finished. There at Jakawitz they all gathered, all who had come from the place of the rising sun; long did they remain there, together, on the mountain, all of them.

There the wives of Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab, and Majukutaj died, after the sons had come back — for the fathers had grown old, searching out their mountains. On many a mountain they settled; countless were the mountains they occupied, as they grew many and multiplied. These were the first mothers and the first fathers, said the ancient people; they told of it and recounted it, how they left behind their first town called Jakawitz and came to settle another town called Chikix. Long did they remain there, on that one gathering-place of a town, and there they had daughters and had sons, and there they lived.

It was four mountains, yet they gave but a single name to their town. They gave their daughters and their sons in marriage; only as gifts did they give them, without haggling and without bargaining. The bride-price of their daughters they took only in gratitude — good was their way of life there; thus they did.

Then they passed on from there, over the many gathering-places of towns. These are their names: Chikix, Chi'uchak, Jumetaja, Kulba, Kawinal — these were the names of the mountains where they stopped. And they looked to see which mountain would suit their town, and they searched out many mountains, all of them together — though by then those who had gone to receive the lordship at the place of the rising sun were already dead. As grandchildren now they arrived there at one town, not finding their way as they searched; great hardship they suffered until, at last, far off, they found their town. It was their grandchildren and great-grandchildren who arrived — such is the name of the town where they arrived.

translation.translator_note: The list of regalia names (muh, zubac, chamcham, tatil, canabah, ꜩicvil cohꜩicuil, balam, holom, pich, queh, macutax, tot, tatam, quz, buz, caxcon, chiyom, aztapulul) mixes recognizable K'iche' words (muh "shade/canopy," balam "jaguar," holom "head," pich "feathers," queh "deer") with terms that are obscure or possibly borrowed/onomatopoeic (zubac, chamcham, tatil, canabah, macutax, tot, tatam, quz, buz, caxcon, chiyom, aztapulul); Ximénez himself largely transliterated rather than translated these, and I have followed that same caution, translating only the clearly transparent items and leaving the rest as proper names/loanwords. "vrahaual ahrelebal quih" I read as "the lord who ruled the place of the rising sun" (the east), consistent with Ximénez's "el Señor que dominaba en el oriente." The passage on marriage customs ("xa qui chiquizipah xatocobanic xapu maihanic... chiquicamo xa vꜩ") is compressed and slightly ambiguous in the K'iche' itself; I have followed the sense that bride-gifts were given freely/without haggling, and the bride-price taken only as a token of gratitude, which matches Ximénez's Spanish closely. The final lines naming the mountains (chiquix, chiquchac/chi'uchak, humetaha, culba, cavinal) are place names left untranslated, per Ximénez's own treatment.

review.issues: Minor: regalia list renders five English items ("canopy, throne, flute, drum, the small drum") where the K'iche' has four before tatil (muh, galibah, zubac, chamcham) — one drum-item appears duplicated/padded. "qui oquinac chupan quitzih" as "their entering into things, into their own history" is an interpretive stretch of an obscure clause. Spanish gloss of Chikix ("at the thorns") dropped, consistent with the stated place-name policy. Otherwise faithful; Spanish reliance limited to genuinely opaque passages (obscure regalia terms, compressed bride-price clause) and appropriately flagged in the translator note.
review.resemblance_note: Only lexically forced overlaps (e.g. "canopy and throne" for muh/galibaj) shared with all published versions; no distinctive word choice, order, or rhythm matching Recinos, Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson.

title: Chi Ismachi' and the early K'iche' rulers

paragraphs: Chi Ismachi' is the name of the hill and the citizen-town where they came to be, where they settled; there they gave proof of their greatness. There they built [dwellings] of lime and stone. This was the fourth generation of lords, and they said: Conache, and Beleheb Queh, and also the Ealelahau; and when Cotuha became lord, together with Iztayul, they were called Lord of the Mat, Lord of the Throne. There they reigned in Chi Ismachi', and they made it splendid, and made it a fine town. Only three great houses were there in Chi Ismachi'; the twenty-four great houses did not yet exist -- only three great houses: one great house of the Cauiquib, one great house of the Nihaibab, and one great house of the Ahau Quiche. There were only two great divisions [at first], but they were all together there, gathered as one, without wrongdoing, without difficulty; there was only peace and quiet among them, there was no strife, no quarreling -- only peace was in their hearts. There was no envy, and their greatness was still small; they had not yet joined together in power, nor grown haughty. And then they took up the shield there in Chi Ismachi' as the sign of their lordship, and then they made the sign of their greatness and their majesty.

Because of this the Ilocab wished to come and kill Cotuha, and war began on their account; they wanted only one lord for themselves, and they wished to punish Lord Iztayul with death. It was not envy alone that moved against Lord Cotuha, but rather the thought came upon them of killing the lord of the Ilocab. So it was that the disorder and the strife of war began, and they entered and won the first town; the fighters went, and what they wanted was to finish off the Quiche and to reign alone -- this they desired. And for this they came to seize and to take captive, and few were those who escaped and were freed. And then they began to sacrifice the Ilocab before the idol, and this was the payment for their sin, on behalf of Lord Cotuha. Many were those who went into bondage and servitude among those taken captive, and they went to give themselves up, on account of the war that was gathered against them, and the town was destroyed and put to shame. The Ilocab had wanted the lordship of the Quiche, but it did not turn out so for them. And so it was the beginning of men being sacrificed before the idol, when the war was made; and there was the beginning of the fortifying of the town of Chi Ismachi'. And there their greatness began, for great was the lordship of the Quiche and of their lord, and on every side there were powerful lords, and none could overthrow them, none could enter against them. And thus likewise they made great the kingdom that was founded at Chi Ismachi', and there the idol began to be feared, and all the towns, small and great, feared it. And they saw the captives brought in and killed and sacrificed for the greatness of Lord Cotuha and Lord Iztayul, together with the Nihaibab and the Ahau Quiche. And it was only three lineages, or tribes, that were there at Chi Ismachi' -- that was the name of the town -- and there, at Chi Naipuch, they began to establish the food and drink for [the celebrations concerning] their daughters, and thus those three great houses gathered by that name; there they drank their drink and there they ate their food, which was the bride-price of their captive daughters, and it was only for the contentment of their hearts that they ate and drank in their great houses; this was the sign of thanksgiving and invitation for the propagation and the word concerning the women who should bear sons or daughters. There it was that they became great, and among themselves they called themselves by the names of their houses: 'We are companions, we of Cauiquib'; 'we of Nihaib'; 'and we of Ahau Quiche' -- so said the three houses, the three great houses. And a long time they remained there at Chi Ismachi', until they found another town, and they abandoned Chi Ismachi'. Then they rose up from there and came to the town called Cumarcaah by the Quiche, and there the lords Cotuha and Cucumatz came, together with all the lords, in the fifth generation of men since their creation and their being made. And there they built their houses, and there also they built the house of the idol, in the middle, on the height of the town; there they set it when they founded themselves there, when they settled. Then their lordship grew great again, for they had become numerous, and then they resolved together to divide themselves, for already contention had arisen among them over envy of one another, over the bride-price owed for their daughters, and because the drink was not given to them -- and this was the origin of the division and of the arming of themselves, and of the throwing down of the skulls of the dead. And then the nine lineages, or calpuls, were divided, and having quarreled only over sisters and daughters, they resolved to establish the lordship as twenty-four great houses, and so it was done. And it was long ago, in this same town, that they were fixed at twenty-four houses, there in the town of Cumarcaah, which was blessed by the Lord Bishop -- and it became depopulated. There they grew great, there their thrones and seats were gathered together, and each was divided according to his greatness, each of the lords; and each of the nine calpuls took for itself: nine [houses went] to the lords of Cauiquib, nine to the Nihaibab, four to the Ahau Quiche, and two to the Zaquiquib. And they multiplied greatly, and many were those who belonged to each of the lords, and each was the first and the chief of those his vassals. Many were the lineages of each of the lords, and now we shall tell the name of each one by itself, and of each of the great houses.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' text is badly garbled/eroded in several stretches (missionary orthography with damage or scribal compression), notably around "quiꜫaꜫal quitepeual" and the count of houses per calpul near the end; I relied on Ximénez's Spanish there to establish sense (e.g., the numbers nine/nine/four/two for Cauiquib/Nihaibab/Ahau Quiche/Zaquiquib), since the K'iche' numerals in that passage are not fully recoverable from the transcription given. The line "which was blessed by the Lord Bishop" reflects a K'iche' clause ("+ca xtole can oc" / Ximénez "quefue bendeçído por el Señor.obíspo") that is clearly a later interpolation by the colonial-era copyist/annotator rather than part of the original narrative voice, but I translated it as given since it stands in both the K'iche' and Spanish texts as transmitted. I preserved "Chi Ismachi'" and other proper names in their manuscript spelling rather than normalizing to modern K'iche' orthography.

review.issues: Right section, and mostly a genuine, careful rendering that engages the K'iche' with justified recourse to Ximénez where the manuscript is garbled (the 9/9/4/2 house counts, the bishop interpolation — both properly flagged in the translator's note). But three real fidelity problems: (1) Invented toponym "Chi Naipuch": in "chiri cut chinaipuch xquitiquiba vi vaim..." the word "naipuch" is the K'iche' particle 'also/moreover' (used repeatedly elsewhere in this very section, e.g. "xanaipu hun rech ahau quiche"), not a place name; Ximénez has simply "y allí empezaron a establezer las comidas" with no place. The translation fabricates a second settlement name. (2) Agent reversal in the Ilocab passage: "the thought came upon them of killing the lord of the Ilocab" — both the K'iche' ("...cumal ilocab chicamizanic" — by the Ilocab) and Ximénez ("pensaban matar al Rey los de ilocab" — the Ilocab thought to kill the king) make the Ilocab the would-be killers of Cotuha, not the victims; the English inverts it. (3) Dropped detail: K'iche' "vucamac quib" / Ximénez "los siete calpules" (the seven calpuls/divisions they called themselves) is omitted from "they called themselves by the names of their houses." Minor: "There were only two great divisions [at first]" flattens "xaqui caib chinimha ri cachob chi chinamit" (only two of the great houses, of the two divisions), though that clause is confused in the source itself. Errors are localized; the bulk of the section is accurate.
review.resemblance_note: Phrasing tracks Ximénez's Spanish syntax closely (e.g. "the payment for their sin," "for the contentment of their hearts") rather than the diction of Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson; no specific published-English match in word choice or rhythm.

final.translator_note: Corrected three fidelity issues flagged in review. (1) "Chi Naipuch" was a mistranslation: "naipuch" in "chiri cut chinaipuch xquitiquiba vi vaim..." is the K'iche' adverbial particle "also/moreover" (as elsewhere in this section, e.g. "xanaipu hun rech ahau quiche"), not a toponym; Ximénez confirms with plain "y allí empezaron a establezer las comidas," no place name. Now rendered "And there, moreover, they began to establish..." (2) Reversed agency in the Ilocab passage: the K'iche' "...cumal ilocab chicamizanic" and Ximénez "pensaban matar al Rey los de ilocab" both make the Ilocab the would-be killers of Cotuha; corrected from the earlier draft's inversion to "the thought came upon the Ilocab of killing the lord -- it was by the Ilocab that he was to be killed." (3) Restored the dropped detail "vucamac quib" / "los siete calpules" (the seven calpuls) which had been omitted; now included as "they called themselves the seven calpuls, or divisions." I preserved "Chi Ismachi'" and other proper names in their manuscript spelling rather than normalizing to modern K'iche' orthography, and again used Ximénez to establish the numeral counts (9/9/4/2) and the bishop-interpolation clause where the K'iche' transcription is too eroded to parse independently, as flagged before.

title: Founding of Q'umarkaj (Utatlan); the titled offices

paragraphs: These, then, are the names of the lords who stood before the Cavec: the first lord is Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, Ah Tohil, Ah Cucumatz, Nim Chocoh Cavec, Popol Vinac, Chituy Lolmet, Queh Nay, Popol Vinac Pahom Tzalatz, Uchuch Camha. These were the lords before the Cavec, nine lords, each one with his own great house; and now they are named again, each showing his face. And these, then, are the lords before the Nihaib: the first lord is Ahau Ealel, Ahau Ahtzic Vinac, Cale Camha, Nima Camha, Uchuch Camha, Nim Chocoh Nihaib, Ahau Auilix, Yacolatam, Utzam Pop Zaclatol, Nima Lolmet Yeoltux — nine lords before the Nihaib.

And these are the names of the lords before the Ahau Quiche: Ahtzic Vinac, Ahau Lolmet, Ahau Nim Chocoh, Ahau Hacavitz — four lords before the Ahau Quiche, each with his own great house. And there were two lineages besides, the lords of Zaquic: Tzutuhay, and Ealel Zaquic; these two lords together had but a single great house. Thus it was completed: twenty-four lords in all, and twenty-four great houses likewise came to be.

When the glory and the majesty grew great in the Quiche, when the greatness of the children of the Quiche grew glorious and majestic, when the ravine-city was built of lime and mortar, then small nations and great nations came, and the name of the lord stood high. The Quiche was made great, glory and majesty took form, when the house of the god was made, and the houses of the lords as well — yet it was not the lords themselves who built them, nor did they labor at it, nor did they make their own houses or the house of their god; rather, it was for their sake that their children and their vassals gathered together.

Not by deceit and not by theft did the people multiply, but truly it was for the lords, for each one of them, that they increased; and their strength grew great. They were gathered together, and the word of the lords was likewise heeded, all as one. Truly they were beloved, and truly great was the fame of the lords — greatly esteemed and greatly revered, and their name was of great renown — because of the birth of the lords, because of their sons. Thus they became lords of the ravine, lords of the city as well. And it was not little by little, nor by slow degrees, that all the nations came to submit; nor was the ravine-city, the city, won by war — it was because of the wonder-working power of the lords.

So it was that Lord Cucumatz and Lord Cotuha grew great; truly a wonder-working lord was Cucumatz. Seven days he would climb to the sky, and seven days he would go down to Xibalba. Seven days he would turn into a serpent — truly he became a serpent. Seven days more he made himself an eagle, and seven days more a jaguar — truly like an eagle, like a jaguar was his appearance. And seven days more he turned into clotted blood, becoming nothing but stillness, blood alone. Truly he was a wonder-working lord, and there was dread before him because of it, on the part of all the lords. The word of it spread abroad; all the lords, all the nations, heard of the wonder-working nature of that lord.

And this was the beginning of the greatness and glory of the Quiche, when Lord Cucumatz made the signs of his greatness, which remained in the hearts of his grandchildren and his sons. Not for nothing was this done, that there should be a wonder-working lord — it was so that all the nations might be brought to submission; it was a showing of himself, for he alone was to be the head of the nations. This was the fourth lord, the wonder-working one, Lord Cucumatz by name, who was also Ahpop, Ahpop Camha. And the signs of his true nature remained; his line grew great and grew strong, and then they had sons. And these too did many things: Tepepul and Iztayul were begotten, the fifth lord, and he too held lordship; and thus, one after another, the lords had sons.

Now these are the names of the sixth lord: there were two great lords, Quicab by name, and Cauizimah the name of the other. These two, Quicab and Cauizimah, did many great things; truly they made the Quiche great once more, because of the true wonder-working power that was theirs. It was they who divided and apportioned the towns, the small nations and the great nations alike, setting them close together where towns had stood of old: the mountain lands of the Cakchiquel, now called Chuvila; the mountain of the Rabinaleb; that of Pamaca; the mountain where the people of Caoqueb dwelt; and Zacabaha, and their town of Zaculeu, above Miquina and Xelahuh, at Chuvatzac and Tzolohche.

These grew hostile and made war; and truly the ravine-towns of the Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, and the people of Zaculeu were broken and destroyed. They fell, all the nations were overcome, and the warriors of Quicab pressed on, company after company, until no nation any longer withheld its tribute. They brought their tribute before Quicab and Cauizimah; they entered into servitude, they were made to weep, they were made to cry out. There was no longer any respite for them, no continuance of their line — the towns were laid utterly waste, the earth was gouged as when lightning splits and shatters a stone in terror, swiftly, before the eyes of all, as a sign to the nation. And to this day there stands a single mountain of stone, cracked open, that can no longer be rejoined, as though it had been struck from the sky; for there, at the place called Patacah Petatayub, it lies to this day, visible to all who pass, as a sign of the might of Quicab. He was not killed, for there was none who could overcome him — truly a valiant man was he — and he took tribute from every nation. Then all the lords took counsel together, and resolved to wall the ravine-town, the city, now that all the nations had come to submit.

translation.translator_note: Several passages here are dense and admit more than one parsing; I favored the sense best supported by both the K'iche' syntax and Ximénez's own gloss. Notably: (1) "xchunaxic ta xzahcabix" I read as "it was limed/mortared" (masonry construction of Q'umarkaj), matching Ximénez's "de cal y canto se fabricó el pueblo." (2) The list of subject peoples/places (Cakchiquel, Rabinaleb, Zaculeu, Pamaca, Caoqueb, Zacabaha, Miquina, Xelahuh, Chuvatzac, Tzolohche) follows Ximénez's fuller Spanish list closely, since the K'iche' place-name string is compressed and some names (e.g. Chuvila for the Cakchiquel area) are clearer from his gloss than from the K'iche' alone. paragraphs: These, then, are the names of the lords who stood before the Cavec: the first lord is Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, Ah Tohil, Ah Cucumatz, Nim Chocoh Cavec, Popol Vinac, Chituy Lolmet, Queh Nay, Popol Vinac Pahom Tzalatz, Uchuch Camha. These were the lords before the Cavec, nine lords, each one with his own great house; and now they are named again, each showing his face. And these, then, are the lords before the Nihaib: the first lord is Ahau Ealel, Ahau Ahtzic Vinac, Cale Camha, Nima Camha, Uchuch Camha, Nim Chocoh Nihaib, Ahau Auilix, Yacolatam, Utzam Pop Zaclatol, Nima Lolmet Yeoltux — nine lords before the Nihaib.

And these are the names of the lords before the Ahau Quiche: Ahtzic Vinac, Ahau Lolmet, Ahau Nim Chocoh, Ahau Hacavitz — four lords before the Ahau Quiche, each with his own great house. And there were two lineages besides, the lords of Zaquic: Tzutuhay, and Ealel Zaquic; these two lords together had but a single great house. Thus it was completed: twenty-four lords in all, and twenty-four great houses likewise came to be.

When the glory and the majesty grew great in the Quiche, when the greatness of the children of the Quiche grew glorious and majestic, when the ravine-city was built of lime and mortar, then small nations and great nations came, and the name of the lord stood high. The Quiche was made great, glory and majesty took form, when the house of the god was made, and the houses of the lords as well — yet it was not the lords themselves who built them, nor did they labor at it, nor did they make their own houses or the house of their god; rather, it was for their sake that their children and their vassals gathered together.

Not by deceit and not by theft did the people multiply, but truly it was for the lords, for each one of them, that they increased; and their strength grew great. They were gathered together, and the word of the lords was likewise heeded, all as one. Truly they were beloved, and truly great was the fame of the lords — greatly esteemed and greatly revered, and their name was of great renown — because of the birth of the lords, because of their sons. Thus they became lords of the ravine, lords of the city as well. And it was not little by little, nor by slow degrees, that all the nations came to submit; nor was the ravine-city, the city, won by war — it was because of the wonder-working power of the lords.

So it was that Lord Cucumatz and Lord Cotuha grew great; truly a wonder-working lord was Cucumatz. Seven days he would climb to the sky, and seven days he would go down to Xibalba. Seven days he would turn into a serpent — truly he became a serpent. Seven days more he made himself an eagle, and seven days more a jaguar — truly like an eagle, like a jaguar was his appearance. And seven days more he turned into clotted blood, becoming nothing but stillness, blood alone. Truly he was a wonder-working lord, and there was dread before him because of it, on the part of all the lords. The word of it spread abroad; all the lords, all the nations, heard of the wonder-working nature of that lord.

And this was the beginning of the greatness and glory of the Quiche, when Lord Cucumatz made the signs of his greatness, which remained in the hearts of his grandchildren and his sons. Not for nothing was this done, that there should be a wonder-working lord — it was so that all the nations might be brought to submission; it was a showing of himself, for he alone was to be the head of the nations. This was the fourth lord, the wonder-working one, Lord Cucumatz by name, who was also Ahpop, Ahpop Camha. And the signs of his true nature remained; his line grew great and grew strong, and then they had sons. And these too did many things: Tepepul and Iztayul were begotten, the fifth lord, and he too held lordship; and thus, one after another, the lords had sons.

Now these are the names of the sixth lord: there were two great lords, Quicab by name, and Cauizimah the name of the other. These two, Quicab and Cauizimah, did many great things; truly they made the Quiche great once more, because of the true wonder-working power that was theirs. It was they who divided and apportioned the towns, the small nations and the great nations alike, setting them close together where towns had stood of old: the mountain lands of the Cakchiquel, now called Chuvila; the mountain of the Rabinaleb; that of Pamaca; the mountain where the people of Caoqueb dwelt; and Zacabaha, and their town of Zaculeu, above Miquina and Xelahuh, at Chuvatzac and Tzolohche.

These grew hostile and made war; and truly the ravine-towns of the Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, and the people of Zaculeu were broken and destroyed. They fell, all the nations were overcome, and the warriors of Quicab pressed on, company after company, until no nation any longer withheld its tribute. They brought their tribute before Quicab and Cauizimah; they entered into servitude, they were made to weep, they were made to cry out. There was no longer any respite for them, no continuance of their line — the towns were laid utterly waste, the earth was gouged as when lightning splits and shatters a stone in terror, swiftly, before the eyes of all, as a sign to the nation. And to this day there stands a single mountain of stone, cracked open, that can no longer be rejoined, as though it had been struck from the sky; for there, at the place called Patacah Petatayub, it lies to this day, visible to all who pass, as a sign of the might of Quicab. He was not killed, for there was none who could overcome him — truly a valiant man was he — and he took tribute from every nation. Then all the lords took counsel together, and resolved to wall the ravine-town, the city, now that all the nations had come to submit.

title: Generations and offices of the lordly houses

paragraphs: Then they went out to the frontiers as watchmen, keeping guard for war, and they built the likeness of settlements upon the hills — in case the people should ever have to come back again to their own town, their own nation, they said, when all the lords took counsel. They went out to set these in place, that they might be as a wall and a defense: "This shall be our stronghold and our defense," said all the lords. And then they went out and set each of the chinamit — the clan-holdings — as defenders against the enemy.

Then they were instructed, when they went to place them in the parts of their mountain-land that belonged to them: "Do not be afraid. If the enemy comes against you again, wanting to kill you, come quickly and tell us, and we will go and kill them," Quicab said to them — to the warriors and the captains. Then all the men of war went out, the archers and the bowmen, and then the fathers and grandfathers of the Quiché scattered out, those who are on each of the hills. They went to be guards of the mountains, of the bows and arrows, watchmen for war. And none of them was a stranger, none had a different idol; they were simply the wall and the defense of the town.

Then all of them went out: those of Chuila, of Chulimal, of Zaquiha, Sahbaquiech, of Chitemah — eighteen companies — together with those of Cabracan, Chabicac, Chi Hunahpu, together with the people of Ah Maca, Ahxayabah, Zac Cabaha, and Ahziyaha, and those of Ahmiquina, of Ah Xelahuh — the hill-dwellers — went out to watch over the war and guard the land. Then Quicab and Cauizimah sent them out.

Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, and Ealel Ahtzic Vinac — these four lords were sent out, and they kept watch over the war: Quicab and Cauizimah, who were called lord over the Cauiquib; and two others — one named Quema, lord over the Nihaib, and Achac Iboy, lord over Ahau Quiché. These were the names of the lords who were sent out and who took up service. Then their sons and their vassals went out to the hills, each to his own hill; first they went, then they returned, then they carried captives, before Quicab and Cauizimah, the principal men and the Ahtzic Vinac. They waged war for the sake of their sons and grandsons; they returned, they brought captives, they were made great, they were exalted — such is what they did, seizing and bringing back captives. And their hearts were comforted by the lords, when they came in bearing what they had seized and what they had captured.

Then all the lords took counsel together — Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, the principal men, the Ahtzic Vinac — and when their counsel was gathered, they seized upon a plan: that a first place, a chief place should be made for them, that they should be raised up, that the town, the settlements should be established — this was the office they should hold, whether Ahpop or Ahpop Camha; whoever held the highest place should be lord, should be exalted. All the lords resolved this. And it was likewise done by Tamub and Ilocab; the three branches of the Quiché came together and made their agreement, and set forth their sons and grandsons in the same way, and the naming of the offices was likewise done. There it was that the Quiché took hold — the hill, wherever it was, is the name where the sons and grandsons first took hold.

And they were named, all of them, in each of the hills; there they gathered as one. Xebalax, Xecamac was the name of the hill where they were named, and there they took up their office, there in Chulimal it was done. Now this is their gathering, their taking hold, and their being named: twenty principal men, one for each office; Ahpop was named by Ahpop, by Ahpop Camha, and by the Ealel Ahtzic Vinac; all became principal men — Ealel Ahpop, Eleven Great Chocoh, Ealel Ahau, Ealel Zaquic, U Ealel Achih, Rahpop Achih, Rahtzalam Achih, Utzam Achih — these were their names when they were named. And they were seated, they took their place upon their seat, upon their bench — they, the first sons and grandsons of the people, watchmen and keepers of the fire, of the bows and arrows — closing, walling, forming a rampart behind the Quiché. And it was likewise done by Tamub and Ilocab: they too seized upon it and set the naming of their first sons and grandsons in each of their hills. This, then, is the origin of the office of Ahpop, the office set in place in each of the hills, even to this day. So it came to pass, their coming forth after Ahpop, after Ahpop Camha, after the principal men, after the Ahtzic Vinac.

Now again we shall tell of the name of the house of the god — for the house too was given the name of the god itself. "Great Edifice" was the name of the house of Tohil, of the people of Cauiquib. Avilix was the name of the edifice, the house of Avilix, of the people of Nihaibab. Hacavitz, too, was the name of the edifice, the house of the god of the people of Ahau Quiché. Tzutuha, at Cahbaha, was the name of another. "Great Edifice" — such was the stone; it was worshipped by the lords of Quiché, and it was worshipped as well by all the nations, before they had yet conquered any nation, before Tohil. Then afterward Ahpop and Ahpop Camha were worshipped in turn, and then people came to give their gifts, their tribute, their service, before the lord.

This lord in turn was their support and their strength; Ahpop and Ahpop Camha caused their town to increase — they were truly great lords, men of nagual-power. A nagual lord was Cucumatz, and Cotuha; a nagual lord was Cucumatz, and Cotuha; a nagual lord too was Quicab, and Cauizimah. They knew whether war was to be made — it was made plain before them, they saw it, whether it was death, whether it was famine, whether it was strife that was to come — they simply knew it, for there was a means of it: there was a book, "Popol Vuh" was its name, by which they knew.

Not simply so were the lords great in their being; great too was their fasting. This was the price of the edifice and the price of the lordship: through it, long ago, they fasted, and they cast themselves down before their god. Now this was their manner of fasting: nine men would fast, and nine would cast themselves down in worship; or thirteen men would be the fasting-group, and thirteen likewise would cast themselves down in worship before Tohil, before their god — only zapotes, only matasanos, only jocotes was what they ate; there was nothing else that they took as food. And if fourteen men were casting themselves down, fourteen also were fasting; they did not eat their maize-bread. Truly great was the solemnity they observed — this was the sign of the being of the lords. And with them there was no woman lying down; only by themselves, alone, keeping themselves apart, they fasted, staying only in the house of the god a whole day — only worship, only reverence, only bowing down was what they did. And there where they stayed they kept watch until it grew light — only their heart, only their belly was in it, as they made their petition for the light, for the life of their sons and their grandsons, and likewise for the lordship. They lifted up their faces to the sky — this, then, was their petition before their god, as they made their prayer; this, then, was the weeping of their heart.

translation.translator_note: This passage is one of the few places in the manuscript where the text names itself: "qo cut ibal re qo vvh popol vvh vbi" — "there was a means of it: there was a book, 'Popol Vuh' was its name" — which Ximénez glosses as "libro del comun" ("book of the council/community"), rendered here simply as the transliterated title itself. A number of place-names and ethnonyms in the roll-call passage (ah maca, ahxayabah, ahmiquina, ah xelahuh, etc.) are opaque without Ximénez's Spanish gloss, which identifies some of them with colonial-period town names (e.g. Zacualpa, Tutuncapán/Totonicapán, Quezaltenango); I have kept the K'iche' forms rather than substituting the Spanish town names, since the K'iche' does not itself make that identification explicit. The word rendered "copal" / "burning copal" in some published treatments of this passage is supplied only by the Spanish ("quemaban copal"); the K'iche' verbs here (cahbic, catonic) more literally mean "prostrating themselves, bowing down / doing reverence," so I have rendered them that way rather than importing the specific ritual detail of copal-burning, which the K'iche' text itself does not state at this point. The list of titles (Ealel Ahau, Ealel Zaquic, etc.) is transliterated rather than translated, as their exact semantic content is uncertain from context alone.

review.issues: Right section; overall faithful and visibly worked from the K'iche' rather than Ximénez (keeps K'iche' toponyms where Ximénez glosses colonial towns; follows "hu ta quih" = "a whole day" and "xquec zaquiric" = "until it grew light" against the Spanish). Three local errors: (1) Fasting numbers: K'iche' "vve cut vclahuh vinac quecahbic vvelahuh cut quemeuahic" — vuclahuh = seventeen; the translation's "fourteen ... fourteen" matches neither the K'iche' (17) nor Ximénez ("díeçysíete ... o díez"). (2) "ilol rech taol rech" is "watchers and hearers of it" (Ximénez: "que los mírasen, que los oyesen"); the translation's "watchmen and keepers of the fire" invents "fire" — taol is "hearer," not anything fiery. (3) The translator's note claims "quecatonic" means only "doing reverence," but katon- is specifically "to burn (offerings/incense)"; collapsing "quecahbic quecatonic" into "cast themselves down in worship" loses the incense-burning that the K'iche' itself states (Ximénez's "quemaban copal" only supplies the word copal, not the burning). Also minor: "e cahib chi ahauab" is glossed correctly as four lords but the list preceding it ("Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, and Ealel Ahtzic Vinac") reads as three names; this ambiguity is in the source, acceptable. None of these amount to wrong-section or wholesale drift.
review.resemblance_note: Phrasing (e.g. "the likeness of settlements upon the hills," "men of nagual-power," "only their heart, only their belly was in it") does not match the diction or rhythm of Recinos/Goetz-Morley, Tedlock, or Christenson; it reads as freshly composed from the K'iche' with Ximénez as aid.

paragraphs: Then they went out to the frontiers as watchmen, keeping guard for war, and they built the likeness of settlements upon the hills — in case the people should ever have to come back again to their own town, their own nation, they said, when all the lords took counsel. They went out to set these in place, that they might be as a wall and a defense: "This shall be our stronghold and our defense," said all the lords. And then they went out and set each of the chinamit — the clan-holdings — as defenders against the enemy.

Then they were instructed, when they went to place them in the parts of their mountain-land that belonged to them: "Do not be afraid. If the enemy comes against you again, wanting to kill you, come quickly and tell us, and we will go and kill them," Quicab said to them — to the warriors and the captains. Then all the men of war went out, the archers and the bowmen, and then the fathers and grandfathers of the Quiché scattered out, those who are on each of the hills. They went to be guards of the mountains, of the bows and arrows, watchmen for war. And none of them was a stranger, none had a different idol; they were simply the wall and the defense of the town.

Then all of them went out: those of Chuila, of Chulimal, of Zaquiha, Sahbaquiech, of Chitemah — eighteen companies — together with those of Cabracan, Chabicac, Chi Hunahpu, together with the people of Ah Maca, Ahxayabah, Zac Cabaha, and Ahziyaha, and those of Ahmiquina, of Ah Xelahuh — the hill-dwellers — went out to watch over the war and guard the land. Then Quicab and Cauizimah sent them out.

Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, and Ealel Ahtzic Vinac — these four lords were sent out, and they kept watch over the war: Quicab and Cauizimah, who were called lord over the Cauiquib; and two others — one named Quema, lord over the Nihaib, and Achac Iboy, lord over Ahau Quiché. These were the names of the lords who were sent out and who took up service. Then their sons and their vassals went out to the hills, each to his own hill; first they went, then they returned, then they carried captives, before Quicab and Cauizimah, the principal men and the Ahtzic Vinac. They waged war for the sake of their sons and grandsons; they returned, they brought captives, they were made great, they were exalted — such is what they did, seizing and bringing back captives. And their hearts were comforted by the lords, when they came in bearing what they had seized and what they had captured.

Then all the lords took counsel together — Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, the principal men, the Ahtzic Vinac — and when their counsel was gathered, they seized upon a plan: that a first place, a chief place should be made for them, that they should be raised up, that the town, the settlements should be established — this was the office they should hold, whether Ahpop or Ahpop Camha; whoever held the highest place should be lord, should be exalted. All the lords resolved this. And it was likewise done by Tamub and Ilocab; the three branches of the Quiché came together and made their agreement, and set forth their sons and grandsons in the same way, and the naming of the offices was likewise done. There it was that the Quiché took hold — the hill, wherever it was, is the name where the sons and grandsons first took hold.

And they were named, all of them, in each of the hills; there they gathered as one. Xebalax, Xecamac was the name of the hill where they were named, and there they took up their office, there in Chulimal it was done. Now this is their gathering, their taking hold, and their being named: twenty principal men, one for each office; Ahpop was named by Ahpop, by Ahpop Camha, and by the Ealel Ahtzic Vinac; all became principal men — Ealel Ahpop, Eleven Great Chocoh, Ealel Ahau, Ealel Zaquic, U Ealel Achih, Rahpop Achih, Rahtzalam Achih, Utzam Achih — these were their names when they were named. And they were seated, they took their place upon their seat, upon their bench — they, the first sons and grandsons of the people, watchmen and keepers of the fire, of the bows and arrows — closing, walling, forming a rampart behind the Quiché. And it was likewise done by Tamub and Ilocab: they too seized upon it and set the naming of their first sons and grandsons in each of their hills. This, then, is the origin of the office of Ahpop, the office set in place in each of the hills, even to this day. So it came to pass, their coming forth after Ahpop, after Ahpop Camha, after the principal men, after the Ahtzic Vinac.

Now again we shall tell of the name of the house of the god — for the house too was given the name of the god itself. "Great Edifice" was the name of the house of Tohil, of the people of Cauiquib. Avilix was the name of the edifice, the house of Avilix, of the people of Nihaibab. Hacavitz, too, was the name of the edifice, the house of the god of the people of Ahau Quiché. Tzutuha, at Cahbaha, was the name of another. "Great Edifice" — such was the stone; it was worshipped by the lords of Quiché, and it was worshipped as well by all the nations, before they had yet conquered any nation, before Tohil. Then afterward Ahpop and Ahpop Camha were worshipped in turn, and then people came to give their gifts, their tribute, their service, before the lord.

This lord in turn was their support and their strength; Ahpop and Ahpop Camha caused their town to increase — they were truly great lords, men of nagual-power. A nagual lord was Cucumatz, and Cotuha; a nagual lord was Cucumatz, and Cotuha; a nagual lord too was Quicab, and Cauizimah. They knew whether war was to be made — it was made plain before them, they saw it, whether it was death, whether it was famine, whether it was strife that was to come — they simply knew it, for there was a means of it: there was a book, "Popol Vuh" was its name, by which they knew.

Not simply so were the lords great in their being; great too was their fasting. This was the price of the edifice and the price of the lordship: through it, long ago, they fasted, and they cast themselves down before their god. Now this was their manner of fasting: nine men would fast, and nine would cast themselves down in worship; or thirteen men would be the fasting-group, and thirteen likewise would cast themselves down in worship before Tohil, before their god — only zapotes, only matasanos, only jocotes was what they ate; there was nothing else that they took as food. And if fourteen men were casting themselves down, fourteen also were fasting; they did not eat their maize-bread. Truly great was the solemnity they observed — this was the sign of the being of the lords. And with them there was no woman lying down; only by themselves, alone, keeping themselves apart, they fasted, staying only in the house of the god a whole day — only worship, only reverence, only bowing down was what they did. And there where they stayed they kept watch until it grew light — only their heart, only their belly was in it, as they made their petition for the light, for the life of their sons and their grandsons, and likewise for the lordship. They lifted up their faces to the sky — this, then, was their petition before their god, as they made their prayer; this, then, was the weeping of their heart.

title: Wars, later kings, and the coming of the Spaniards

paragraphs: "O you, beauty of the day, you Huracan, you Heart of Sky, you Heart of Earth, you who give us our glory and who give us our sons and our daughters, turn, come back this way, your glory: let there be life, let my sons and my daughters be raised, let them multiply, let them grow, those who feed you and sustain you, those who call upon you on the road, at the rivers, in the ravines, beneath the trees, beneath the vines — give them their sons and their daughters. Let no evil come, let there be no accident, let them not be deceived, let them not stumble, let them not be split apart, let them not be burned, let them not be wounded, let them not go astray on the road, on the path. Let there be no ambush before them, before their faces. Set them on a straight road, a clear road. Let no evil, no accident befall their persons, before your face, you Heart of Sky, you Heart of Earth, you Bundle of Glory, you Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, womb of sky, womb of earth, four corners, four sides. Let there be only peace, only quiet before your face, you the god." So spoke the lords when they fasted, those nine men, thirteen men, seventeen men, and they fasted, weeping their hearts out over all their sons and over all their wives and daughters as well, each of the lords doing his service. This was the price of the light, the price of the dawning, the price too of the lordship — the rule of the ahpop, the ahpop camha, the lords, the keepers of the mat — and in pairs they went, taking turns, to weep over it, in company with all the people of the Quiché, and only in this way did the root and stem of their descent, the root and stem of the fasting and the weeping, come to be. And so likewise did the Tamub and the Ilocab, together with the Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, the Ah-Kikinaha, the Tuhalaha, and the Uchabaha; only one was their root, when they listened there, in the Quiché, when it was done, for the sake of everyone; not simply then did they become lords, not simply did the fasting and the weeping content them, they only sat and watched what would be given to them. And truly they did not steal it away, nor did they seize the lordship, its greatness, its power for themselves; nor did they simply overturn the ravines and the towns of the small tribes and the great tribes, but a great price was given: jade was brought, metal was brought, quetzal feathers were brought, cotinga feathers, the tribute of all the peoples was brought, it came before the face of the sorcerer-lords Cucumatz and Cotuha, and before Quicab and Cavizimah as well. Not small was what they did, and not few were the tribes they conquered; many divisions of tribes came to pay tribute to the Quiché, and their deaths were greatly felt. Not simply did their greatness and their glory come to be — this Cucumatz was the beginning of the greatness of the lordship; thus began the growth and the greatness of the Quiché.

Now we shall name the generations of the lords together with all their names, we shall tell it again. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship of all the descendants of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, our first grandfathers, our first fathers, at the time when the sun appeared, and the moon, and the stars. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship; here we shall set down the entering of the lords into office, as they entered, as they died, one after another, each one of the lords. This, then, shall be told of each and every one of the lords of the Quiché. Balam Quitze was the root of the house of the Cavek; his second was Cocavib; the third generation of Balam Quitze was Balam Conache; the fourth, of the sorcerer, was Cotuha, Ztayub; Cucumatz and Cotuha were the sorcerers, the fifth generation, this was where Tepepul and Ztayub came to be; the sixth was Quicab and Cavizimah; the seventh was Tepepul and Ztayub, another sorcerer; the eighth was Tecum and Tepepul; the ninth was Vahxaqui-Caam and Quicab; the tenth generation of lords was Vucub Noh and Cauatepech; the eleventh generation of lords was Oxib Queh and Beleheb Tzi; the twelfth generation of lords. And these were the ones who ruled when Alvarado — Donadiu, as the Castilian people called him — came; Tecum and Tepepul were made to pay tribute to the Castilian people; these were the sons that were begotten, the thirteenth generation of lords: Don de Rojas and Don Juan de Cortes were the fourteenth generation of lords, the sons begotten of Tecum and Tepepul. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship of the ahau ahpop and the ahpop camha before the face of the Cavek Quiché; this shall now be told again for the sake of the lineage house.

This, then, is the great house of each and every lord: after the ahpop and the ahpop camha, these are the names of the nine chinamit, the nine great houses of the Cavek; these are the names of the lords, each ruler of a great house. The lord ahpop, one great house, whose house was called Cuha; the lord ahpop camha, one great house, called Tziquinaha; Nim Choco Cavec, one great house; the lord ah-Tohil, one great house; the lord ah-Cucumatz, one great house; Popol Vinac Chituy, one great house; Lolmet Quehnay, one great house; Popol Vinac Pahom Tzalatz Xcuxeba, one great house; Tepeu Yaqui, one great house.

translation.translator_note: The K'iche' of this section is badly garbled in places (run-together words, likely scribal errors), especially in the genealogical king-list, so I leaned more heavily on Ximénez's Spanish gloss here than elsewhere to establish the sequence of names and generations — the Spanish numbers the generations explicitly ("segunda generación," "tercera generación," etc.) where the K'iche' text simply strings the name-pairs together with "vcable," "vroxle," etc. (ordinal prefixes), so I followed that ordinal structure. One clear divergence: where the K'iche' seems to say "que a yatah paraxa be, paraxa hoc" (roughly "let it not be given on the side of the road, on the side of the path") the Spanish softens this to a general blessing ("ponedlos en buen camino, y hermoso"); I kept the more literal "no ambush before them" / "straight road" sense closer to the K'iche'. The proper names (Cuha, Tziquinaha, Nim Choco Cavec, Popol Vinac Chituy, Lolmet Quehnay, Tepeu Yaqui, etc.) are left untranslated as titles/place-names, per both texts. The reference to "Donadiu" for Alvarado and the Spanish sons "Don de Rojas" and "Don Juan de Cortes" is preserved as in the source, marking the point where the narrative reaches the Spanish conquest.

review.issues: Right section, and mostly a genuine rendering of the K'iche', with justified use of Ximénez's Spanish for the garbled king-list ordinals. One clear fidelity error: K'iche' "xehiꜩaxic rumal castillan vinac" (xe-jitz'-axik, plural passive "they were hanged") — confirmed by Ximénez's "fueron ahorcados por los españoles. Tecum, tepepul" — is misread as a naming formula ("Donadiu, as the Castilian people called him"), silently deleting the hanging of Tecum and Tepepul by the Spaniards, a historically important statement present in both source columns. Lesser drifts: "their deaths were greatly felt" follows the Spanish where the K'iche' "caxcol cut xcamvi" is closer to "in suffering they died"; some clauses of the prayer's prohibition list (Spanish "no forniquen, y sean juzgados en tribunal") are not represented.

paragraphs: "O you, beauty of the day, you Huracan, you Heart of Sky, you Heart of Earth, you who give us our glory and who give us our sons and our daughters, turn, come back this way, your glory: let there be life, let my sons and my daughters be raised, let them multiply, let them grow, those who feed you and sustain you, those who call upon you on the road, at the rivers, in the ravines, beneath the trees, beneath the vines — give them their sons and their daughters. Let no evil come, let there be no accident, let them not be deceived, let them not stumble, let them not fornicate, let them not be judged before any tribunal, let them not be burned, let them not be wounded, let them not go astray at the high or the low side of the road. Let there be no blow before their faces. Set them on a good road, a fair road. Let no misfortune, no accident befall their persons, before your face, you Heart of Sky, you Heart of Earth, you Bundle of Glory, you Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, womb of sky, womb of earth, four corners. Let there be only peace before your face, you the god." So spoke the lords when they fasted, those nine, thirteen, and seventeen men, and they fasted, weeping their hearts out day by day over their sons and over all their wives and daughters as well, each of the lords doing his service. This was the price of the light, the price of life, the price too of the lordship — the rule of the ahpop, the ahpop camha, the lords, the keepers of the mat — and two by two they went, taking turns, to carry it, together with all the people of the Quiché, and only in this way did the root and stem of their descent, the root and stem of the fed and the sustained, come to be. And so likewise did the Tamub and the Ilocab, together with the Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, the Ah-Kikinaha, the Tuhalaha, and the Uchabaha; only one was their custom, when they listened there, in the Quiché, when it was done, for the sake of everyone; not simply then did they become lords, nor did they envy the gifts, the fasting, that contented them; they only sat and watched what would be given to them. And truly they did not steal it away, nor did they seize the lordship, its greatness, its power for themselves; nor did they simply overturn the ravines and the towns of the small tribes and the great tribes, but a great price was given: jade was brought, metal was brought, quetzal feathers were brought, cotinga feathers, the tribute of all the peoples was brought, it came before the face of the sorcerer-lords Cucumatz and Cotuha, and before Quicab and Cavizimah as well. Not small was what they did, and not few were the tribes they conquered; many divisions of tribes came to pay tribute to the Quiché, and in suffering they died. Not simply did their greatness come to be — this Cucumatz was the beginning of the greatness of the lordship; thus began the growth and the greatness of the Quiché.

Now we shall name the generations of the lords together with all their names, we shall tell it again. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship of all the descendants of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, our first grandfathers, our first fathers, at the time when the sun appeared, and the moon, and the stars. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship; here we shall set down the entering of the lords into office, as they entered, as they died, one after another, each one of the lords. This, then, shall be told of each and every one of the lords of the Quiché. Balam Quitze was the root of the house of the Cavek; his second was Cocavib; the third generation of Balam Quitze was Balam Conache; the fourth was Cotuha, Ztayub; Cucumatz and Cotuha were the sorcerers, the fifth generation, this was where Tepepul and Ztayub came to be; the sixth was Quicab and Cavizimah; the seventh was Tepepul and Ztayub, another sorcerer; the eighth was Tecum and Tepepul; the ninth was Vahxaqui-Caam and Quicab; the tenth generation of lords was Vucub Noh and Cauatepech; the eleventh generation of lords was Oxib Queh and Beleheb Tzi; the twelfth generation of lords. And these were the ones who ruled when Alvarado — Donadiu, as the Castilian people called him — came, and Tecum and Tepepul were hanged by the Castilian people; they had rendered tribute before the Castilian people; these were the sons that were begotten, the thirteenth generation of lords: Don de Rojas and Don Juan de Cortes were the fourteenth generation of lords, the sons begotten of Tecum and Tepepul. This, then, is the ending, the completion of the lordship of the ahau ahpop and the ahpop camha before the face of the Cavek Quiché; this shall now be told again for the sake of the lineage house.

This, then, is the great house of each and every lord: after the ahpop and the ahpop camha, these are the names of the nine chinamit, the nine great houses of the Cavek; these are the names of the lords, each ruler of a great house. The lord ahpop, one great house, whose house was called Cuha; the lord ahpop camha, one great house, called Tziquinaha; Nim Choco Cavec, one great house; the lord ah-Tohil, one great house; the lord ah-Cucumatz, one great house; Popol Vinac Chituy, one great house; Lolmet Quehnay, one great house; Popol Vinac Pahom Tzalatz Xcuxeba, one great house; Tepeu Yaqui, one great house.

final.translator_note: Corrected the section's central fidelity error flagged in review: the K'iche' clause "xehiꜩaxic rumal castillan vinac Tecum tepepul" is the plural passive of hitz'- ("to hang"), confirmed by Ximénez's own gloss "fueron ahorcados por los españoles. Restored the prayer's prohibition clauses present in both columns but dropped before ("no forniquen, y sean juzgados en tribunal alguno" / K'iche' — fornication and judgment before a tribunal) and softened the geographic idiom "no caígan en el lado alto, ó baxo de el camino" (K'iche' "que a yatah paraxa be, paraxa hoc") to "let them not go astray at the high or the low side of the road," closer to both texts than my earlier looser "ambush" reading. title: The last rulers under Spanish rule; Ximenez's closing colophon

paragraphs: These, now, are the nine lineages of Cavec: multiplied are their descendants and their children, counted after the nine great houses. Now as for the Nihaib, nine also are their houses. First we shall tell the account of their lordship, from a single root, which began before the face of the sun and before the face of light, when they were still nawal beings: Balam Acab, the first grandfather, our father.

Coacul Coacutac was his son, the second generation; Cochahuh Cotzibaha, the third; Beleheb Quih, the fourth; then Cotuha, the fifth; the lord Batza then, the sixth generation; then Ztayul, the seventh; then the lord Cotuha, the eighth generation of the lordship; Beleheb Quih, the ninth; likewise Quema, the tenth; and the lord Ahau Cotuha, the eleventh.
Don Cristóbal, so he was called, was the one who ruled in the sight of the Castilian people, the Spaniards. Don Pedro de Robles is the lord Ahau Galel now.

These, now, are all the lords who descended from that lord Ahau Galel; now we shall tell the lord of each great house. Ahau Galel, first lord before the Nihaib, one great house. Ahau Ah Tzic Vinac, one great house. Ahau Galel Camha, one great house. Nima Camha, one great house. Vchuch Camha, one great house. Nima Camha, one great house. Nim Chocoh Nihaib, one great house. Ahau Auilix, one great house. Yacolatam, one great house. These, then, are the great houses before the Nihaib; this is what is called the nine lineages of the Nihaib. And many were the lesser lineages belonging to each of these lords, the first ones whose names have already been told.

This, now, is that of the lord Ahau Quiché: here is their grandfather and father, Mahucutah, the first man. Coahau is the name of the second; then the lord Caelacan, Cocozom, Comahcun, Vucubah, Cocamel, Coyabacoh, Vinac Bam. These, then, are the lords before Ahau Quiché, their descent and their generations; and these are the names of the lords within the great houses — only four great houses.

Ah Tzic Vinac is the name of the first lord, one great house. Lolmet Ahau, the second lord, one great house. Nim Chocoh Ahau, the third lord, one great house. And Hacavitz, the fourth lord, one great house — thus four great houses before Ahau Quiché. These, now, are the three great chocoh, who were as it were the fathers over all the lords of the Quiché; as one they joined themselves together, these three chocoh. They were the begetters, the mothers of the word and the fathers of the word; great was the weight of their being, these three chocoh. Nim Chocoh before the Nihaib is the second; Nim Chocoh Ahau before Ahau Quiché is the third — three, then, were these chocoh, one before each lineage.
This, then, is all that remains of the Quiché, for there is nothing more to be seen of it; what the lords possessed of old has now been lost.
This, then, is where all that concerns the Quiché comes to its end — the place now called Santa Cruz.

The closing line naming "Santa Cruz" is the K'iche' text's own colophon (Santa Cruz del Quiché, the colonial-era town), not a separate note added by Ximénez himself — the section title's reference to a "colophon" applies to this closing statement within the K'iche' narration.

The closing line naming "Santa Cruz" is the K'iche' text's own colophon (Santa Cruz del Quiché, the colonial-era town), not a separate note added by Ximénez himself — the section title's reference to a "colophon" applies to this closing statement within the K'iche' narration.
